## VITTORIA COLONNA, ILLUSTRIOUS
### MARCHIONESS OF
### PESCARA, FROM ANDREA
### OF ASOLA. <note>Andrea Torresano of Asola (1451–1529) was a prominent Venetian printer and the father-in-law of Aldus Manutius. After Aldus's death in 1515, Andrea took over the management of the Aldine Press.</note>

Having recently reprinted, most Illustrious <term>Lady</term><note>original: "Madonna." Here used as a formal title of respect for a noblewoman.</note>, the divine poet Dante—who is inferior to none of the other writers, whether ancient or modern (if one looks with a discerning eye at the height and grandeur of his verse, and at the many and varied sciences contained within it)—it did not seem right to me to release it under any name more distinguished than that of <term>Your Ladyship</term><note>original: "V. S." (Vostra Signoria), a formal honorific.</note>.

And in this, not only has my long-standing service toward your most Noble house spurred me on; but even more so the living fame of your immortal and divine beauties: which from day to day grow along with your youthful age, surpassing themselves so much that it is truly believed, and the world speaks of it, that neither in this age of ours nor in any other has a more beautiful or more accomplished woman been seen. 

And although this [physical beauty] is infinite, the beauties of the soul are in no way less than those of the body; indeed, they far surpass them: because those physical traits possess nothing that is not natural, while these spiritual traits hold art no less than nature united within them. # HELL

<meta>catchword "a 2" at bottom right; faint ink bleed-through from reverse page</meta>

In the middle of the journey of our life
I found myself within a dark wood; <note>original: "selua oscura". This famous setting represents a state of spiritual error and moral confusion. The "journey of our life" refers to the age of 35, the midpoint of the biblical three-score and ten years.</note>
For the straight path was lost:
And how hard a thing it is to say what it was like,
This wood, wild and rugged and harsh;
Which, in thought, renews the fear.
So bitter is it, that death is little more so.
But to treat of the good that I found there;
I will tell of the other things that I perceived.
I cannot rightly retell how I entered there;
So full of sleep was I at that moment,
That I abandoned the true way.
But after I had reached the foot of a hill,
There, where that valley ended,
Which had pierced my heart with fear;
I looked up; and I saw its shoulders
Clothed already in the rays of the planet <note>original: "pianeta". In the medieval Ptolemaic system, the Sun was classified as a planet. Its light here symbolizes divine grace or reason.</note>
That leads others straight along every path.
Then the fear was a little quieted,
Which in the lake of my heart <note>original: "lago del cor". A medieval anatomical concept where the heart was thought to have a reservoir for blood; here, it symbolizes the deep interior space where his terror pooled.</note> had endured
Through the night that I passed with such anguish.
And like one who, with gasping breath,
Having come out of the deep sea to the shore,
Turns to the dangerous water and gazes;
So my spirit, which was still fleeing,
Turned back to look again upon the pass
That never let any living person leave.
After I had rested my tired body a little;
I resumed the way across the deserted slope,
So that the firm foot was always the lower. <note>original: "pie fermo". Dante describes the mechanics of climbing: the "firm" or weight-bearing foot remains lower than the one stepping up. Some scholars interpret this "firm foot" as representing the soul's lower, earth-bound appetites.</note>

**Vocabulary:** Dante Alighieri, Hell, <term>dark wood</term> (a landscape of sin), <term>journey of our life</term> (the human lifespan), hill, planet.

And behold, almost at the beginning of the steep slope,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;A leopard, <note>original: "lonza". While often translated as leopard, it likely refers to a generic spotted feline. In Dante's allegory, this beast is widely interpreted as representing the sin of Lust or Fraud.</note> light and very swift,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which was covered with a spotted coat.
And it did not move from before my face:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Rather, it so hindered my path,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That I turned many times to go back.
It was the time of the beginning of the morning:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And the sun was rising with those stars
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That were with him when divine love <note>original: "amor diuino". Dante refers to the Christian belief that the universe was created in the spring, with the sun in the constellation of Aries.</note>
First moved those beautiful things;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So that the hour of the day and the sweet season
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Gave me cause for good hope
Against that wild beast with the gaily-marked skin:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But not so much that I did not feel fear
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;At the sight of a lion <note>symbolizing the sin of Pride, appearing with "head held high."</note> that appeared to me.
This one seemed to be coming against me
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;With head held high, and with ravenous hunger,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So that it seemed the air trembled at him:
And a she-wolf; <note>original: "lupa". The most dangerous of the three beasts, representing Avarice (Greed). This was a particularly sharp political and moral critique in Dante's time, as he saw greed as the root of Italy's corruption.</note> who appeared laden
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;With all cravings in her leanness;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And who has already made many people live in misery.
She brought such heaviness upon me
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;With the terror that came from the sight of her,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That I lost the hope of reaching the height.
And like one who eagerly gains,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And the time arrives that makes him lose,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Who in all his thoughts weeps and is saddened;
Such did that restless beast make me,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which, coming against me little by little,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Was pushing me back to where the sun is silent. <note>original: "doue'l sol tace". A famous example of synesthesia, where the lack of light is described as the absence of sound, signifying the deep, dark abyss where divine grace does not reach.</note>

<summary>Dante encounters three symbolic beasts—a leopard, a lion, and a she-wolf—which represent different categories of sin and prevent him from climbing the sunlit mountain of salvation. Terrified, he is driven back toward the darkness of the valley.</summary>

**W**hile I was rushing down to a lower place,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Before my eyes, one offered himself to me,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Who through long silence seemed faint. <note>original: "fioco". This can mean "faint" to the sight or "hoarse" of voice. It suggests that Virgil—the voice of Reason—has been silent or ignored by Dante for a long time.</note>
**W**hen I saw him in the great desert,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;"Have mercy on me!" <note>original: "Miserere di me". Dante cries out in Latin, the language of the Church and of Virgil himself, using the opening words of Psalm 51.</note> I cried to him,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;"Whatever you may be, whether a shade or a certain man."
**H**e answered me: "Not a man; I was once a man,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And my parents were Lombards,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Mantuans by birth, both of them.
**I** was born under Julius, <note>original: "sub Iulio". Referring to Julius Caesar. Virgil was born in 70 BCE.</note> although it was late;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And I lived in Rome under the good Augustus,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In the time of the false and lying gods.
**P**oet I was; and I sang of that just
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Son of Anchises <note>The hero Aeneas, the protagonist of Virgil's epic poem, the *Aeneid*.</note> who came from Troy,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;After proud Ilium <note>Another name for the city of Troy.</note> was burned.
**B**ut you, why do you return to such distress?
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Why do you not climb the delectable mountain,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which is the beginning and cause of all joy?"
"**A**re you then 그 Virgil, and 그 source
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which spreads so wide a river of speech?"
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I answered him with a bashful brow.
"**O** honor and light of other poets,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;May the long study and the great love avail me,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which has made me search through your volume.
**Y**ou are my master and my author:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;You alone are the one from whom I took
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The beautiful style that has done me honor.
**S**ee the beast <note>Referring to the she-wolf mentioned on the previous page.</note> for which I turned back;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Help me against her, famous sage,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For she makes my veins and my pulses tremble."

### a 4

**A** different path you must pursue,"
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;He answered, after he saw me weeping,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;"If you wish to escape this wild place;
**F**or this beast, for which you cry out, <note>Referring to the She-wolf, who represents the vice of avarice or greed.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Does not let anyone pass along her way,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But so obstructs them that she kills them;
**A**nd she has a nature so wicked and cruel
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That she never sates her greedy will,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And after feeding, she is hungrier than before.
**M**any are the animals she mates with, <note>In this allegory, the "mating" suggests how greed interacts with and corrupts other vices or worldly powers.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And there will be more still, until the Greyhound <note>original: "veltro". This is one of the most famous prophecies in literature. The Greyhound is a future savior—perhaps a political leader or a holy figure—who will drive corruption out of the world.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Comes, who shall make her die in pain.
**H**e shall not feed on land or wealth, <note>original: "peltro". Literally pewter or tin, used here to represent coinage and material riches.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But on wisdom, love, and virtue;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And his birth shall be between Feltro and Feltro. <note>A cryptic geographical clue. It may refer to the towns of Feltre and Montefeltro in Italy, or to the "felt" cloth used in the election of magistrates.</note>
**H**e shall be the salvation of that humble Italy,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For which the virgin Camilla,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Euryalus, Turnus, and Nisus died of their wounds. <note>Dante lists four characters from Virgil's own epic poem, the *Aeneid*, who died during the founding of the Roman civilization in Italy.</note>
**H**e shall hunt her through every city,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Until he has driven her back into Hell,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;From whence envy first released her.
**T**herefore, for your own good, I think and judge
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That you should follow me; and I shall be your guide,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And lead you from here through an eternal place;
**W**here you shall hear the desperate shrieks,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And see the ancient spirits in pain,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Who each cry out for the second death; <note>The "second death" refers to the finality of damnation—the death of the soul—following the first death of the physical body.</note>
**A**nd you shall see those who are content
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Within the fire, because they hope to come,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Whenever it may be, to the blessed people. <note>A reference to the souls in Purgatory. Unlike those in Hell, they suffer with hope because their pain is temporary and leads eventually to Heaven.</note>

### a 4

To those [heights] then, if you wish to ascend,
*A soul more worthy of this than I shall be:* <note>This refers to Beatrice, Dante's deceased beloved and the symbol of Divine Grace, who will take over as his guide for the final part of the journey because Virgil, as a pagan, cannot enter Paradise.</note>
I will leave you with her when I depart;
For that Emperor who reigns on high, <note>Dante frequently refers to God as an "Emperor" and Heaven as His "City."</note>
*Because I was a rebel to his law,* <note>Virgil lived before Christ; therefore, he did not follow the Christian "law" or baptism, which prevents him from entering the presence of God.</note>
Does not want me to enter into his city.
He rules everywhere, and there he reigns;
*There is his city and his high throne:*
O happy is the one whom he elects to be there!
And I to him: "Poet, I entreat you
*By that God whom you did not know,*
So that I may flee this evil and worse, <note>The "evil" of the dark forest of sin, and the "worse" of eternal damnation.</note>
That you lead me there, where you just said,
*So that I may see the gate of Saint Peter,* <note>original: "la porta di san Pietro". This refers to the entrance of Purgatory, guarded by an angel acting on behalf of St. Peter.</note>
And those whom you describe as so sorrowful."
Then he moved on, and I followed behind him.

->C A N T O. II.<-

The day was departing, and the darkening air
*Was taking the creatures that are on earth*
Away from their labors; and I, alone,
Was preparing myself to endure the war,
*Both of the journey and of the pity,* <note>Dante describes the upcoming experience as a "war" because it will be a physical struggle to travel and an emotional struggle to witness the suffering of the damned.</note>
Which my memory, which does not err, shall retrace.
O Muses, O high genius, now help me! <note>Following the tradition of ancient epic poets like Homer and Virgil, Dante calls upon the Muses—the goddesses of inspiration—to help him tell his story.</note>
*O memory, that wrote down what I saw,*
Here your nobility shall be shown.
I began: "Poet, who guides me,
*Look at my strength, if it is powerful enough,*
Before you trust me to the difficult pass.

<meta>This page continues Dante’s dialogue with Virgil at the beginning of Canto II. Having just agreed to follow Virgil through the afterlife, Dante now pauses, overcome by a second thought. He compares himself to Aeneas and Saint Paul, questioning why he, a mere mortal and a sinner, should be granted the same divine privilege of visiting the spirit realm.</meta>

# HELL

->H E L L.<-

You say that the father of Silvius, <note>Silvius was the son of Aeneas. Dante refers to Aeneas, the hero of Virgil’s *Aeneid*, who traveled to the underworld while still alive.</note>
*While still subject to death, went to the*
Immortal world, and was there physically.
Therefore, if the Adversary of all evil <note>original: "l’auersario d’ogni male". A poetic way of referring to God, who is the opposite of all that is wicked.</note>
*Was gracious to him, considering the high effect*
That would come from him, and who and what he was;
It does not seem unworthy to a man of intellect:
*For he was chosen in the empyrean heaven*
As the father of noble Rome and her empire:
Which [Rome] and which [Empire], to tell the truth,
*Were established for the holy place*
Where the successor of the great Peter sits. <note>Dante argues that Aeneas’s journey to the underworld was divinely ordained because Aeneas was to found Rome, which would eventually become the seat of the Papacy (the "successor of Peter").</note>
Through this journey, for which you give him credit,
*He learned things that were the cause*
Of his victory and of the papal mantle.
Afterward, the Chosen Vessel went there, <note>original: "lo uas d’elettione". This refers to Saint Paul (from Acts 9:15), who was "caught up to the third heaven."</note>
*To bring back comfort to that faith*
Which is the beginning of the way of salvation.
But I, why should I come there? Or who permits it?
*I am not Aeneas, I am not Paul;*
Neither I nor others believe me worthy of this.
Therefore, if I resign myself to coming,
*I fear that the coming may be folly;*
You are wise; you understand better than I can speak.
And just like one who unwills what he willed,
*And changes his purpose because of new thoughts,*
So that he withdraws completely from what he started;
Such I became on that dark slope;
*Because by thinking, I wasted the undertaking*
That had been so quick in its beginning.

<summary>Dante expresses his deep self-doubt to Virgil, arguing that while Aeneas and Saint Paul were worthy of visiting the afterlife for their roles in founding the Empire and the Church, he is not. He characterizes his own hesitation as a "folly" that makes him want to abandon the journey before it truly begins.</summary>

<keywords>Dante, Virgil, Aeneas, Saint Paul, Rome, Papacy, doubt, cowardice, Canto II, underworld journey</keywords>

S e i if I have rightly understood your words,
Replied that shadow of the high-souled one; <note>Virgil, the "magnanimous" or great-souled poet, begins his rebuttal of Dante's fear.</note>

### III.

"Through me you go into the city of woe:
Through me you go into eternal pain:
Through me you go among the lost people.
Justice moved my high maker:
Divine power made me,
The highest wisdom, and the primal love. <note>original: "somma sapientia, e'l prim'amore." These terms refer to the Holy Trinity: Power (the Father), Wisdom (the Son), and Love (the Holy Spirit), indicating that Hell was created by a just and balanced God.</note>
Before me there were no created things,
Save those eternal; and I eternal endure:
Abandon all hope, you who enter."
These words of dark color
I saw written above a gate:
Wherefore I: "Master, their sense is hard for me." <note>Dante finds the message "hard" both because it is difficult to understand and because it is terrifyingly harsh.</note>
And he to me, like a person of discernment:
"Here all suspicion must be left behind;
All cowardice must here be dead.
We have come to the place where I told you
That you would see the woeful people
Who have lost the <term>good of the intellect</term>:" <note>In medieval philosophy, the "good of the intellect" is the ultimate truth, which is the vision of God. To lose it is to be eternally separated from the source of all knowledge and peace.</note>

they had an appearance neither sad nor joyful.
**L**o, the good master began to say:
"Look at him with that sword in hand,
who comes before the three as if he were their lord.
**Q**uegli is Homer, the sovereign poet; <note>original: "Homero poeta sourano." Homer is depicted with a sword because he is the poet of epic war (the Iliad).</note>
the next is Horace the satirist;
Ovid is the third, and the last is Lucan." <note>Horace, Ovid, and Lucan were, along with Virgil and Homer, considered the greatest poets of the classical world by medieval scholars.</note>

*That the single voice cried out,* <note>The "single voice" refers to the cry "Honor the highest poet!" heard on the previous page. The "name" they share is that of "Poet."</note>

*Of that lord of the highest song,* <note>original: "altissimo canto." The "lord" is Homer, who leads the group of poets.</note>

*Of great authority in their appearance;*
*They spoke seldom, with gentle voices.*
**W**e moved then to one of the sides,
*Into an open place, bright and high,*

**T**here, directly upon the green enamel, <note>original: "verde smalto." This refers to the vibrant, evergreen grass of the meadow where the souls of the virtuous pagans reside.</note>

**I** saw Electra with many companions;
Among whom I recognized both Hector and Aeneas;
Caesar, fully armed, with hawk-like eyes. <note>Electra was the mother of Dardanus, founder of Troy; Hector and Aeneas represent the Trojan lineage that led to the founding of Rome. Caesar is depicted as a man of action even in the afterlife.</note>
**C**amilla I saw, and Penthesilea
On the other side; and I saw King Latinus,
Who sat with Lavinia, his daughter. <note>Camilla and Penthesilea were famous warrior queens of antiquity. Latinus and Lavinia represent the local Italian roots of the Roman people.</note>
**I** saw that Brutus who drove out Tarquin;
Lucretia, Julia, Marcia, and Cornelia;
And alone, apart, I saw Saladin. <note>Saladin, the 12th-century Sultan of Egypt and Syria, is placed here despite being a Muslim because of his legendary reputation for chivalry and justice. He sits "apart" because he does not belong to the Greco-Roman lineage.</note>
**W**hen I raised my eyes a little higher,
I saw the master of those who know,
Sitting among a philosophical family. <note>original: "il maestro di color, che sanno." This is Aristotle, whom Dante and his contemporaries regarded as the ultimate authority on logic, science, and ethics.</note>
**A**ll look to him, all do him honor.
There I saw both Socrates and Plato,
Who stand closer to him than the others;
**D**emocritus, who attributes the world to chance;
Diogenes, Anaxagoras, and Thales;
Empedocles, Heraclitus, and Zeno; <note>This list includes the major pre-Socratic and Stoic philosophers of Greece.</note>
**A**nd I saw the good collector of qualities,
I mean Dioscorides; and I saw Orpheus,
Tully, and Linus, and moral Seneca; <note>Dioscorides was a Greek physician known for his study of herbs. "Tully" is Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator. Orpheus and Linus are legendary poets and musicians.</note>
**E**uclid the geometer, and Ptolemy;
Hippocrates, Avicenna, and Galen;
Averroes, who made the great commentary. <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a medieval Islamic philosopher famous for his extensive commentaries on Aristotle.</note>

Because the long theme so drives me
That many times the word falls short of the fact.
**T**he company of six is reduced to two:
By another way the wise guide leads me
Out of the quiet into the air that trembles: <note>The "company of six" (Dante, Virgil, Homer, Horace, Ovid, and Lucan) splits; Dante and Virgil leave the other poets to continue their journey deeper into Hell. The "air that trembles" signifies the transition from the relative peace of Limbo back into the regions of active suffering.</note>

And I come to a place where no light shines. <note>original: "E t uegno in parte; oue non è, chi luca." This line marks the exit from the luminous "Noble Castle" of Limbo into the eternal darkness of the lower circles.</note>

### V.

**T**hus I descended from the first circle
Down into the second; which girds less space,
But so much more pain, that it stings to wailing.
**T**here stands Minos, horrific and snarling:
He examines the offenses at the entrance;
He judges and dispatches according to how he girds himself. <note>Minos was a legendary King of Crete, famous for his wisdom. In Dante's Hell, he is transformed into a demonic judge who uses his long tail to signal which level of Hell a soul is destined for.</note>
**I** say, that when the ill-born soul
Comes before him, it confesses all;
And that connoisseur of sins
**S**ees what place in Hell is for it:
He wraps himself with his tail as many times
As the number of levels he wants it to be sent down.
**A**lways many stand before him:
They go in turn, each to the judgment;
They speak, and they hear, and then are cast downward.
**"O**h you, who come to this sorrowful hospice,"
Said Minos to me, when he saw me,
Leaving behind the act of such a great office:
**"L**ook how you enter, and in whom you trust;
Let not the width of the entrance deceive you!"
And my leader <term>duca: leader or guide (referring to Virgil)</term> said to him: "Why do you also cry out?
**D**o not hinder his fated journey:
It is willed so there, where there is power
To do what is willed; and ask no more." <note>original: "Vuolsi cosi cola, doue si puote / Cio che si uuole." This is Virgil’s standard formula for silencing the monsters of Hell, asserting that Dante’s journey is mandated by Heaven.</note>
**N**ow the sorrowful notes begin
To make themselves heard; now I have come
Where much weeping strikes me.

**Minos:** The judge of the underworld; **leader:** Virgil, Dante's guide; **hell:** the realm of the damned; **sins:** moral failings being judged; **judgment:** the sentence passed by Minos; **fated journey:** Dante's divine mission.

<summary>Dante descends into the second circle of Hell, where he encounters the judge Minos, who sentences souls to their respective circles. Despite Minos's warnings, Virgil secures passage for Dante as they enter the realm of the Lustful.</summary>

I came into a place mute of all light;
Which bellows like the sea in a tempest,
If it is combated by opposing winds.
The infernal storm, which never rests,
Drives the spirits with its rapine:
Wheeling and striking, it molests them.
When they arrive before the ruin; <note>The "ruin" (*ruina*) likely refers to a collapsed section of the abyss caused by the earthquake at Christ's crucifixion.</note>
There are the shrieks, the mourning, and the lamentation:
There they blaspheme the divine power.
I understood that to such a torment
Are condemned the carnal sinners,
Who subject reason to desire. <note>original: "talento." In this context, it refers to instinctual desire or carnal appetite overstepping rational control.</note>

In the cold season, in a broad and full flock;
So does that blast carry the evil spirits.
Here, there, down, and up it drives them:
No hope ever comforts them—
Not of rest, but even of lesser pain.
And as the cranes go singing their lays, <note>Cranes were often used in medieval literature to symbolize long, wailing cries and orderly movement.</note>

Coming to us through the malignant air;
So powerful was the affectionate cry.

We passed over the shadows, which the heavy
> rain beats down; and we placed the soles of our feet
> upon their emptiness, which appears as human bodies.
They were all lying on the ground,

**A**nd he to me: "After long contention

I tell you no more, and no more will I answer you." <note>The "sweet world" is the world of the living. Souls in the Inferno often beg to be remembered on Earth, as fame is the only shadow of life they have left.</note>
**H**is straight eyes he then twisted into a squint:
he looked at me a moment, then bowed his head:
he fell with it to the level of the other blind souls.

"**O** Pope Satan, O Pope Satan, Aleppe!" <note>original: "Pape Satàn, pape Satàn aleppe." These famous opening words are a nonsensical, menacing invocation. While scholars debate their meaning, they serve to show Pluto's monstrous, irrational nature.</note>

<meta>This page continues Virgil’s explanation of the spiritual failures of the Avaricious and the Prodigal. **M**aster," I said to him, "now tell me also:
This Fortune, of whom you speak to me,
What is she, who holds the world's goods so tightly in her claws? <note>original: *branche*. Literally "claws" or "talons," personifying Fortune as a grasping beast.</note>
**A**nd he to me: "O foolish creatures,
How great is the ignorance that harms you!
Now I wish you to take in my judgment. <note>original: *sententia*. Here meaning a formal teaching or definitive opinion.</note>
**H**e, whose wisdom transcends all things,
Made the heavens, and gave them those who guide them, <note>In medieval cosmology, God created angelic intelligences to move and "guide" the celestial spheres.</note>
So that every part shines upon every other part,
**D**istributing the light equally.
In a similar way, for worldly splendors, <note>original: *splendor mondani*. This refers to earthly riches, status, and power.</note>
He ordained a general minister and guide;
**W**ho might shift at the proper time those empty goods
From nation to nation, and from one bloodline to another,
Beyond the reach of human wisdom. <note>original: *oltre la difension d’e senni humani*. Meaning that no human planning or intelligence can prevent the shifts of Fortune.</note>
**F**or this reason one nation rules and another languishes,
Following the judgment of her [Fortune];
Which is hidden, like a snake in the grass.
**Y**our knowledge has no defense against her:
She foresees, judges, and carries out
Her reign, as the other gods <note>original: *altri Dei*. Virgil, a pagan, uses the word "gods" to refer to the angelic powers that govern the universe under the One God.</note> do theirs.
**H**er changes have no truce:
Necessity makes her swift;
So often does someone come who wins his turn.
**T**his is she who is so often crucified <note>original: *posta in croce*. A metaphor for being heavily criticized or vilified.</note>
Even by those who should give her praise,
Giving her wrongful blame and an ill name.
**B**ut she is blessed, and does not hear this:
Happy among the other primal creatures, <note>original: *prime creature*. The angels, the first beings created by God.</note>
She turns her sphere, and in her bliss enjoys herself."

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the second ring of the Seventh Circle of Hell. Having entered the pathless forest of the suicides, Dante is confused by the disembodied wailing he hears. This section contains the famous encounter where Dante breaks a branch from a thornbush, revealing the soul of Pier delle Vigne, a former advisor to Emperor Frederick II.</meta>

->INF.<-

I heard wails being drawn from every side;
And I saw no person who might be making them:
Wherefore, completely bewildered, I stopped.
I believe that he believed that I believed <note>Dante uses a complex rhetorical figure here (polyptoton) to mirror his own mental confusion: "Io credo ch'ei credette ch'io credesse."</note>
That so many voices were coming from among those trunks
From people who were hiding from us:
Therefore, the master said, "If you break off
Some small twig from one of these plants;
The thoughts you have will all be cut short." <note>The Master (Virgil) realizes Dante thinks people are hiding behind the trees; by breaking a branch, Dante will realize the trees *are* the people.</note>
Then I reached my hand forward a little;
And I plucked a small branch from a great thornbush:
And its trunk cried out: "Why do you tear me?"
After it became dark with blood;
It began to cry out again: "Why do you mangle me?
Have you no spirit of pity at all?
Men we were, and now we are made into brushwood. <note>original: "sterpi"; refers to dry, gnarled, or thorny undergrowth.</note>
Surely your hand should have been more merciful;
Even if we had been the souls of serpents."
As from a green log that is burned
At one of its ends; which at the other end groans,
And hisses because of the air escaping; <note>original: "per uento, che ua uia"; Dante compares the sound of the soul speaking through the bleeding branch to the whistling of sap and steam escaping a burning branch.</note>
So from that broken splinter issued forth
Both words and blood: wherefore I let the tip
Fall; and stood like a man who is afraid.
"If he had been able to believe before,"
My sage replied, "O wounded soul,
What he has seen only through my verse; <note>Virgil refers to his own epic poem, the *Aeneid* (his "rima"), specifically the episode of Polydorus who was similarly turned into a bleeding plant.</note>
He would not have stretched out his hand against you:
But the thing being so incredible made me
Induce him to an act that weighs upon my own heart." <note>Virgil expresses regret for making Dante hurt the soul, but explains it was the only way for the mortal Dante to truly believe the reality of this punishment.</note>

<summary>Dante, confused by voices in the Wood of the Suicides, breaks a branch from a bush at Virgil's urging. The bush bleeds and speaks, revealing that the souls of suicides are encased in thorny plants; Virgil apologizes to the shade, explaining he needed Dante to see the truth for himself.</summary>

**B**ut tell him who you were, so that instead
Of some penance he may refresh your fame
In the world above, where he is permitted to return.
**A**nd the trunk: "You lure me so with your sweet speech
That I cannot remain silent; may it not trouble you
If I am drawn into speaking at some length.
**I** am he who held both keys
Of Frederick’s heart <note>Emperor Frederick II (1194–1250). The speaker is Pier delle Vigne, the Emperor’s most trusted advisor and diplomat.</note>, and I turned them,
Locking and unlocking so gently,
**T**hat I excluded almost every other man from his confidence.
I remained so faithful to that glorious office
That I lost both my sleep and my life for it. <note>original: "le uene e' polsi" (the veins and pulses); a metaphor for his vital strength and life force.</note>
**T**he harlot <note>Envy personified. In the context of a royal court, envy is described as a prostitute who never leaves the "house of Caesar" (the imperial court).</note> who never from the house
Of Caesar turned her shameless eyes—
That common death and vice of courts—
**I**nflamed all minds against me;
And those inflamed ones so inflamed Augustus <note>A title used here for Emperor Frederick II, linking him to the Roman Emperors.</note>

**M**y mind, in a scornful mood,
Thinking to escape scorn by dying,
Made me unjust toward my own just self. <note>Pier explains the paradox of his suicide: by killing himself to escape the unjust accusations of the court, he committed a sin (an injustice) against himself, despite being innocent of the original crimes.</note>
**B**y the new roots of this tree,
I swear to you that I never broke faith
With my lord, who was so worthy of honor.
**A**nd if either of you returns to the world,
Restore my memory, which still lies prostrate
From the blow that envy dealt it."
**H**e waited a moment, and then, since the soul was silent,
The poet <note>Virgil.</note> said to me: "Do not lose the moment;
But speak, and ask him more, if it pleases you."

Wherefore I said to him: "Ask him further

Then the trunk blew strongly; and afterwards 
That wind was converted into this voice: 
"Briefly shall you be answered. 
When the fierce soul departs 
From the body from which it has uprooted itself, 
Minos <note>The mythological judge of the underworld who assigns souls to their specific circle of Hell based on their sins.</note> sends it to the seventh abyss. 
It falls into the forest, and no specific place is chosen for it; 
But there, where fortune flings it: 
There it sprouts like a grain of spelt <note>original: "gran di spelta"; a hardy species of wheat. Dante uses this to emphasize the soul's loss of human form and its reduction to a mere plant.</note>. 
It rises into a sapling and into a wild plant: 
The Harpies <note>Mythological monsters with the faces of women and bodies of birds. In this circle, they symbolize the remorse that "eats away" at the spirit.</note>, feeding then upon its leaves,

For it is not just for a man to have what he takes from himself. 
Here we shall drag them; and through the mournful 
Forest our bodies shall be hung, 
Each on the thorn-bush of its own troublesome shade."
We were still attentive to the trunk, 
Believing that it wished to say more, 
When we were surprised by a noise—

**D**ownward from there, he is all of chosen iron,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;except that the right foot is made of baked clay;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;and he stands more upon that foot than on the other. <note>The statue's feet are often interpreted as symbols of the pillars of society: the iron left foot representing the Empire (strength) and the clay right foot representing the Church, which Dante viewed as fragile or corrupted by earthly concerns.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;by a fissure <note>original: "fessura"</note> that drips with tears,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;which, once collected, bore through this cavern.
**T**heir course cascades down into this valley:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;they form Acheron, Styx, and Phlegethon; <note>These are the major rivers of the underworld in Greek mythology, adapted by Dante into a single connected hydraulic system fed by human suffering.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;then the water flows down through this narrow conduit

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;therefore, if something new appears to us,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;it should not bring a look of wonder to your face."

**"L**ethe you shall see, but not in this abyss;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;rather, where the souls go to wash themselves

### XV.

Now one of the hard margins carries us along;
And the steam of the stream casts a shadow above,
So that it shields the water and the banks from the fire.
Just as the Flemings between Wissant and Bruges, <note>Wissant (Guizante) and Bruges (Bruggia) were key points on the coast of Flanders (modern-day France and Belgium).</note>
Fearing the tide that rushes toward them,
Build a bulwark so that the sea might be driven back;
And as the Paduans do along the Brenta river, <note>Padua is a city in Northern Italy; the Brenta is a river that often flooded when Alpine snows melted.</note>
To defend their villas and their castles,
Before the heat is felt in Carinthia; <note>original: "Chiarentana"; a mountain region in the Eastern Alps. Dante refers to the spring thaw when the river swells.</note>
In such a likeness were these banks made,
Though the master—whoever he may have been—
Made them neither so high nor so thick.
Already we were so far removed from the wood
That I could not have seen where it was,
Even if I had turned back to look;
When we encountered a troop of souls
Who came along the bank; and each one
Looked at us, as one is wont at evening
To look at another under a new moon;
And they sharpened their brows toward us,
As an old tailor does at the eye of his needle. <note>This famous simile illustrates the souls squinting through the dim light and the steam to recognize the travelers.</note>
Being thus eyed by such a company,
I was recognized by one, who took me
By the hem of my garment and cried out: "What a marvel!"

### XVI.

running, from a troop that was passing

We descended toward the right side;
and we took ten steps along the very edge

close to the edge of the void <note>original: "luogo scemo"; referring to the jagged edge where the solid ground drops off into the next circle.</note>.

Thus I went further along the outer boundary

to where the sorrowful people were sitting.
Their grief burst forth from their eyes.
With their hands they fended off the heat,
now from the falling fire, and now from the scorching ground.
They acted just like dogs in the summer,
now with their paws, now with their snouts, when they are bitten

Then I became more terrified of the sheer drop,
because I saw fires and heard wailing;
at which, trembling, I shrank back completely.

who, seeing neither lure <note>A "lure" (logoro) was a leather tool used by falconers to recall their birds.</note> nor bird,

### XVIII.

There is a place in Hell called Malebolge <term>Malebolge: Derived from the Italian words "male" (evil) and "bolge" (pouches, ditches, or pockets). This is the Eighth Circle of Hell, reserved for those who committed various forms of fraud.</term>,
all made of stone and of an iron-grey color,
like the circular wall that surrounds it.
Right in the center of this malignant field
there yawns a pit, exceedingly wide and deep,
whose structure I will describe in its proper place.
The belt of land that remains, then, is circular,
between the pit and the foot of the high, hard bank,
and has its floor divided into ten valleys.
Just as, where many ditches encircle a castle
to protect its walls,
the ground there takes on a certain shape;

Is sufficient to see it without climbing onto the back
Of the arch, where the rock hangs at its highest.
We came to that point; and from there down in the ditch
I saw people submerged in <term>excrement</term><note>In Dante's system of "contrapasso" (the punishment fitting the crime), flatterers are immersed in filth because their false praises on earth were "shitty" or foul talk.</note>
That seemed to have been moved from human latrines.
And while I searched down there with my eyes,
I saw one with a head so fouled with filth
That it was not clear if he was a layman or a cleric.
He cried out to me: "Why are you so greedy
To look at me more than the other filthy ones?"
And I to him: "Because, if I remember correctly,
I have seen you before with dry hair,
And you are **Alessio Interminei of Lucca**<note>A member of a prominent White Guelph family in Lucca, known for his political maneuvering and excessive flattery.</note>:
That is why I eye you more than all the others."
And he then, beating his own skull, replied:
"Down here the flatteries have submerged me,
Of which my tongue never grew tired."
After this, my leader said: "Make sure you push
Your gaze a little further forward,
So that your eyes may clearly reach the face
Of that filthy and disheveled <term>wench</term><note>This refers to Thais, a character from the Roman play "The Eunuch" by Terence. In the Middle Ages, she was often used as the archetypal example of a flatterer.</note>
Who scratches herself there with dung-filled nails,
And now she crouches, and now she stands upright."

<summary>Dante and Virgil cross into the second ditch of the eighth circle, where flatterers are immersed in human excrement. Dante identifies Alessio Interminei of Lucca and observes the filthy state of the courtesan Thais.</summary>
<keywords>Malebolge, Flatterers, Alessio Interminei, Lucca, Thais, Contrapasso, Second Ditch</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the description of the second ditch of the eighth circle, where flatterers are punished, and begins the transition into the third ditch, where the "Simonists"—those who sold sacred offices for money—are tormented.</meta>

->HELL<-

Thais is the whore who responded 
To her paramour when he said: "Do I have 
Great favor with you?"; "Indeed, marvelous!": 
And with this, let our sight be satisfied. <note>original: "Thaidà è la puttana..." Dante is referencing a character from the Roman play *The Eunuch* by Terence. She is placed among the flatterers because of her excessive, false gratitude to her lover. In the medieval view, this was considered a form of linguistic corruption.</note>

### XIX.

O **Simon Magus**, o wretched followers; 
Who, being greedy, prostitute for gold 
And silver the things of God, which 
Ought to be the brides of goodness; 
Now it is necessary that the trumpet sound for you, 
Because you reside in the third <term>bolgia</term><note>A ditch or pouch in the eighth circle of Hell.</note>. 
We had already climbed to the next tomb, 
Rising onto that part of the rocky bridge 
Which hangs exactly over the middle of the trench. 
O Supreme Wisdom, how great is the art 
That You show in earth, in heaven, and in the evil world; 
And how justly Your power distributes its rewards. 
I saw along the sides and across the bottom 
The livid-colored stone full of holes, 
All of one width; and each was round. 
They seemed to me no less wide, nor larger, 
Than those that are in my beautiful **San Giovanni** 
Made as standing-places for the <term>baptizers</term><note>Dante refers to the stone baptismal fonts in the Baptistery of San Giovanni in Florence. Priests stood in these holes to protect themselves from the crowds while performing baptisms.</note>: 
One of which, not many years ago, 
I broke for the sake of one who was drowning inside: 
And let this be the seal that clears up every man's error. <note>Dante includes this personal anecdote to defend himself against a historical rumor that he had committed sacrilege by damaging the holy font; he explains he did it only to save a child's life.</note> 
From the mouth of each hole there protruded 
A sinner's feet, and the legs as far as 
The calf; and the rest of the body stayed inside.

<summary>Dante concludes the scene of the flatterers with the figure of Thais and enters the third ditch, where Simonists are buried upside-down in holes resembling baptismal fonts.</summary>

The soles of both feet were set on fire for all of them:
> Because of this, their joints twitched so violently,
> That they would have snapped cords of fiber or hemp. <note>original: "ritorto & strambe" refers to ropes made of twisted vines or sturdy marsh grass; the image conveys the intense physical agony of the sinners.</note>

Just as the flaming of oily objects usually
> Moves only along the outermost surface;
> So it was there, from the heels to the toes.

"Master, who is that one who is so tormented,
> Twitching more than his companions,"
> I said, "and who is sucked by a redder flame?" <note>Dante notices one sinner who seems to suffer more intensely than the others, his feet flickering with a brighter, hotter fire.</note>

And he said to me: "If you wish for me to carry you
> Down along that bank which lies lower;
> You shall hear from him about himself and his misdeeds."

And I: "What pleases you is good to me:
> You are my lord; and you know I do not stray
> From your will; and you know that which is left unsaid."

Then we arrived upon the fourth embankment:
> We turned and descended on the left-hand side
> Down into the narrow bottom, full of holes.

And the good master did not yet set me down from his hip,
> Until he brought me to the cleft
> Of the one who was lamenting with his legs. <note>original: "zanca" is a somewhat vulgar or dialectal term for a leg or shank, used here to emphasize the undignified nature of the sinner's position.</note>

"O whoever you are, who keeps your upper part down,
> Sad soul planted like a stake,"
> I began to say; "If you are able, speak a word."

I stood there like the friar who confesses
> The treacherous assassin, who, once fixed in the hole,
> Calls him back so that his death is delayed: <note>In medieval Florence, "treacherous assassins" were executed by being buried alive upside down, a practice called *propaggine*. The criminal would often call the priest back to confess more sins just to gain a few more moments of life.</note>

And he cried out: "Are you already standing there,
> Are you already standing there, **Boniface**?
> The writing lied to me by several years." <note>The sinner is Pope Nicholas III. He mistakes Dante for Pope Boniface VIII, whom he expects to join him in this hole in the year 1303. Since the poem is set in 1300, the "writing" (the divine prophecy known to the damned) seems to have misled him regarding the timing of Boniface's arrival.</note>

But the time during which I have cooked my feet

<meta>This page continues the speech of Dante to Pope Nicholas III. In the previous lines, Nicholas III confessed his identity as a member of the Orsini family and his punishment for simony. Dante now responds with a fierce condemnation of papal corruption, comparing the current state of the Church to biblical examples of greed and idolatry.</meta>

# INF.

He will be a new Jason; of whom we read
*In the Book of the Maccabees: and as to that one was indulgent*
*His king, so shall be to him the one who rules France.* <note>original: "Iason... Machabei." Jason was a biblical figure who purchased the High Priesthood through bribery (2 Maccabees 4). Dante uses him as a type for Pope Clement V, who secured the papacy through the influence of King Philip the Fair of France.</note>
I do not know if I was perhaps too bold here,
*For I replied to him in this very meter:*
*"Pray, tell me now, how much treasure did*
Our Lord demand from Saint Peter at the first,
*Before he placed the keys into his keeping?*
*Surely he asked for nothing but: 'Follow me.'* <note>Referring to Matthew 4:19, where Jesus calls Peter to be a "fisher of men" without any exchange of money.</note>
Neither Peter nor the others asked of Matthias
*Gold or silver, when he was chosen by lot*
*To the place that the guilty soul had lost.* <note>Matthias was the apostle chosen to replace Judas Iscariot (the "guilty soul"). Dante emphasizes that this holy office was not bought.</note>
Therefore stay there, for you are rightly punished;
*And guard well that ill-gotten money*
*That made you so bold against Charles;* <note>Pope Nicholas III was accused of accepting bribes from the Byzantine Emperor to support a rebellion against Charles of Anjou, King of Naples and Sicily.</note>
And were it not that I am still restrained
*By the reverence for those supreme keys*
*Which you held in the glad life above,*
I would use even harsher words than these;
*For your avarice afflicts the whole world,*
*Trampling the good and exalting the wicked.*
You shepherds the **Evangelist** had in mind, <term>Evangelist: Specifically Saint John, the author of the Book of Revelation.</term>
*When she who sits upon the waters*
*Was seen by him to play the harlot with the kings;* <note>A reference to the "Whore of Babylon" in Revelation 17, which Dante interprets as a prophecy of the corrupt, worldly Papacy.</note>
She who was born with the seven heads,
*And from the ten horns had her strength,*
*So long as virtue pleased her spouse.* <note>The "spouse" is the Pope. The heads and horns represent the foundations of the Church (often interpreted as the Seven Sacraments and the Ten Commandments) which only provide strength when the leadership is virtuous.</note>
You have made yourselves a god of gold and silver;
*And what else stands between you and the idolater,*
*Save that he worships one, and you a hundred?*

<summary>Dante delivers a scathing rebuke to Pope Nicholas III, contrasting the poverty of the Apostles with the greed of contemporary Popes. He uses the biblical Whore of Babylon as an allegory for a Church corrupted by political alliances and "idolatrous" wealth.</summary>

# INF. 45

Ah, Constantine, of how much ill was the mother,
> Not your conversion, but that dowry
> Which the first wealthy father took from you! <note>original: "Constantin." Dante refers to the "Donation of Constantine," a forged decree where Emperor Constantine supposedly granted the Pope (the "wealthy father," Sylvester I) temporal power over Rome. Dante believed this wealth corrupted the Church.</note>

> Whether anger or conscience bit him,
> He kicked out fiercely with both his feet.
I believe truly that it pleased my leader;
> With such a contented expression he always listened
> To the sound of the true words I expressed. <note>original: "duca." Referring to Virgil, Dante's guide through Hell.</note>

> And once he had me entirely upon his chest,
> He climbed back up the path by which he had descended:
Nor did he tire of holding me close to him,
> Until he bore me to the summit of the arch,
> Which is the passage from the fourth to the fifth embankment. <term>embankment: The "argine" or stony wall that separates the various ditches (bolge) within the eighth circle of Hell.</term>
There he gently set down his burden;
> Gently, because of the rugged and steep ridge,
> Which would be a difficult passage even for goats:

### XX.

Of new punishment I must now make verses,
> And give material to the twentieth canto
> Of the first song, which is of the submerged souls. <note>original: "uentesimo canto... prima canzon." The "first song" refers to the Inferno, the first part of the Divine Comedy.</note>
I was already fully prepared
> To look down into the uncovered bottom,
> Which was bathed in anguished tears;
And I saw people through the circular valley
> Coming silent and weeping, at the slow pace

<meta>This page continues Canto XX of the Inferno. # INF.

As my gaze descended lower upon them,
Each appeared to be strangely distorted
Between the chin and the start of the chest: <note>original: "casso." This refers to the trunk or torso of the body.</note>
For the face was turned toward the shoulders,
And they were forced to walk backward,
Because the power to see ahead was taken from them.
Perhaps by some great force of paralysis <term>paralysis: original "parlasia." Dante uses a medical term to emphasize the physical impossibility of this twisting.</term>
Someone has been so completely turned about;
But I have never seen it, nor do I believe it happens.
So may God let you, Reader, gather fruit
From your reading, now think for yourself,
How I could ever keep my own face dry;
When I saw our human image so close at hand,
So twisted that the tears from their eyes
Bathed their buttocks at the cleft. <note>Dante uses this graphic imagery to show the total degradation of the human form, emphasizing that these sinners have lost the "upright" dignity of man.</note>
Certainly I wept, leaning against one of the rocks
Of the hard crag, so much so that my escort <note>original: "scorta." Referring to the poet Virgil, who guides Dante through Hell.</note>
Said to me: "Are you still among the other fools?
Here pity lives when it is well dead. <note>original: "Qui uiue la pieta, quand' è ben morta." This is a famous wordplay in Italian. "Pietà" can mean both "pity" and "piety" (devotion to God). Virgil is saying that true "piety" toward God's justice requires that "pity" for the damned must be dead.</note>
Who is more wicked than he
Who brings his own passion to oppose divine judgment?
Lift up your head, lift it; and see him for whom
The earth opened before the eyes of the Thebans,
When they all cried out: 'Where are you falling,
Amphiaraus? Why do you leave the war?' <note>Amphiaraus was one of the seven kings who attacked Thebes. As a seer, he foresaw his own death and tried to flee, but the earth opened up and swallowed him. Dante places him here for using his prophetic powers to try to escape his fate.</note>
And he did not stop rushing down the valley
Until he reached Minos, who seizes every soul. <note>In Greek mythology and Dante’s Hell, Minos is the monstrous judge of the underworld who wraps his tail around himself to indicate which level of Hell a sinner must go to.</note>
Look how he has made a breast of his shoulders:
Because he wanted to see too far ahead,
He now looks behind and walks a backward path."

# INF.

See **Tiresias**, who changed his appearance <note>original: "muto sembiante." Tiresias was a famous blind prophet of Thebes in Greek mythology.</note>
When he became a woman from a man,
Changing every one of his limbs;
And afterward, he had to strike again
The two coiled serpents with his wand <term>wand: original "verga." The instrument of a magician or augur.</term>
Before he could regain his masculine plumage. <note>original: "maschili penne." A poetic way of describing his male form or perhaps his beard.</note>

Who, in the mountains of **Luni**, where the laborer
Of **Carrara**—who dwells below—hoes the earth, <note>Luni was an ancient Etruscan city near the famous white marble quarries of Carrara.</note>

For his dwelling; from there, his view 
Of the stars and the sea was never cut off.

Which you cannot see, with her loose tresses,
And has all her hairy skin on the other side,
Was **Manto**; who searched through many lands,
Then settled there, where I was born: <note>Virgil is referring to his own birthplace, Mantua.</note>
So it pleases me that you listen to me for a while.
After her father departed from this life,
And the city of **Bacchus** became enslaved, <note>original: "citta di Baco." This refers to the city of Thebes, the birthplace of the god Bacchus (Dionysus).</note>
She wandered through the world for a long time.
Up in beautiful **Italy** lies a lake

By a thousand springs and more, I believe, the water

<meta>This page continues Virgil’s detailed geographical and historical account of the founding of Mantua, his birthplace. He is explaining to Dante how the waters of Lake Garda (Benaco) flow into the Mincio river and create the marshy land where the prophetess Manto eventually settled.</meta>

# INF.

**Peschiera** sits, a beautiful and strong fortress <note>original: "arnese." Literally "tool" or "equipment," but here referring to a defensive fortification.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To face the people of **Brescia** and **Bergamo**;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Where the surrounding shore lies lowest.
There it is necessary that all the water falls,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Whatever cannot stay in the lap of **Benaco**, <term>Benaco: The classical name for Lake Garda.</term>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And it becomes a river down through green pastures.
As soon as the water starts to flow;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;It is no longer called **Benaco**, but the **Mincio**
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Until **Governo**, where it falls into the **Po**. <note>Governo is the modern town of Governalo, the confluence of the Mincio and Po rivers.</note>
It has not run far before it finds a low flat; <term>low flat: original "lama." A term for a marshy depression or stagnant pool.</term>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In which it spreads out and turns into a swamp;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And in summer it is sometimes unwholesome. <note>original: "grama." Likely referring to the foul smells or malaria associated with stagnant marshes in the heat.</note>
Passing through there, the wild virgin <note>This refers to Manto, the "cruel" or "wild" (cruda) daughter of Tiresias, who was a practitioner of sorcery.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Saw land in the middle of the bog,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Untilled and stripped of inhabitants.
There, to flee all human company,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;She stopped with her servants to practice her arts; <note>original: "far su arti." Refers to her magical or prophetic rituals.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And there she lived; and there she left her empty body.
Then the men who were scattered around
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Gathered at that place; for it was strong
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Because of the swamp it had on all sides.
They built the city over those dead bones;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And after her, who first chose the place,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;They called it **Mantua** without any other omen. <note>original: "senz'altra sorte." In ancient times, the naming of a city often involved casting lots or seeking omens; Virgil claims Mantua was simply named after Manto.</note>
Formerly its people within were more numerous;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Before the foolishness of **Casalodi** <note>original: "Mattia da Casalodi." Refers to the count Alberto da Casalodi, who was tricked into exile in 1272.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Was deceived by **Pinamonte**. <note>Pinamonte de' Bonacolsi, who seized power in Mantua by tricking the Casalodi family.</note>
Therefore I warn you, so that if you ever hear
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;My city’s origin told otherwise;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Let no lie defraud the truth.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Dante and Virgil in the Fourth Bolgia of the Eighth Circle of Hell, where the Soothsayers and Diviners are punished. Virgil has just finished explaining the origins of his home city, Mantua, to correct any false mythological accounts.</meta>

# I N F.

**A**nd I said: "Master, your explanations
Are so certain to me, and so command my faith,
That any others would be like cold, spent coals to me.
**B**ut tell me of the people who are passing by;
If you see any among them worthy of note:
For my mind is fixed on that alone."
**T**hen he said to me: "That one, who from his cheek
Spreads his beard over his dark shoulders,
Was—at the time when Greece was so empty of men
**T**hat they hardly remained even for the cradles—
An augur; <term>augur: A religious official in ancient Rome and Greece who interpreted omens, particularly the flight of birds.</term> and with Calchas he gave the signal
In Aulis to cut the first cable to set sail. <note>Aulis was the port where the Greek fleet gathered before the Trojan War. They could only sail once the gods were appeased.</note>
**E**urypylus was his name; and my high tragedy
Sings of him in a certain place:
You know it well, since you know the whole poem by heart. <note>Virgil refers to his own epic poem, the *Aeneid*, as a 'high tragedy' because of its noble style and subject matter.</note>
**T**hat other one, who is so thin around the flanks,
Was Michael Scot; who truly
Understood the game of magical deceptions. <term>Michael Scot: A 13th-century Scottish scholar and philosopher at the court of Frederick II, legendary for his supposed supernatural powers.</term>
**S**ee Guido Bonatti; see Asdente,
Who now wishes he had stayed focused on his leather
And his twine; but he repents too late. <note>Guido Bonatti was a famous astrologer. Asdente was a shoemaker from Parma who gained fame as a prophet.</note>
**S**ee the wretched women who left the needle,
The shuttle, and the spindle, and became diviners;
They performed sorceries with herbs and with wax images.
**B**ut come along now: for already Cain and his thorns
Occupies the border of both hemispheres
And touches the wave beneath Seville. <note>original: "Cain e le spine." In medieval folklore, the "Man in the Moon" was Cain, punished by carrying a bundle of thorns. Virgil is using the moon's position over Seville (the western edge of the world) to indicate it is about 6:00 AM.</note>
**A**nd already last night the moon was full:
You should remember it well, for it did you no harm
When you were in the deep woods." <note>Referring to the 'dark woods' of Canto I, where the moonlight helped Dante find his way before meeting Virgil.</note>

### XXI.

Thus from bridge to bridge we went, talking of other things
Which my comedy does not care to sing; <note>Dante refers to his work as a "comedy" because it begins in misery (Hell) but ends in happiness (Paradise), and is written in the vernacular rather than "high" Latin. This mirrors Virgil's reference to his own "high tragedy" on the previous page.</note>
We arrived; and held the summit of the bridge; when
We stopped to see the next fissure
Of <term>Malebolge: Literally "Evil-Ditches" or "Evil-Pouches," this is the eighth circle of Hell, divided into ten concentric trenches where different types of fraud are punished.</term>, and the other vain laments:
And I saw it marvelously dark.
As in the <term>Arsenal of the Venetians: In Dante’s time, the state-run shipyard in Venice was the largest industrial complex in Europe. Its massive operations are used here as a vivid metaphor for the scale of the infernal activity.</term>
The sticky pitch boils in winter
To caulk their damaged ships,
Which they cannot sail; and in its place
One builds his ship anew; and another plugs
The ribs of that which has made many voyages;
One hammers at the prow, and another at the stern;
Others make oars, and others twist the ropes;
Another repairs the small foresail and the mainsail;
So, not by fire, but by divine art
A thick tar was boiling down there,
Which coated the bank on every side.
I saw it; but I saw nothing in it
Except the bubbles that the boiling raised;
And the whole mass swelling, and then settling back down.
While I was gazing down there fixedly;
My leader, saying, "Look out, look out!"
Pulled me to himself from the place where I stood.
Then I turned; like a man who is anxious
To see what he must flee from;
And whom a sudden fear unnerves;

...who, for the sake of seeing, does not delay his departure. <note>Dante describes himself as being like a man who is terrified but still looks back to see what he is running from.</note>
And I saw behind us a black Devil
Running up along the crag.
Ah, how fierce he was in his appearance;
And how bitter he seemed to me in his actions,
With wings outspread, and light upon his feet.
His shoulder, which was sharp and high,
Was laden with a sinner by both haunches;
And he held gripped the tendon of his feet.
From our bridge he said: "O <term>Malebranche: Literally "Evil-Claws," these are the cruel, winged demons who guard the Fifth Bolgia and torment the souls within.</term>,
Here is one of the elders of <term>Santa Zita: The patron saint of the city of Lucca. The "elders" were the city's high-ranking magistrates.</term>!
Put him under, for I am returning again
To that city, which is well supplied with them:
Every man there is a <term>barrator: Someone who commits "barratry"—the sin of trading public office for money or taking bribes. It is the political equivalent of Simony.</term>, except for Bonturo;
There, for money, they turn 'No' into 'Yes.'" <note>Dante is being deeply sarcastic here; Bonturo Dati was actually the most corrupt politician in Lucca, not the only honest one.</note>
Down there he threw him; and along the hard crag
He turned back; and never was a mastiff unleashed
With such haste to pursue a thief.
That one plunged in, and came back up doubled over;
But the Demons, who were sheltered by the bridge,
Cried: "Here the <term>Holy Face: A famous ancient wooden crucifix in the Cathedral of Lucca, believed to have been carved by Nicodemus.</term> has no place!
Here one swims differently than in the <term>Serchio: The river that flows through Lucca.</term>!
Therefore, if you do not want our claws,
Do not poke yourself above the pitch."
Then they bit into him with more than a hundred hooks;
They said: "It is best that you dance here covered up,
So that, if you can, you may grab things secretly." <note>This is a cruel joke by the demons: just as the barrator took bribes in secret during life, he must now stay hidden beneath the pitch.</note>
Not otherwise do cooks make their assistants
Dip the meat into the middle of the cauldron
With hooks, so that it does not float.

The good master—so that it might not be apparent
That you are here—said to me: "Crouch down low
Behind a crag, so that you have some protection.
And regardless of any offense that may be directed at me,
Do not be afraid; for I have these matters well in hand,
Because I was at such a <term>skirmish: The Italian word "baratta" means a fight or brawl, but Dante uses it here as a pun on "barratry," the sin being punished in this circle.</term> once before." <note>Virgil refers to his previous journey to the lower depths of Hell, mentioned in Canto IX, when he was summoned by the witch Erichtho.</note>
Then he passed beyond the head of the bridge;
And as he reached the sixth bank,
He had need of a steady brow.
With the same fury and the same storm
With which dogs rush out at a beggar
Who suddenly asks for alms where he stops,
Those demons rushed out from under the little bridge
And turned all their <term>hooks: "Roncigli" were long-handled grappling irons used to pull sinners back under the boiling pitch.</term> against him;
But he cried out: "Let none of you be hostile!
Before your hook takes hold of me,
Let one of you step forward to hear me,
And then decide if you wish to hook me."
They all cried out: "Let <term>Malacoda: Literally "Evil-Tail," the leader of this group of demons.</term> go!"
Whereupon one moved, and the others stood still;
And he came to him, saying: "What good does this do him?"
"Do you believe, Malacoda, that you see me
Having come here," said my master,
"Safe already from all your defenses,
Without divine will and a favorable fate?
Let us pass: for it is willed in Heaven
That I show another this wild path."
Then his pride was so fallen
That he let the hook drop to his feet,
And said to the others: "Now, let him not be struck."

**A**nd I said to the Guide: "Tell him not to slip away; <note>original: "duca" (leader/guide), referring to Virgil.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And ask what crime thrust him down here:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For I once saw him as a man of blood and rages."
**A**nd the sinner, who heard, did not pretend;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But directed his mind and his face toward me;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And he was painted with a sad shame:
**T**hen he said: "It pains me more that you have caught me
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In the misery where you see me now,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Than when I was taken from the other life.
**I** cannot deny that which you ask:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I am put so far down because I was
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;A thief in the sacristy of the beautiful ornaments; <note>In 1293, Vanni Fucci stole the treasure of San Jacopo from the Cathedral of Pistoia.</note>
**A**nd falsely it was once blamed on someone else.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But so that you do not enjoy such a sight,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;If you ever find yourself outside these dark places,
**O**pen your ears to my announcement, and hear:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Pistoia first thins herself of the 'Blacks'; <note>The "Blacks" and "Whites" were opposing political factions (Guelphs). This refers to the expulsion of the Black Guelphs from Pistoia in 1301.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Then Florence renews her people and her ways.
**M**ars draws a vapor from the Val di Magra, <note>Mars represents war; the "vapor" is a metaphor for the commander Moroello Malaspina.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which is wrapped in murky clouds:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And with a storm, impetuous and bitter,
**O**ver the Picene field shall it be fought: <note>Refers to the siege of Pistoia (the Campo Piceno) where the White Guelphs were defeated.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Whereby it shall suddenly break through the mist,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So that every 'White' shall be wounded by it:
**A**nd I have said this, so that it might cause you grief." <note>Vanni Fucci provides this prophecy of Dante’s own political party's defeat purely to spite the poet.</note>

At the conclusion of his words, the thief
Raised his hands with both "the figs," <note>An obscene gesture made by placing the thumb between the index and middle fingers, intended here as a profound insult to God.</note>

Clenching itself so tightly in front
That he could not even give a shrug with them.
Ah, Pistoia, Pistoia! Why do you not decree
To incinerate yourself so that you last no longer,

Then they stuck together, as if they

**H**e stared at the serpent, and it at him;

Such that both forms were ready

**T**he legs and the thighs fastened themselves 
Together so closely that soon the joint

**T**he split tail took on the very shape
That the other was losing; its skin

**T**hen, tossing its tip to and fro, 
as if it were the very tongue that spoke, 
it cast out a voice and said: "When 
**I** departed from Circe, who withheld 
me for more than a year there near Gaeta, 
before Aeneas had given it that name; <note>original: "Circe." The sorceress who turned Ulysses’s men into swine. Gaeta is a city in central Italy which, according to Virgil's Aeneid, was named by Aeneas after his nurse, Caieta.</note>

I had to gain experience of the world, 
and of human vices and of human worth. 
**B**ut I set out upon the deep, open sea 
with only a single ship and that small 
company of men who had not deserted me. 
**I** saw both shores as far as Spain, 
as far as Morocco, and the island of Sardinia, 
and the others bathed by that sea. 
**I** and my companions were old and slow 
when we reached that narrow strait 
where Hercules set up his markers, <note>original: "foce stretta." The Strait of Gibraltar. The "markers" are the Pillars of Hercules, which in antiquity were considered the boundary of the known world, beyond which no one should sail.</note>
**s**o that man should not venture further. 
On the right hand, I left Seville behind; 
on the other, Ceuta had already been passed. <note>original: "Sibilia" and "Setta." Seville in Spain and Ceuta in North Africa.</note>

perils have reached the west; to this so brief 
**v**igil of your senses that remains to you, 
do not choose to deny the experience— 
following the sun—of the world that has no people. <note>original: "mondo senza gente." The uninhabited hemisphere, which in Dante's geography was thought to be covered entirely by water.</note>

**B**ut because no one ever returned from this depth,
If what I hear is true,
Without fear of infamy I answer you.
**I** was a man of arms, and then a Franciscan friar, <note>original: *cordigliero*. Members of the Franciscan order were called "cordeliers" because of the simple knotted cord they wore as a belt.</note>
Believing that, so girded, I could make amends;

**I**f it were not for the High Priest <note>Pope Boniface VIII, whom Dante blamed for much of the corruption in the Church and his own exile from Florence.</note>—may evil take him!—

And how and why <note>original: *quare* (Latin for "why").</note>, I want you to hear from me.
**W**hile I was still made of the bones and flesh
That my mother gave me, my deeds
Were not those of a lion, but of a fox.
**T**he clever tricks and the hidden ways,
I knew them all; and I managed their art so well,
That my fame spread to the ends of the earth.
**W**hen I saw myself reaching that part
Of my life where every man should
Lower the sails and gather in the ropes, <note>A metaphor for retiring from worldly ambitions and preparing for death in old age.</note>
**T**hat which pleased me before now grieved me;
And repentant and confessed, I gave myself to God.
O wretch that I am! It would have been enough.
**T**he Prince of the new Pharisees, <note>Another reference to Pope Boniface VIII, suggesting he shared the hypocrisy of the biblical Pharisees.</note>

**F**or every enemy of his was a Christian;
And none of them had been to the conquest of Acre, <note>The Fall of Acre in 1291 was the final loss of the Crusader kingdom; the Pope is criticized for fighting fellow Christians instead of defending the Holy Land.</note>

**N**either his high office nor his sacred orders
Did he respect in himself, nor in me that cord
Which used to make its wearers thin. <note>The Franciscan cord was a symbol of poverty and fasting; Guido suggests the Pope disregarded the sanctity of the monastic life.</note>

<meta>This page continues the confession of Guido da Montefeltro in the eighth circle of Hell. ### HELL

**B**ut as Constantine sought out Sylvester
Within Soracte to cure his leprosy; <note>A reference to the legend that Emperor Constantine the Great sought out Pope Sylvester I on Mount Soracte to be baptized and cured of leprosy, leading to the "Donation of Constantine" which granted the Church secular power.</note>
So this man sought me out as a master
To cure the fever of his pride:
He asked me for advice; and I remained silent,
Because his words seemed like those of a drunkard:
**A**nd then he said to me: "Let your heart not fear:
From this moment I absolve you; now teach me how
To level Palestrina to the ground. <note>original: *Penestrino*. This refers to the stronghold of the Colonna family, which Pope Boniface VIII was determined to destroy during their bitter feud.</note>
I have the power to lock and unlock Heaven;
As you well know: for the keys are two, <note>The "Keys of St. Peter," symbolizing papal authority to forgive or retain sins.</note>
Which my predecessor did not hold dear." <note>A reference to Pope Celestine V, who abdicated the papacy in 1294, "refusing" the keys and the responsibility of the office.</note>
**T**hen his weighty arguments pushed me
To the point where silence seemed the worse choice:
And I said: "Father, since you wash me
Of that sin into which I must now fall;
A long promise with a short fulfillment <note>Guido's advice was to offer the Colonna family a full amnesty (the long promise) but then break the agreement once they surrendered (the short fulfillment).</note>
Will make you triumph upon the high seat."
**F**rancis came for me later, once I was dead, <note>St. Francis of Assisi, founder of the order Guido had joined.</note>
But one of the black Cherubim <note>A fallen angel; Dante often depicts demons as "black" counterparts to the celestial hierarchy.</note>
Said to him: "Do not take him: do not do me wrong.
**H**e must come down among my minions;
Because he gave the fraudulent advice,
Since which time I have been at his hair:
For one cannot be absolved who does not repent;
Nor can one repent and will the sin at once,
Because the contradiction does not allow it." <note>A point of scholastic logic: you cannot have the "will to sin" and "repentance for that sin" in your heart at the same moment; therefore, the Pope’s preemptive absolution was invalid.</note>
**O** miserable me, how I shuddered,
When he seized me, saying to me: "Perhaps
You did not think that I was a logician!"

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In wonder forgetting their martyrdom. <note>Dante often notes how the souls in Hell are so shocked by the sight of a living body that they momentarily forget their eternal agony.</note>
"**N**ow tell Fra Dolcino then, to arm himself,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;You who perhaps will see the sun shortly,

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Does not bring victory to the Novarese,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which otherwise would not be easy to win." <note>Muhammad warns Fra Dolcino, the leader of the "Apostolic Brethren" who advocated for communal property. **A**fter he had lifted one foot to go on,

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which was crimson on the outside in every part, <note>The physical mutilations of these shades reflect their sins: they used their tongues and ears to spread scandal and discord, so those organs are now hacked away.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Unless too much resemblance deceives me; <note>original: *terra Latina*. This refers to Italy, specifically the Romagna region where this shade lived.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That slopes from Vercelli to Marcabò." <note>Pier da Medicina was a notorious political meddler in the Romagna. The "sweet plain" he describes is the Po Valley, bounded by Vercelli in the west and the castle of Marcabò in the east.</note>

i 3

I made the father and the son rebels to each other;
**Ahithophel** did no more for **Absalom**
And for **David** with his wicked goadings. <note>original: "punzelli"—referring to the biblical story where Ahithophel incited Absalom to rebel against his father, King David. Dante parallels this with Bertran de Born, who encouraged the "Young King" Henry to rebel against Henry II of England.</note>
Because I parted persons so joined,
I carry my brain parted, alas,
From its source, which is in this trunk:
Thus is observed in me the <term>contrapasso</term>. <note>The law of "contrapasso" (retribution) is the guiding principle of Dante's Inferno: the punishment either mirrors the sin or stands in direct contrast to it. Here, because Bertran divided a family, his own body is divided.</note>

### XXIX.

The many people and the diverse wounds
Had made my eyes so "drunken," <note>original: "innebbriate"—Dante uses the metaphor of intoxication to describe the sensory and emotional overload caused by the sight of so much suffering.</note>
That they were eager to stay and weep;
But **Virgil** said to me: "What are you still gazing at?
Why does your sight still rest
Down there among the sad, mutilated shadows?
You did not do this at the other <term>bolge</term>; <note>A "bolgia" (plural "bolge") is a "ditch" or "pouch" in the eighth circle of Hell, where different types of fraud are punished.</note>
Consider, if you think to count them,
That the valley winds for twenty-two miles; <note>Dante provides specific measurements for the geography of Hell to give it a sense of physical reality; this ditch is 22 miles in circumference.</note>
And already the moon is beneath our feet;
The time allowed to us is short now,
And there is more to see than what you perceive."
"If you had," I replied thereafter,
"Attended to the reason why I was looking,
Perhaps you would have permitted me to stay longer."
Part of him was already going, and I followed behind him,
Already making my reply to the leader,
And adding: "Within that cavern,
Where I held my eyes so fixedly,
I believe a spirit of my own blood weeps <note>This refers to Geri del Bello, a first cousin of Dante's father, who was murdered and whose death had not yet been avenged by his family, according to the social codes of the time.</note>
The guilt that costs so much down there."

Then the master said: "Do not let your thoughts
