Right to the bottom, if there were more light.
When we were above the final cloister
Of **Malebolge**, <term>Malebolge</term> <note>Literally "Evil Pouches" or "Evil Ditches," this is the eighth circle of Hell where various types of fraud are punished.</note> so that its "lay brothers" <note>original: "conversi"—Dante uses monastic terminology (cloister and lay brothers) ironically to describe the ditch and the sinners trapped within it.</note>
Could be seen by our sight;
Diverse laments shot at me like arrows,
Which had their shafts tipped with pity;
So that I covered my ears with my hands.
Such pain as there would be if the illnesses
From the hospitals of **Valdichiana**, between July and September,
And of **Sardinia**, and the **Maremma**, <note>In Dante’s time, these three marshy regions of Italy were infamous for malaria and other pestilent diseases, especially during the heat of late summer.</note>
Were all together in one ditch;
Such it was here; and such a stench came from it
As usually comes from festering limbs.

Down toward the bottom, where the minister
Of the High Lord, infallible Justice,
Punishes the **falsifiers** <term>falsifiers</term> <note>In this final ditch of the eighth circle, Dante finds those who practiced various forms of deception that "corrupted" the world. I do not believe it was a greater sorrow to see
The entire people of **Aegina** <note>Aegina is a Greek island. Dante refers to a myth from Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* in which a plague sent by the goddess Juno wiped out the island's inhabitants. As the poets hold for certain,

The spirits languishing in various heaps.

One lay upon his belly, another upon the shoulders
Of his companion; and another on all fours
Shifted himself along the dismal path.
Step by step we went without speech,
Looking at and listening to the sick,
Who could not lift their own bodies.

I saw two sitting propped against each other,
As one props pan against pan to warm them,
Spotted from head to foot with scabs.
And I never saw a curry-comb <note>original: "stregghia"—a metal-toothed comb used for grooming horses.</note> handled
By a stable-boy whose master is waiting for him,
Nor by one who stays awake against his will,
As each of these plied the bite
Of his nails over himself, because of the great fury
Of the itching, which has no other relief.

**A**t the time when **Juno** <note>In Roman mythology, Juno was the queen of the gods, often portrayed as vengeful toward the lovers of her husband, Jupiter.</note> was enraged
For the sake of **Semele** against the **Theban** bloodline,

**S**eizing the one who was named **Learchus**,

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;see how it cuts across your great chest."

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;we found another giant, much fiercer and larger.

<note>The "beautiful planet" is Venus, associated with love, which appears as the morning star. The "Pisces" (the Fish) are dimmed by her light.</note>

<note>The "other pole" is the South Pole. The "four stars" are often interpreted as symbols of the four Cardinal Virtues: Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance. The "first people" refers to Adam and Eve, who lived in the Earthly Paradise at the top of this mountain before their fall.</note>
The heavens seemed to rejoice in their flames.
O widowed northern region,

When I had turned away from gazing at them,

There, where the Great Bear had already disappeared;
<note>original: "carro." Literally the "cart" or "wagon," referring to the Big Dipper/Ursa Major, which is not visible from the Southern Hemisphere.</note>

In order to return here another time," I said. 
<note>Casella was a renowned singer and composer in Florence and a friend of Dante. Dante suggests that by making this pilgrimage now, he hopes to secure his eventual return to Purgatory after death.</note> 
"But how has so much time been taken from you?" 
**A**nd he to me: "No wrong has been done to me, 
If he who takes up whom and when he pleases 
Has many times denied me this passage; 
**F**or his will is moved by a just power. 
Truly, for three months now, he has taken 
All who wished to enter, in total peace. 
<note>Casella refers to the "Celestial Pilot" (the angel) and the Jubilee year of 1300. During this holy year, the grace of the Church was expanded, allowing souls who had delayed their repentance to be transported to Purgatory more quickly.</note> 
**S**o I, who was then turned toward the seashore 
Where the water of the Tiber becomes salt, 
<note>original: "Teuere." The Tiber River flows from Rome to the sea at Ostia; Dante follows the tradition that the souls of the saved gather at the Tiber's mouth to be collected by the angel.</note> 
Was kindly gathered up by him."

<summary>Dante attempts to embrace the spirit of his friend, the musician Casella, and learns how the souls of the saved gather at the mouth of the Tiber to be transported to Purgatory.</summary>

<note>Acheron is the river in Greek mythology and Dante’s Inferno that the damned must cross to enter Hell. In contrast, those destined for Heaven gather at the mouth of the Tiber in Rome.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;My soul; which, coming here with its physical body,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Is so very exhausted."
<note>Dante is the only person in Purgatory who possesses a physical body of flesh and bone, which makes the climb and the journey much more tiring for him than for the spirits.</note>

<note>original: "Amor che ne la mente mi ragiona." This is the opening line of a poem Dante himself wrote, which his friend Casella had previously set to music.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Crying out: "What is this, you laggard spirits?
<note>The "venerable old man" is Cato of Utica, the guardian of the shores of Purgatory. He represents stoic discipline and moral rigor.</note>

<note>original: "scoglio." Literally a "slough" or the discarded skin of a snake. Cato uses this metaphor to describe the remnants of earthly sin that the souls must shed.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Because they are seized by a greater concern;
**S**o I saw that fresh company
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Leave the song, and go toward the slope,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Like a man who goes, and knows not where he will end:

<note>Vocabulary: **Acheron** (river of Hell), **Love who speaks within my mind** (Dante's poem), **laggard spirits** (those slow to repent), **Purgatory**, **Dante**, **Casella** (the singer), **Cato** (the guardian).</note>

->III<-

**A**lthough the sudden flight
    Scattered them across the plain,

<note>The "mountain" is Mount Purgatory. The souls are "goaded" or spurred by divine justice to begin their purification process after being scolded for their delay.</note>
**I** drew closer to my faithful companion:
    And how would I have run without him?

**H**e seemed to me remorseful within himself:
    O dignified and pure conscience,
    How bitter a sting is a small fault to you!
<note>Virgil feels guilty because he, the guide and symbol of Reason, allowed himself to be distracted by the beauty of Casella's song instead of focusing on the spiritual journey.</note>
**W**hen his feet left behind that haste,
    Which robs every act of its dignity;
    My mind, which before was restrained,
**W**idened its focus, as if eager;
    And I turned my face toward the hill
    That rises highest toward heaven out of the sea.
**T**he sun, which was flaming red behind me,
    Was broken in front of me by my shape,
    For I formed a barrier to its rays.
<note>Dante is physically alive, so his body blocks the light. In the afterlife, this is a startling sight because the spirits do not cast shadows.</note>
**I** turned to the side with fear
    Of being abandoned; when I saw
    The ground dark only in front of me:
**A**nd my comfort began to say to me,
    Turning fully: "Why do you still distrust?
    Do you not believe I am with you and that I guide you?
**I**t is already evening there, where the body
    Is buried within which I used to cast a shadow:
    Naples has it, and from Brindisi it was taken."
<note>Virgil explains that his physical body is buried in Naples. He died in Brindisi (Branditio) in 19 BCE while returning from Greece. Because he is now a spirit, the sun's rays pass through him without casting a shadow.</note>

<summary>As the souls rush toward the mountain of Purgatory, Dante notices he is the only one casting a shadow and fears Virgil has left him. Virgil reassures him, explaining that his own physical body is buried in Naples and that spirits do not block light.</summary>

# PURGATORY

### CANTO III

**N**ow no shadow falls before me;
    Do not marvel at this more than at the heavens,
    Where one sphere does not block the light of another.
**T**o suffer torments, heat, and frost,
    The Divine Power ordains such bodies as ours;
    How it does so, it does not wish to reveal to us.
<note>Virgil explains that although spirits are "airy" and do not cast shadows, God has granted them the ability to feel physical sensations like heat and cold so they may undergo purgation.</note>
**M**ad is he who hopes that our reason
    Can traverse the infinite path
    Held by one Substance in three Persons.
<note>This refers to the Mystery of the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit). Virgil warns that human logic cannot fully grasp divine truths.</note>
**S**tay content, human race, with the <term>quia</term>;
    For if you had been able to see everything,
    There was no need for Mary to give birth;
<note>The term <term>quia</term> (Latin for "because" or "the fact that") refers to a philosophical distinction: knowing *that* something is true without knowing the underlying *why*. Virgil argues that if humans could understand everything, Faith and the Incarnation of Christ would have been unnecessary.</note>
**A**nd you have seen desiring without fruit
    Those men whose desire would otherwise have been calmed,
    But which is now given to them as eternal grief:
**I** speak of Aristotle, and of Plato,
    And of many others"; and here he bowed his head,
    And said no more; and remained troubled.
<note>Virgil is "troubled" because he himself resides in Limbo with these great philosophers. Their "eternal grief" is the longing to see God, a desire that can never be satisfied because they lacked Christian faith.</note>
**W**e came, meanwhile, to the foot of the mountain;
    There we found the cliffside so steep
    That even the nimblest legs would be useless.
**B**etween Lerici and Turbia, the most deserted,
    The most solitary rock-fall is a staircase
    Easy and open, compared to that slope.
<note>Lerici and Turbia are the two ends of the rugged Ligurian coastline in Italy. Virgil uses this comparison to emphasize that the mountain of Purgatory is far steeper and more difficult to climb than the most treacherous cliffs on Earth.</note>
**"N**ow, who knows on which side the slope declines,"
    Said my master, halting his step,
    "So that he who travels without wings might climb?"
**A**nd while he, keeping his face cast down,
    Was searching his mind for a path,
    And I was looking up around the rock;

<summary>Virgil explains the limits of human reason regarding divine mysteries like the Trinity and describes the impossibility of climbing the steep base of Mount Purgatory through human effort alone.</summary>

On the left hand there appeared to me a crowd
Of souls, who moved their feet toward us;
And yet they did not seem to move, so slowly did they come.
"Lift," I said to the Master, "your eyes:
Look over here, those who will give us counsel,
If you cannot have it from your own self."
<note>Dante, seeing his guide Virgil is uncertain for the first time, points out a group of spirits who might know the path up the mountain.</note>
He looked at me then; and with a clear expression
He replied: "Let us go there, for they come slowly;
And you, strengthen your hope, sweet son."
That company was still as far away—
I mean after a thousand of our steps—
As a good thrower could reach with his hand,
<note>Dante uses the distance of a stone’s throw to emphasize that although the souls are moving toward them, their progress is incredibly slow and hesitant.</note>
When they all huddled against the hard rocks
Of the high cliff, and stood still and close together,
As one who walks in doubt stops to look.
"O souls who ended well, O spirits already chosen,"
Virgil began, "by that peace
Which I believe is awaited by you all,
<note>Virgil addresses them as "spirits already chosen" because, unlike those in Hell, these souls are destined for Heaven after their purification.</note>
Tell us where the mountain slopes
So that it may be possible to go upward;
For the loss of time most displeases him who knows most."
<note>Virgil’s remark that "loss of time displeases him who knows most" reflects the medieval idea that time is a precious gift from God, and every moment in Purgatory is a step toward salvation.</note>
As the little sheep come out from the fold
By ones, by twos, by threes; and the others stand
Timidly, casting down their eyes and muzzles;
And what the first one does, the others do,
Huddling against her if she stops,
Simple and quiet; and they do not know the why;
<note>This famous simile compares the souls to a flock of sheep. It illustrates their newfound humility and their need for leadership, contrasting with the prideful nature they might have had in life.</note>
So I saw then the head move to come
Of that fortunate flock,
Modest in face, and dignified in movement.

<note>Virgil reassures the souls that Dante’s presence is divinely ordained, using "this wall" to refer to the steep, seemingly impassable cliffs of the mountain.</note>

<note>This explains the rule of "Ante-Purgatory": those who delayed their repentance must wait outside the gates for a period thirty times longer than the time they lived in rebellion against the Church.</note>

<note>Constance was Manfred's daughter. He asks Dante to tell her he is in Purgatory (saved) rather than Hell, so she may pray for him.</note>

<note>Manfred highlights the "doctrine of suffrage," the belief that the prayers of the living can shorten the time a soul spends in Purgatory.</note>

### CANTO IV

->P V R G.<-

m 2

When, through delights or perhaps through pains,
    Which any one of our faculties perceives,
    The soul gathers itself entirely to that one;
<margin>P</margin> It seems to attend to no other power:
    And this refutes that error which believes
    That one soul is kindled above another within us.
<note>Dante is arguing against the Platonic idea that humans have multiple souls (vegetative, sensitive, and intellectual). He follows the Aristotelian/Thomistic view that the soul is a single unit; when we are fully focused on one sense, the whole soul is "bound" to it.</note>
<margin>E</margin> And therefore, when something is heard or seen
    That keeps the soul strongly turned toward it,
    Time passes, and the man does not realize it;
<margin>C</margin> For the power that listens is one thing,
    And that which keeps the soul whole is another:
    The latter is as if bound, and the former is free.
<margin>D</margin> I had a true experience of this
    While listening to that spirit and marveling;
    For the sun had already climbed fully
<margin>L</margin> Fifty degrees, and I had not noticed,
    When we came to where those souls, as one,
    Cried out to us: "Here is what you requested."
<note>In Dante’s time, the sky was measured in degrees. Since the sun moves 15 degrees per hour, "fifty degrees" means about three hours and twenty minutes have passed since sunrise.</note>
<margin>M</margin> A man from the village often closes
    A larger gap in a hedge with a small forkful
    Of his thorns, when the grapes are darkening,
<margin>C</margin> Than was the narrow path through which
    My leader climbed, and I after him, alone,
    Once the troop of spirits had departed from us.
<margin>V</margin> One can go to San Leo; one can descend to Noli;
    One can climb to the very peak of Bismantova
    With just their feet; but here, a man must fly—
<note>Dante names three notoriously steep or difficult places in Italy: San Leo (a fortress on a cliff), Noli (a town on the Ligurian coast reached by steep paths), and Bismantova (a massive rock plateau).</note>
<margin>D</margin> I mean with the swift wings and with the feathers
    Of great desire, following behind that guide
    Who gave me hope and provided light.

### CANTO IV

->P V R G.<-

We were climbing through the broken rock;
    And from every side the edge hemmed us in;
    And the ground below required both feet and hands.
<note>The ascent is so steep that Dante must scramble on all fours, using his hands for leverage.</note>
When we reached the top edge of the high bank, 
    Out upon the open slope;
    "My Master," I said, "what way shall we take?"
And he to me: "Let none of your steps fail;
    Just keep gaining ground up the mountain behind me,
    Until some wise guide appears to us."
The summit was so high it defeated my sight;
    And the slope was far steeper by far
    Than a line from the midpoint of a quadrant to the center.
<note>Dante uses a geometric metaphor here. A quadrant is 90 degrees; half of that is 45 degrees. He is saying the mountain's incline is much steeper than a 45-degree angle.</note>
I was weary, when I began:
    "O sweet father, turn and look
    How I remain alone, if you do not stop."
"O son," he said, "pull yourself up as far as here,"
    Pointing out a ledge a little higher up,
    Which circles the whole mountain on that side.
His words so spurred me on
    That I forced myself to crawl after him
    Until the ledge was beneath my feet.
There we both sat down,
    Facing the east, from where we had ascended;
    For looking back usually brings comfort to a man.
First I directed my eyes to the low shores;
    Then I raised them to the sun, and I was amazed
    That we were being struck by its rays from the left.
<note>Dante is confused because he is now in the Southern Hemisphere. In the North, if you face East, the sun appears to your right (the South). Here, the sun appears to his left (the North).</note>
The poet well noticed that I stood
    Completely bewildered by the chariot of light,
    Where it entered between us and the north wind.
<note>original: "aquilone" — This is a classical term for the North Wind, used here to indicate the direction of the North.</note>

### CANTO IV

->P V R G.<-

To which he replied to me: "If Castor and Pollux
    Were in the company of that mirror
    Which conducts its light both up and down,
<note>Castor and Pollux represent the constellation Gemini. Virgil is explaining that if the Sun (the 'mirror') were currently in the sign of Gemini—which is closer to the summer solstice—it would appear even further to the North from their current position in the Southern Hemisphere.</note>

<note>The 'Bears' refers to Ursa Major and Minor, the constellations used to find the North Star. The 'ancient path' is the Ecliptic, the sun's apparent path through the sky.</note>

<note>original: "Pheton". In Greek myth, Phaethon was the son of Apollo who lost control of the sun-chariot. Virgil uses this to describe the Ecliptic (the sun's path). He explains that Purgatory and Jerusalem are at exact opposite points on the globe.</note>

    Which is called the Equator in certain sciences,

<note>Dante realizes he is looking at the celestial equator. Because they are in the Southern Hemisphere, the sun appears to the north, whereas in Jerusalem (the North), it appears to the south.</note>
For the reason you say, departs from here

<note>original: "Hebrei". Dante uses the Hebrews to represent the inhabitants of the Northern Hemisphere (centered on Jerusalem). The 'warm region' refers to the South.</note>
But if it pleases you, I would willingly know
    How far we have to go; for the hill rises
    Higher than my eyes can reach."
And he to me: "This mountain is such,
    That it is always difficult at the start below;
    But the further one climbs, the less it hurts.
<note>Virgil provides a famous spiritual lesson: the climb toward virtue is exhausting and painful at first, but as a person purifies themselves of sin, the ascent becomes natural and effortless.</note>

    That the upward journey feels as light
    As a ship moving downstream with the current;
<note>Virgil explains a spiritual law of Purgatory: as a soul is purified of sin, the physical effort of the climb decreases.</note>
**T**hen you will be at the end of this path:
    There, you may expect to rest your weariness:
    I answer no more; and this I know for truth."
**A**nd as he had finished saying these words,
    A voice sounded nearby: "Perhaps
    You will have need of sitting down before then."
<note>This voice introduces the character of Belacqua, whose defining trait is his extreme lethargy.</note>
**A**t the sound of it, each of us turned;
    And we saw on the left a great rock,
<note>original: "petrone". A large, rugged stone or boulder.</note>
    Which neither I nor he had noticed before.
**W**e drew near to it: and there were people
    Who were standing in the shade behind the rock,
    Just as a man through negligence might position himself.
<note>original: "neghienza". These are the Negligent, those who delayed their repentance out of laziness or preoccupation until their final moments.</note>
**A**nd one of them, who seemed weary to me,
    Was sitting and embracing his knees,
    Holding his face down low between them.
"**O** my sweet lord," I said, "look there
    At him, who shows himself more negligent
    Than if Laziness herself were his sister."
<note>original: "pigritia". Dante is mocking the soul's posture, which embodies the vice of sloth.</note>
**T**hen he turned toward us, and paid attention,
    Moving his face only up along his thigh,
    And said: "Go on up then, you who are so valiant."
**I** knew then who he was; and that breathlessness,
<note>original: "angoscia". Here meaning the physical distress and heavy breathing caused by the steep climb.</note>
    Which still made my breathing a bit heavy,
    Did not prevent me from going to him; and after
**I** had reached him, he barely raised his head,
    Saying: "Have you truly seen how the sun
    Drives his chariot past your left shoulder?"
<note>Belacqua is teasing Dante. Earlier, Dante was amazed by the sun's position in the Southern Hemisphere; Belacqua mocks him for being so fascinated by basic celestial facts while ignoring the people around him.</note>

<summary>Virgil explains that the climb will become easier as they ascend, only to be interrupted by the sarcastic voice of Belacqua, a lethargic friend of Dante found among the Negligent.</summary>
<keywords>Belacqua, Ante-Purgatory, Negligence, Sloth, Virgil, celestial geography, Southern Hemisphere</keywords>

->P V R G.<-

His lazy gestures and his brief words
> Moved my lips a little to a smile;
> Then I began: "Belacqua, I do not grieve
For you anymore; but tell me, why are you seated
> Right here? Are you waiting for an escort?
> Or has your old habit simply overtaken you again?"
<note>Belacqua was a Florentine instrument maker known for his extreme indolence; Dante is relieved to find his friend among the saved, even if he is in the waiting area of Purgatory.</note>
And he: "Brother, what is the use of going up?
> For the bird of God, who sits upon the gate,
> Would not let me pass through to the penances."
<note>original: "L'uccel di Dio". This refers to the Angel Porter who guards the entrance to Purgatory proper.</note>
"First, the heavens must circle around me
> Outside that gate, for as long as they did in life,
> Because I delayed my holy sighs until the end;"
<note>Those who waited until the very end of their lives to repent must wait in Ante-Purgatory for a duration equal to their lifespan on Earth.</note>
"Unless a prayer helps me first,
> One that rises from a heart that lives in grace;
> What value has any other, which is not heard in heaven?"
And already the poet was climbing ahead of me,
> And saying: "Come now; see that the sun
> Has touched the meridian, and from the shore,
> Night already covers Morocco with her foot."
<note>Dante uses astronomical positioning to tell time: if the sun is at the meridian (noon) in Purgatory, it is midnight in Jerusalem and evening in Morocco (the western edge of the known world).</note>

### V.

I had already departed from those shades,
> And was following the footsteps of my leader,
> When behind me, pointing his finger,
One cried out: "Look, the ray of light does not seem
> To shine on the left of the one below;
> And he moves as if he were still alive!"
<note>The souls are shocked to see that Dante casts a shadow, which signifies he is a living man of flesh and blood, unlike their own translucent spirit-bodies.</note>
I turned my eyes at the sound of these words,
> And I saw them watching in amazement
> Only me, only me, and the light that was broken.
<note>original: "il lume, ch'era rotto". The "broken light" is the shadow Dante's body casts on the ground.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Thought always pushes his goal further away,

### VI.

When the game of <term>Zara</term> breaks up,
<note>Zara was a popular medieval game played with three dice. It was a game of chance and skill often played in taverns.</note>
The one who loses remains behind, grieving,
Repeating the throws, and sadly learns his lesson;
With the winner, all the people go along:
One goes in front, another grabs him from behind,
Another at his side reminds him of himself;
He does not stop, and listens to this one and that;
Those to whom he gives his hand no longer press him;
And so he defends himself from the crowd:
<note>Dante compares himself to a winning gambler being mobbed by hangers-on. The "hand" he gives is a promise to pray for them or carry news of them back to the living.</note>
Such was I in that dense throng,
Turning my face to them here and there,
And by promising, I freed myself from them.
There was the Aretine, who at the fierce arms
Of <term>Ghin di Tacco</term> met his death;
<note>Ghin di Tacco was a famous "gentleman thief" or brigand of the era who murdered the judge Benincasa of Arezzo (the "Aretine") in revenge for the execution of his family members.</note>
And the other, who drowned while giving chase.
There Federigo Novello was praying with outstretched hands;
And the one from Pisa,
Who made the good Marzucco appear strong.
<note>This refers to Farinata degli Scornigiani. His father, Marzucco, showed "strength" by either forgiving his son's murderer or by showing extraordinary stoicism at his funeral.</note>
I saw Count Orso; and the soul divided
From its body through spite and envy,
As he said, and not for any fault committed:
<note>Count Orso was murdered by his cousin. The "soul divided... through spite" refers to Pierre de la Brosse, a chamberlain to the King of France, who claimed he was framed and executed due to the envy of the Queen.</note>

<summary>This page concludes the stories of those who died by violence with the poignant plea of Pia de' Tolomei, then transitions into Canto VI, depicting Dante being mobbed by souls seeking the prayers of the living.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Canto VI of the Purgatorio. On the previous page, Dante was mobbed by the souls of those who died by violence but repented at the last moment. ->P V R G.<-
<note>Abbreviation for *Purgatorio* (Purgatory).</note>

**P**ierre de la Brosse, I say; and let the Lady of Brabant
<note>original: "Pier da la Broccia." Pierre was the chamberlain of King Philip III of France, executed in 1278. The "Lady of Brabant" is Mary of Brabant, the queen, who was accused by some of being responsible for his death. Dante suggests she should repent now to avoid a worse fate in the afterlife.</note>
See to it, while she is still here,
So that for this she does not end up in a worse flock.
**A**s soon as I was free from every one of
Those shades, who prayed only that others might pray for them,
So that their progress toward holiness might be hastened;
**I** began: "It seems to me that you deny,
O my light, expressly in a certain text,
That the decree of heaven can be bent by prayer;
<note>Dante is referring to a line in Virgil's *Aeneid* (Book VI, 376), where the Sibyl tells the shade Palinurus that the decrees of the gods cannot be changed by human entreaty.</note>
**A**nd yet these people pray for exactly this.
Would their hope, then, be in vain?
Or is your meaning not fully clear to me?"
**A**nd he to me: "My writing is plain,
And the hope of these souls does not fail,
If one looks closely with a sound mind:
**F**or the high peak of justice is not lowered
Because the fire of love fulfills in a single moment
The debt that those who stay here must satisfy.
<note>Virgil explains that while the "decree" (Justice) remains firm, a prayer from a living person—motivated by love—can satisfy the "debt" of time a soul owes in Purgatory instantly, rather than through years of waiting.</note>
**A**nd in that place where I established that point,
The fault could not be mended by prayer,
Because the prayer was disconnected from God.
<note>original: "perche 'l prego da Dio era disgiunto." Virgil clarifies that the prayers mentioned in his poem, the *Aeneid*, were pagan and lacked the grace of the Christian God, making them ineffective.</note>
**T**ruly, regarding such a profound doubt,
Do not settle your mind until she tells you—
She who shall be a light between the truth and the intellect.
**I** do not know if you understand: I speak of Beatrice;
You shall see her above, on the summit
Of this mountain, smiling and happy."
**A**nd I: "Good Guide, let us go with greater speed,
For I no longer grow weary as I did before;
And see how the mountain already casts its shadow."
<note>Dante notices the sun is shifting. In Purgatory, souls can only climb while the sun (symbolizing God's grace) is shining.</note>

<summary>Dante questions Virgil about whether prayer can truly change divine decrees, as Virgil's own poetry once suggested it could not. Virgil explains that the power of love in Christian prayer can satisfy divine justice, but reminds Dante that Beatrice will provide the final clarity on the matter.</summary>

"We shall go forward with this day,"

Ship without a pilot in a great storm,
Not lady of provinces, but a brothel!
<note>original: "bordello." Dante uses this harsh term to describe how Italy, once the ruler of the Roman world, has sold herself to various political factions and foreign interests.</note>
That noble soul was so ready,
Only for the sweet sound of his land,
To welcome his fellow citizen here:

--- Page 211 ---
<meta>This page continues Dante’s famous invective against Italy in Canto VI. On the previous page, the shade of Sordello embraced Virgil simply because they were both from Mantua. This display of civic love prompted Dante to contrast it with the bitter civil wars currently tearing Italy apart.</meta>

->P V R G.<-
<note>Abbreviation for *Purgatorio* (Purgatory).</note>

**A**nd now within you, those who live do not stay
Without war; and one gnaws at the other,
Even of those whom one wall and one moat enclose.
<note>Dante laments that even within the same fortified city, citizens are killing one another in civil strife.</note>
**S**earch, wretched one, all around the shores
Of your seas; and then look into your own heart,
To see if any part of you enjoys peace.
**W**hat does it matter that Justinian repaired
The bit, if the saddle is empty?
Without that law, the shame would at least be less.
<note>Justinian (reigned 527–565 AD) was the Byzantine Emperor who codified Roman law. Dante argues that having good laws (the "bit") is useless if there is no Emperor (the rider) to enforce them; in fact, having the law makes the lawlessness even more shameful because the people know better.</note>
**A**h, people who ought to be devout,
And let Caesar sit in the saddle,
If you well understood what God marks out for you!
<note>Dante addresses the Church leadership, who he believes should stay out of secular politics ("let Caesar sit") and focus on spiritual matters as commanded by the Gospel.</note>
**L**ook how this beast has become wild and wicked,
By not being corrected by the spurs,
Ever since you laid your hand upon the bridle.
<note>The "beast" is Italy. The "bridle" represents the control the Church has taken over secular government, which Dante believes has prevented the Emperor from "riding" and ruling effectively.</note>
**O** Albert the German, you who abandon
This woman who has become untamed and savage,
When you should have bestridden her saddle-bows;
<note>Albert I of Anjou (reigned 1298–1308) was the Holy Roman Emperor who never traveled to Italy to be crowned, leaving the country to descend into chaos.</note>
**M**ay a just judgment fall from the stars
Upon your blood; and let it be strange and clear,
Such that your successor may have fear of it:
<note>Dante is writing after Albert's assassination in 1308, seeing it as a divine punishment that should serve as a warning to the next Emperor, Henry VII.</note>
**F**or you and your father, through greed
For territories back there, have suffered
The garden of the Empire to be laid waste.
<note>original: "costa' distretti." Albert and his father, Rudolph I, were accused of being too concerned with their German/Austrian lands ("back there") to care for Italy, which Dante calls the "garden of the Empire."</note>
**C**ome to see the Montagues and the Capulets,
The Monaldi and the Filippeschi, O man without care:
Those already grieving, and these in fearful suspicion!
<note>These were famous feuding families of the time. The Montagues and Capulets (Montecchi and Cappelletti) were rival factions in Verona; the Monaldi and Filippeschi were rival factions in Orvieto. Dante uses them as examples of the ruinous effects of political neglect.</note>
**C**ome, cruel man, come and see the oppression
Of your nobles; and tend to their wounds;
And you shall see how secure is Santa Fiora!
<note>Santa Fiora was a county near Siena, once powerful but at this time ruined and lawless due to the absence of Imperial authority. Dante uses "secure" sarcastically.</note>

<summary>Dante delivers a scathing political critique of Italy, lamenting its civil wars and blaming the Holy Roman Emperor Albert I for neglecting his duties. He uses the metaphor of an unridden, wild horse to describe the lawless state of the Italian peninsula.</summary>
<keywords>Justinian, Albert I of Germany, Caesar, Montecchi, Cappelletti, Monaldi, Philippeschi, Santa Fiora, Italian politics, Holy Roman Empire, Canto VI</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Dante’s scathing address to the political leaders of his time and his lament over the state of Italy. Having previously criticized the Emperor Albert for neglecting the "garden of the Empire," Dante now turns his gaze toward Rome and his own home city of Florence.</meta>

->P V R G.<-
<note>Abbreviation for *Purgatorio* (Purgatory).</note>

**C**ome see your Rome, who weeps,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;A lonely widow, and calls day and night:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;“My Caesar, why do you not stay with me?”
<note>Dante personifies Rome as a widow because it was abandoned by both the Popes (who had moved to Avignon) and the Holy Roman Emperors (who remained in Germany).</note>
**C**ome see the people, how much they love one another!
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And if no pity for us moves you,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Come to feel shame for your own reputation.
<note>This is biting sarcasm; Dante refers to the bloody civil wars between rival factions like the Guelphs and Ghibellines.</note>
**A**nd if it is permitted for me, O supreme Jove,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Who was crucified on earth for our sake,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Are your righteous eyes turned elsewhere?
<note>original: "sommo Gioue" (Supreme Jove). Dante frequently uses the name of the king of the Roman gods to refer to the Christian God, reflecting the Renaissance bridge between Classical and Christian thought.</note>
**O**r is it a preparation that you make,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In the abyss of your counsel, for some good purpose
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Completely cut off from our understanding?
**F**or the cities of Italy are all full
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Of tyrants; and every peasant who plays the partisan
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Becomes a Metellus.
<note>Metellus was a Roman tribune who unsuccessfully tried to prevent Julius Caesar from seizing the state treasury. Dante uses him here to describe low-born, local agitators who suddenly seize power and act like grand political figures.</note>
**M**y Florence, you may well be content
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;With this digression, which does not touch you—
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Thanks to your people, who are so industrious!
<note>Dante pivots to a deeply ironic "praise" of Florence, his home city, which he believes is the worst example of political instability.</note>
**M**any have justice in their hearts, but it shoots late,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For they do not come to the bow without careful counsel;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But your people have it right on the tip of their tongues.
**M**any refuse the public burden;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But your people answer eagerly
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Without being called, and say, "I'll take it on!"
**N**ow make yourself happy, for you have good reason:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;You rich, you at peace, you so wise!
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;If I speak the truth, the result does not hide it.
**A**thens and Lacedaemon, which made
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The ancient laws and were so civilized,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Made only a small hint at living well
<note>Lacedaemon is the ancient name for Sparta. Dante suggests that even the greatest law-giving civilizations of history were nothing compared to the "reforms" of Florence—a statement meant as a mocking insult.</note>

<summary>In this passage from Canto VI of Purgatorio, Dante continues his political invective, calling upon the Emperor to witness the desolation of Rome and using heavy irony to mock the political chaos and self-righteousness of Florence.</summary>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Does not even reach mid-November.

### VII.

**A**fter the greetings, dignified and joyful,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Were repeated three and four times,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Sordello drew back and said: "Who are you?"
**"B**efore the souls worthy of ascending to God
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Were turned toward this mountain,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;My bones were buried by Octavian.
<note>original: "Ottauian" refers to Octavian, better known as the Emperor Augustus, who ruled when Virgil died in 19 BCE.</note>
**I** am Virgil; and for no other sin
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Did I lose heaven, than for not having faith."
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Thus did my leader then reply.
**L**ike one who suddenly sees something
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Before him, which makes him marvel,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Who believes and does not, saying: "It is, it is not";
**S**o did that one appear: and then he lowered his brow,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And humbly turned back toward him,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And embraced him where the inferior takes hold.
<note>To show deep respect and acknowledge Virgil's superior status, Sordello embraces Virgil's knees or feet rather than his chest.</note>
**"O** glory of the Latins," he said, "through whom
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Our language showed all that it could do;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;O eternal honor of the place where I was born,
<note>original: "Latin." In this context, it refers to the Italian people and the Roman heritage they shared.</note>

<summary>This page concludes Dante's satirical attack on the instability of Florence before beginning Canto VII, where Virgil identifies himself to Sordello, prompting a display of profound reverence from the later poet.</summary>

--- Page 214 ---
<meta>This page continues the encounter between Sordello and Virgil. Sordello, having just discovered the identity of his fellow Mantuan, expresses his awe. Virgil then describes his eternal dwelling in Limbo and asks for guidance toward the gate of Purgatory.</meta>

->PVRG.<-
<note>Abbreviation for *Purgatorio*.</note>

"What merit, or what grace shows you to me?
If I am worthy to hear your words;
Tell me if you come from Hell, or from what cloister."
<note>original: "chiostra" (cloister). Sordello asks which specific circle or "enclosure" of the afterlife Virgil inhabits.</note>
**P**hrough all the circles of the sorrowful kingdom,
He replied to him, "I have come here:
Power from heaven moved me; and with it I come.
**N**ot for doing, but for not doing <note>Virgil refers to his lack of Christian faith, rather than any active sin.</note> I lost
The sight of the high Sun, which you desire,
And which was known by me too late.
<note>The "Sun" is a frequent metaphor in the Divine Comedy for God and Divine Illumination.</note>
**L**ow down there is a place not saddened by torments,
But by darkness only; where the laments
Do not sound like wails, but are only sighs.
<note>Virgil describes Limbo, the first circle of Hell, where the inhabitants do not suffer physical pain but feel the eternal grief of being separated from God.</note>
**T**here I stay with the innocent little ones
Bitten by the teeth of death before
They were exempt from human guilt.
<note>original: "humana colpa." This refers to unbaptized infants who, according to medieval theology, still bore the weight of Original Sin.</note>
**T**here I stay with those who did not clothe themselves
In the three holy virtues, yet without vice
Knew the others, and followed every one.
<note>The "three holy virtues" are the theological virtues of Faith, Hope, and Charity. The "others" are the four cardinal virtues: Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance.</note>
**B**ut if you know, and are permitted, give us
Some sign; so that we may arrive more quickly
There, where Purgatory has its true beginning."
**H**e replied: "No fixed place is set for us:
It is permitted for me to go up, and around:
As far as I may go, I join you as a guide.
**B**ut see now, how the day declines;
And to go up by night is not possible:
Therefore it is good to think of a fine resting place.
<note>The "Rule of the Mountain": in Dante's Purgatory, souls can only ascend while the sun is shining, symbolizing that one cannot progress toward God without the light of Divine Grace.</note>
**T**here are souls to the right here, set apart:
If you permit me, I will lead you to them;
And not without delight will they be known to you."

<summary>Virgil explains to Sordello that he dwells in Limbo among the virtuous pagans and unbaptized infants. Sordello explains that they cannot ascend the mountain after sunset and offers to lead them to a valley of noble souls for the night.</summary>
<keywords>Virgil, Sordello, Limbo, Virtues, Rule of the Mountain, sunset, Purgatorio, Divine Grace</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Virgil and the Mantuan poet Sordello on the lower slopes of Mount Purgatory. Following Virgil's explanation of his residence in Limbo, the conversation shifts to the practicalities of ascending the mountain.</meta>

->PVRG.<-
<note>Abbreviation for *Purgatorio*, the second part of Dante Alighieri’s *Divine Comedy*.</note>

"How is that?" was the reply: "If one wished
To climb at night, would he be hindered
By another? Or is it that he simply could not?"
And the good Sordello <note>A 13th-century troubadour and poet who acts as a guide for Dante and Virgil in this section of the poem.</note> traced his finger on the ground,
Saying, "Look; not even this line
Would you cross once the sun has departed;
Not that anything else would offer hindrance
To going upward, except the darkness of night:
That, by the lack of power, thwarts the will.
<note>Sordello explains the "Law of the Mountain": in Purgatory, souls can only ascend while the sun is shining. The Sun represents Divine Grace, without which human effort cannot move toward God.</note>
One could indeed go downward during it,
And wander around the mountainside,
As long as the horizon keeps the day shut away."
Then my lord <note>Dante's address for Virgil.</note>, as if in wonder,
Said, "Lead us, then, to where you say
That one may find delight while waiting."
We had gone but a short distance from there,
When I noticed that the mountain was hollowed out,
In the same way that valleys are hollowed here on earth.
"There," said that shade, "we shall go,
Where the slope makes a lap of itself;
And there we shall await the new day."
Between the steep and the level was a winding path,
Which led us to the side of that hollow,
To the point where the rim almost disappears.
Gold and fine silver, scarlet dye <note>original: "cocco." A red dye derived from insects, highly valued in the Middle Ages.</note> and white lead <note>original: "biacca." A white pigment used in painting.</note>,
Shining and clear Indian wood <note>original: "Indico legno." Thought to refer to ebony or perhaps indigo, representing deep blues or dark lustrous tones.</note>,
Fresh emerald at the moment it is split,
By the grass and by the flowers placed within that fold,
Would each be surpassed in color,
As the lesser is always surpassed by the greater.

<meta>This page continues the scene in the Valley of the Rulers. Virgil and Dante are being guided by Sordello, who is about to identify the famous monarchs who delayed their repentance due to the burdens of statecraft.</meta>

<note>Abbreviation for *Purgatorio*.</note>

**N**ature had not only painted there with colors;
But from the sweetness of a thousand scents,
She made there a single, blended fragrance.
<note>Dante describes how the valley appeals to all senses, not just sight.</note>
**H**ail, Queen <note>original: "Salve Regina." A Latin antiphon or hymn to the Virgin Mary, traditionally sung at Compline (the final prayer of the day), fitting for the twilight setting.</note> on the green grass and among the flowers,
I saw souls sitting there and singing;
Who, because of the valley's depth, were not visible from without.

**T**he other, who appears to comfort him,
Ruled the land where the water is born

**H**is name was Ottokar <note>Ottokar II of Bohemia, a rival of Rudolf.</note>; and even in swaddling clothes

**A**nd that small-nosed one <note>Philip III "the Bold" of France.</note>; who seems in close counsel

<note>Philip III died in retreat during the Aragonese Crusade; the "lily" refers to the fleur-de-lis of the French monarchy, which Dante suggests he shamed.</note>
**L**ook there, see how he beats his breast.
See the other, who, sighing, has made a bed
For his cheek with the palm of his hand.

### PURGATORIO
<note>Abbreviation for Purgatorio, the second part of Dante Alighieri’s Divine Comedy.</note>
<meta>Catchword: The one</meta>

**I**t was already the hour that turns back the longing 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Of those at sea, and softens the heart 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On the day they have said goodbye to their sweet friends;

**W**hen I began to render my hearing 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Useless, and to gaze at one of the souls

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Fixing her eyes toward the East,

<note>Dante often pauses to warn the reader that the literal story hides a deeper allegorical meaning.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Were their robes, which, struck by green wings, 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Were trailed behind and fanned by the breeze.

"Oh," I said to him, "through your lands

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Now here, now there, to the side that recedes." <note>This narrow, winding path requires the travelers to physically adjust to the shape of the rock, symbolizing the "art" or discipline required to navigate the difficult start of their spiritual ascent.</note>

There was storied the high glory
Of the Roman prince, whose great worth
Moved Gregory to his great victory: <note>original: "gran vittoria"; This refers to the medieval legend that Pope Gregory the Great was so moved by the justice of Emperor Trajan that he prayed for Trajan's soul to be released from Limbo and returned to life so he could convert and be saved.</note>

I speak of the Emperor Trajan;
And a poor widow was at his bridle,
In an attitude of tears and of grief.

Around him the space seemed trampled and full
Of knights; and the eagles in gold <note>The "aquila," the standard of the Roman Empire.</note>
Above him, to the sight, moved in the wind.

The poor woman, among all these,
Seemed to say: “Lord, grant me vengeance
For my son who is dead, for which my heart breaks.”

And he answered her: “Now wait
Until I return.” And she: “My lord,”
Like a person in whom grief is urgent,

“If you do not return?” And he: “He who will be where I am
Will do it for you.” And she: “What will another’s
Good deed be to you, if you forget your own?”

Whereupon he: “Now be comforted, for it is right
That I fulfill my duty before I move:
Justice wills it, and pity holds me back.”

He who never saw a new thing <note>This refers to God, the Creator, to whom all things across time are known.</note>
Produced this **visible speech**, <note>original: "visibile parlare"; Dante describes the carvings as a divine miracle where the art is so perfect that it communicates sound and movement directly to the mind.</note>
New to us, because it is not found here on earth.

While I delighted in looking
At the images of such great humilities,
And, for their Craftsman’s sake, dear to see; <note>The "Craftsman" is God, who carved these reliefs into the mountain.</note>

“Behold, on this side—but they take slow steps,”
The poet murmured, “many people:
These will direct us to the high stairs.” <note>The stairs leading to the second terrace of Purgatory.</note>

### XI.

O our Father, you who dwell in the heavens,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Not limited by space, but through the greater love
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;You have for your first creations up above; <note>God is "not circumscribed" (non circonscritto) because He is infinite; He dwells in the highest heavens because of His love for the "first effects"—the angels and the celestial spheres.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;By every creature, as it is only right
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To give thanks to your sweet breath. <note>original: "dolce uapore"; This term refers to the Holy Spirit or the divine grace that emanates from God like a life-giving mist.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;If it does not come to us, despite all our intellect.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Of their own will to you, singing **Hosanna**; <note>original: "Osanna"; A Hebrew cry of praise meaning "Save, we pray." In the liturgy, it represents the joyful submission of the angels to God's will.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So may men do the same with theirs.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;He who most labors to advance goes backward.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Kind as you are, and look not at our merit.
Our virtue, which is easily overcome,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Do not put to the test with the ancient adversary; <note>original: "antico auersaro"; The Devil or Satan.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But deliver us from him who so goads it.

### XII.

Side by side, like oxen that go in a yoke,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I moved along with that burdened soul,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As long as my sweet teacher <term>pedagogo</term> <note>original: "pedagogo"; used here in the classical sense of a tutor or guardian who guides a child.</note> permitted it;

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;With my body; although my thoughts
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Remained both bowed down and diminished. <note>Though Dante physically straightens up, his mind remains humbled by the examples of the prideful souls he has encountered.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The steps of my master; and both of us
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Already showed how light we were;

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;It will be good for you, to ease the journey,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To see the bed beneath the soles of your feet."

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Like a bolt of lightning on one side. <note>This is Lucifer, whose fall from grace is the ultimate example of pride punished.</note>

<margin>B</margin>He well knew what the mute one <note>Dante refers to himself; though he had not spoken, his facial expression revealed his inner conflict at watching the blind souls.</note> meant to say: and therefore he did not wait for my question, but said: "Speak, and be brief and to the point."

<margin>V</margin>Virgil was walking along that side of the terrace from which one could fall, because it is not circled by any railing <note>The outer edge of the terrace has no parapet, leaving it open to the sheer drop of the mountain.</note>;

<margin>D</margin>on the other side were the devout shades, who through that horrible stitching were pressing so hard that they bathed their cheeks with tears.

<margin>V</margin>I turned to them and began, "O people certain of seeing the High Light <note>The "High Light" refers to the vision of God, which these souls are guaranteed to reach eventually.</note>, which is the only thing your desire cares for;

<margin>S</margin>so may grace soon dissolve the scum of your conscience <note>Dante prays that God's grace will quickly purify their sins, allowing their memories and thoughts to become clear and holy.</note>, so that the river of the mind may flow clearly through it;

<margin>D</margin>tell me (for it will be gracious and dear to me) if any soul is here among you who is Latin <note>original: "Latina"; in this context, Dante is asking if any of the souls are from Italy.</note>: and perhaps it will be good for them if I learn of it."

<margin>O</margin>"O my brother, each one is a citizen of a true city <note>The soul's response emphasizes that in the afterlife, earthly nationalities no longer matter; they are all citizens of the Heavenly Jerusalem.</note>: but you mean one who lived in Italy as a pilgrim <note>Medieval theology viewed life on earth as a "pilgrimage" toward the soul's true home in heaven.</note>."

<margin>Q</margin>This I seemed to hear as an answer somewhat further on than where I was standing: so I made myself heard even further in that direction.

<summary>Dante describes the Envious, whose eyes are sewn shut with iron wire, and seeks to find an Italian soul among them. A spirit responds by correcting Dante's earthly perspective, noting that all souls are now citizens of the City of God.</summary>

Just as a ray of light comes to a bright body.

The eternal value grows above it.

<meta>This page continues the conversation between Dante and the soul of Marco Lombardo in the Third Terrace of Purgatory. On the previous page, Dante expressed his confusion regarding the cause of human wickedness—whether it stems from the influence of the stars or from human choice. Marco now begins his profound explanation of free will.</meta>

->PURGATORY<-

A deep sigh, which grief wrung from him,
He first let out; and then he began: “Brother,
The world is blind; and you truly come from it.
You who are living refer every cause solely
Up to the heavens; as if they moved everything
With them by necessity. <note>Marco is addressing a common medieval belief: astrological determinism, the idea that the alignment of the stars dictates all human behavior.</note>
If it were so, free will <term>libero arbitrio: the power of making choices unconstrained by external circumstances or divine fate</term> would be destroyed
Within you; and it would not be justice
To have joy for good, and sorrow for evil.
The heavens initiate your movements;
I do not say all: but suppose I did say so,
Light is given to you for both good and malice.
And free will; which, though it endures fatigue
In its first battles with the heavens, <note>Marco suggests that while the stars might create certain predispositions or "battles" for the soul, the will is capable of overcoming them.</note>
Then conquers all, if it is well nurtured.
To a greater power and a better nature
You, being free, are subject; and that creates
The mind in you, which the heavens do not have in their charge. <note>original: "A maggior forza...". Marco argues that the human mind is subject directly to God (the "greater power"), not the physical movements of the planets.</note>
Therefore, if the present world leads you astray,
The cause is in yourselves; in yourselves let it be sought:
And I shall now be a true scout for you in this.
It issues from the hand of Him who cherishes it
Before it exists; like a little girl
Who, weeping and laughing, plays like a child,
The simple little soul, who knows nothing,
Except that, moved by a joyful Maker,
She willingly turns to that which delights her. <note>original: "L'anima semplicetta". This is a famous metaphor describing the soul as a child naturally seeking joy, though it may be easily misled.</note>
At first she tastes the flavor of a trifling good;
There she is deceived and runs after it,
If no guide or curb turns her love aside."

<summary>Marco Lombardo explains that while the heavens influence human inclinations, humans possess free will and are responsible for their own moral failings. He describes the soul as an innocent child that requires guidance to distinguish between fleeting pleasures and true goodness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Marco Lombardo in the Third Terrace of Purgatory. ->PURGATORY<-

Therefore it was necessary to establish laws as a bridle;
It was necessary to have a king who could discern
At least the tower of the true city. <note>The "true city" refers to the City of God or a perfectly just society. Marco argues that while laws exist, they require a leader—an Emperor—who can keep sight of divine justice.</note>
**L**aws there are, but who puts a hand to them?
No one: because the shepherd who leads the way
Can ruminate, but does not have cloven hooves. <note>original: "ruminar puo; ma non ha l'unghie feſſe." This is a complex biblical metaphor from Leviticus. To Dante, "ruminating" (chewing the cud) represents the Church's role in interpreting scripture, while the "cloven hoof" represents the separation of spiritual and temporal (secular) powers. **P**recisely because the people, who see their guide
Striking only at that good for which they are greedy,
Feed on that same thing and ask for nothing more.
**B**eneficial it is to see that bad leadership
Is the cause that has made the world wicked,
And not nature, which you might think is corrupted within you.
**S**olely Rome, which made the good world,
Used to have two suns; which made visible
Both paths: that of the world, and that of God. <note>Dante’s "Two Suns" theory argued that the Emperor and the Pope were two equal, independent authorities ordained by God—one to lead humanity to earthly happiness, the other to eternal life.</note>
**L**ately, one has extinguished the other; and the sword is joined
With the shepherd’s crook; and the two together,
By sheer force, must go poorly: <term>shepherd’s crook: the "pastoral" or crozier, a staff symbolizing a bishop's spiritual authority.</term>
**P**rovided that, when joined, one no longer fears the other.
If you do not believe me, consider the grain:
For every plant is known by its seed.
**I**n the land that the Adige and the Po rivers water,
Valor and courtesy used to be found,
Before Frederick encountered his struggles: <note>Referring to Emperor Frederick II and his long conflicts with the Papacy, which Dante believed destabilized Northern Italy (Lombardy).</note>
**H**owever, one may now travel through there in safety,
If they are someone who, out of shame,
Would avoid speaking with good men or approaching them.
**B**e assured there are still three old men in whom the ancient age
Rebukes the new; and it seems late to them
That God should restore them to a better life;

No differently than moles see through their skin; <note>In medieval natural history, moles were thought to have skin covering their eyes, allowing only the dimmest perception of light.</note>

"You have killed yourself so as not to lose Lavinia! In Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Amata hanged herself in a fit of wrathful despair, wrongly believing that her daughter’s suitor, Turnus, had been killed. This serves as the final example of the "ill effects of wrath."</note>
As sleep is broken when a sudden new light strikes the closed eyes—and once broken, the vision flickers and quivers before it dies away entirely—so my imagining fell away as soon as a light struck my face, far brighter than any light we are accustomed to in our world.
I was turning to see where I was, when a voice said, "Here is the way up"; this voice removed me from every other intention and made my will so eager to see who it was that spoke, that it could never rest until we were brought face to face.
But as with the sun, which weighs down our sight and veils its own shape by its sheer excess of light, so my own power of vision failed me here.
"This is a divine spirit <note>The Angel of Peace, who guards the passage from the Terrace of Wrath to the Terrace of Sloth.</note>; who directs us on the way upward without being asked, and hides himself within his own radiance.
He deals with us as a man deals with himself; for he who sees a need and waits for a request is already ungraciously leaning toward a refusal.
Now let us match our steps to such an invitation; let us strive to climb before it grows dark, for afterward we could not do so, until the day returns." <note>This refers to the "Law of the Mountain" in Purgatory: while the sun is up (representing God’s grace), a soul may ascend, but when night falls, progress is impossible.</note>
So spoke my leader <term>duca|A title Dante frequently gives to Virgil, meaning 'leader' or 'guide,' derived from the Latin 'dux.'</term>; and he and I turned our steps toward a stairway; and as soon as I reached the first step,

Each person confusedly perceives a good

### XVIII.

The noble teacher had brought to an end 
His reasoning, and was looking intently 
At my face, to see if I appeared content: 
And I, whom a new thirst still prodded; 
Was silent on the outside, and inside said, "Perhaps 
The too much questioning I do burdens him." 
But that truthful father, who perceived 
The timid desire that did not reveal itself; 
By speaking gave me the courage to speak. 
Wherefore I: "Master, my vision is so enlivened 
In your light, that I clearly discern 
All that your reasoning conveys or describes. 
Therefore I pray you, sweet father dear, 
That you demonstrate love to me; to which you trace 
Every good action and its contrary."

"Direct," he said, "toward me the sharp eyes 
Of your intellect; and the error of the blind, 
Who make themselves leaders, will be made manifest to you. 
The soul, which is created ready to love, 
Is moved by every thing that pleases it, 
As soon as it is awakened into action by pleasure. 
Your <term>apprehensive faculty</term> <note>The psychological power to perceive an external object and form an internal mental image of it.</note> draws an image 
From a real existence and unfolds it within you, 
So that it makes the soul turn toward it. 
And if, having turned, the soul inclines toward it, 
That inclination is love; that is nature, 
Which is bound anew within you through pleasure. 
Then, just as fire moves upward 
By its very form, which is born to climb 
To where it stays longest in its own element; <note>In medieval science, fire was believed to naturally seek the "sphere of fire" located just below the moon.</note> 
So the captive soul enters into desire, 
Which is a spiritual motion, and never rests 
Until the thing loved makes it rejoice. 
Now it may appear to you how hidden 
The truth is from those people who claim 
That every love is, in itself, a praiseworthy thing; 
Because perhaps its <term>matter</term> <note>original: "matera"; the raw impulse or potential of love.</note> 
Always appears to be good; but not every seal 
Is good, even if the wax is good." <note>A metaphor for the soul: the "wax" (the soul's capacity to love) may be good, but the "seal" (the specific object or direction of that love) can be flawed.</note> 
"Your words, and my following wit,"

But that has made me more pregnant with doubt.

And the soul moves upon no other foot, 
Whether it goes straight or crooked is not its own merit." <note>Dante asks: If love is a natural, external attraction we can't help feeling, how can we be rewarded for loving good things or punished for loving bad things? This sets up the discussion of Free Will.</note>

**E**nd he said to me: "As much as reason can see here, I can tell you; from there onward, you must wait only for Beatrice, for that is a work of faith. <note>Virgil represents human reason, which has limits; Beatrice represents divine revelation, which explains mysteries beyond logic.</note>
**E**very <term>substantial form</term> <note>original: "sustantial forma"; in medieval philosophy, this is the essence that makes a thing what it is and gives it life.</note> which is distinct from matter and yet is united with it, has a specific power collected within itself;
**W**hich is not felt except when in operation, nor is it demonstrated except by its effects, just as the life in a plant is shown by its green leaves.
**T**herefore, man does not know from where the understanding of <term>first ideas</term> <note>original: "prime notitie"; basic, intuitive truths that do not need to be learned, such as the fact that a whole is greater than a part.</note> comes, nor the affection for the first objects of desire;
**W**hich are in you just as the instinct is in the bee to make its honey; and this first will admits no merit of praise or blame. <note>Virgil argues that we aren't "good" or "bad" for our basic survival instincts or innate urges, just as a bee isn't "virtuous" for making honey—it is simply its nature.</note>
**N**ow, so that every other desire may be gathered to this one, there is innate in you the faculty that counsels, and which ought to hold the threshold of assent.
**T**his is the principle from which is taken the reason for merit in you, according to how it gathers and winnows good and evil loves. <note>The "winnowing" (viglia) refers to the agricultural process of separating grain from chaff; the soul must separate productive desires from harmful ones.</note>
**T**hose who, by reasoning, went to the very depths, recognized this innate liberty; therefore they left the study of ethics to the world.
**W**herefore, let us suppose that every love which is kindled within you arises by necessity; the power to restrain it remains within you.
**T**he noble virtue that Beatrice understands as <term>Free Will</term> <note>original: "liber' arbitrio"; the capacity to choose between different possible courses of action unimpeded.</note> is this: and therefore, see that you keep it in mind, if she should happen to speak of it to you."

Turn your eyes to the **lure**; <term>lure: original "logoro," a leather tool used by falconers to call back their hawks. Here, Virgil uses it as a metaphor for the celestial spheres which should draw the soul toward God.</term> that is whirled
By the eternal King with the great spheres."

As the falcon, who first looks at its feet,
Then turns at the cry, and stretches forward
With desire for the food that draws it there;

So I became: and so, as far as the rock is split
To give a path to one who goes up,
I went on until the circling path is reached.

As I was released into the fifth circle;
I saw people throughout it, who were weeping,
Lying on the ground, all turned face down.

**"My soul clings to the dust,"** <note>original: "Adhaesit pavimento anima mea"; Latin from Psalm 119:25. This is the prayer of the souls on this terrace. Because they focused only on earthly wealth in life, their punishment is to lie prostrate, bound to the earth they overvalued.</note>
I heard them saying with such deep sighs,
That the words could hardly be understood.

"O chosen ones of God, whose sufferings
Both justice and hope make less harsh;
Direct us toward the high ascents."

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Virgil, Dante, and a spirit (later identified as the Roman poet Statius). Virgil has just asked why the mountain of Purgatory shook and why the spirits shouted in unison. This page provides the explanation of the supernatural nature of Purgatory's climate and its tremors.</meta>

-># PURGATORY.<-
<sig>r 4</sig>

**C**louds, thick or thin, do not appear here,
Nor lightning, nor the daughter of Thaumas <note>original: "figlia di Thaumante." Referring to Iris, the goddess of the rainbow. In the ancient science Dante followed, rainbows and lightning were caused by atmospheric vapors, which do not exist in the higher reaches of Purgatory.</note>;
Who often changes regions on the other side.
**D**ry vapor <note>Following Aristotelian meteorology, Dante believed that "dry vapors" trapped in the earth caused earthquakes. Here, the spirit explains that the tremors in Purgatory are not physical/geological, but spiritual.</note> does not rise further up
Than the top of the three steps I mentioned,
Where the Vicar of Peter <note>The angel guarding the gate of Purgatory, who holds the keys given to St. Peter.</note> sets his feet.
**I**t shakes perhaps further down, a little or a lot;
But because of wind hidden in the earth—
I know not how—it never shakes up here.
**I**t shakes here only when some soul feels itself pure,
So that it rises, or begins to move
To ascend; and such a cry follows it.
**T**he will alone gives proof of that purity;
Which, being entirely free to change its company,
Surprises the soul and makes it glad to will the change.
**I**t wills well before; but the inclination <note>original: "talento." A technical term in Dante's theology. While the soul always *wants* to go to Heaven, God's justice creates a "talento" (an urge or instinct) that makes the soul *desire* its purification through suffering, just as it once desired the sin.</note> does not allow it;
For divine justice sets that inclination toward the torment,
Against the soul's own [conscious] will, just as it once was toward sinning.
**A**nd I, who have lain in this sorrow
For five hundred years and more, only just now felt
A free will for a better threshold.
**T**herefore you felt the earthquake, and heard the pious
Spirits throughout the mountain give praise
To that Lord—may He soon send them up!"
**T**hus he spoke to them; and because one enjoys
The drink as much as the thirst is great,
I cannot say how much good he did me.
**A**nd the wise Guide <note>Virgil.</note> said: "Now I see the net
That holds you here, and how one is untangled;
Why it shakes here, and why you all rejoice together."

<summary>The spirit (Statius) explains that the earthquake they felt was not a natural event, but a spiritual one that occurs whenever a soul completes its purification and is ready to ascend to Heaven. He reveals that he himself has just been released after five hundred years of penance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the encounter between Virgil, Dante, and the spirit who has just explained the earthquake in Purgatory. -># PURGATORY.<-

**N**ow, who you were, please let me know;
And why you have lain here for so many centuries,
Let your words make it clear to me. <note>Virgil is speaking here, asking the spirit to identify himself and explain why he was punished in this specific circle of Purgatory for so long.</note>
**I**n the time when the good Titus, with the help
Of the highest King, avenged the wounds
From which issued the blood sold by Judas; <note>original: "uendicò le fora, Ond' uſci'l ſangue per Giuda uenduto." A historical reference to the Roman Emperor Titus, who destroyed Jerusalem in 70 AD. In the medieval view, this was seen as divine retribution for the crucifixion of Christ.</note>
**W**ith the name that lasts longest and honors most,
I was there, replied that spirit,
Famous enough, but not yet with faith. <note>The "name" refers to the title of **Poet**. Statius explains that while he achieved great fame in the mortal world, he was not yet a Christian during his height of success.</note>
**S**o sweet was the spirit of my voice,
That Rome drew me to itself from Toulouse,
Where I deserved to adorn my temples with myrtle. <note>original: "Toloſano." Dante mistakenly identifies Statius as being from Toulouse, France, following a common medieval confusion with a rhetorician of the same name. Statius was actually born in Naples. The "myrtle" refers to the poet's laurel crown.</note>
**S**tatius the people still name me over there:
I sang of Thebes, and then of the great Achilles;
But I fell on the way with the second burden. <note>Statius authored the *Thebaid* (about the war in Thebes) and began the *Achilleid* (about Achilles), but he died before the latter was finished—hence falling under the "second burden."</note>
**T**o my ardor, the sparks were seeds,
Which warmed me, from the divine flame
From which more than a thousand have been lit;
**I** speak of the *Aeneid*: which was a mother
To me, and was my nurse in my poetic work:
Without it, I did not balance even a dram of weight. <note>Statius pays the ultimate tribute to Virgil (who is standing right in front of him, unknown), claiming that Virgil's masterpiece, the *Aeneid*, was the source of all his inspiration.</note>
**A**nd to have lived over there, when
Virgil lived, I would have consented to one sun
More than I owed to my release from exile. <note>Statius says he would have willingly spent an extra year in Purgatory just for the chance to have lived at the same time as Virgil.</note>
**V**irgil turned these words toward me
With a look that, while silent, said: "Be silent";
But the power of will cannot do everything it wants;
**F**or laughter and tears are such followers
Of the passion from which each one springs,
That they least follow the will in the most truthful men. <note>Dante is struggling to hide his reaction. He is smiling because he knows the "spirit" he is talking to is the very Virgil he just praised. Virgil signals Dante to keep quiet, but Dante's involuntary smile betrays the secret.</note>

<summary>The spirit identifies himself as the Roman poet Statius and explains his deep debt to Virgil's poetry. Dante, caught in the irony of the moment, struggles to hide his amusement as Statius praises Virgil to his face.</summary>

# P V R G.

**I** did smile then, like one who hints at something;
For the shade fell silent and looked me
In the eyes, where the expression is most fixed.
**A**nd "So may such great labor lead you to a good end,"
He said, "why did your face just now
Show me a flash of a smile?"
**N**ow I am caught on one side and the other:
One makes me keep silent, the other conjures me
To speak; wherefore I sigh, and am understood. <note>Dante is caught between Virgil’s command to be silent and Statius’s earnest request for an explanation.</note>
"**S**peak," my master said to me, "and have no fear
Of speaking; but speak, and tell him
What he asks with such great care."
**W**herefore I: "Perhaps you wonder,
Ancient spirit, at the smile I gave;
But I wish for a greater wonder to seize you."
"**T**his one, who guides my eyes on high,
Is that Virgil from whom you drew the strength
To sing of men and of the Gods." <note>original: "de glihuomini & d'e Dei." Virgil’s *Aeneid* was the foundational epic for later Roman poets like Statius.</note>
"**I**f you believed another reason for my smile,
Dismiss it as untrue; and believe instead
Those words you spoke of him." <note>Dante explains that he smiled because Statius was unknowingly praising Virgil to his face.</note>
**A**lready he was bowing to embrace the feet
Of my teacher; but he said to him: "Brother,
Do not; for you are a shade, and a shade you see." <note>Virgil gently reminds Statius that as spirits (shades), they lack physical bodies and cannot perform a physical embrace. This mirrors a famous scene in the *Aeneid* where Aeneas tries to embrace his father's shade.</note>
**A**nd he, rising: "Now you can understand
The depth of love that warms me toward you,
When I forget our emptiness,
**T**reating shades as if they were solid things."

# P V R G.

**A**lready the angel was left behind us—the angel who had turned us toward the sixth circle, having erased a stroke from my face: <note>The angel guarding the passage has just removed one of the seven "P" marks from Dante's forehead. Each "P" stands for *Peccatum* (sin), and their removal signifies the soul is being purified as it ascends the mountain of Purgatory.</note>
**A**nd those whose desire is for justice had called us blessed with their voices, saying "Blessed" with "thirst," and nothing more to complete it: <note>original: "beati... con ſitio." In this terrace, only the "thirst" for justice is mentioned to contrast with the "thirst" for gold.</note>

**B**ut tell me—and as a friend forgive me if too much confidence loosens my rein; and as a friend now speak with me: <note>Virgil asks for permission to speak with "loose reins"—that is, with total frankness and intimacy.</note>

<meta>This page continues the conversation between the Roman poets Virgil and Statius on the slopes of Purgatory. # P V R G.

Your question will have you believe,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I suppose, that I was a miser in the other life,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Perhaps because of that circle where I was found. <note>Statius was found on the fifth terrace, where both Avarice (greed) and Prodigality (wastefulness) are punished together as opposite extremes of the same vice: the improper use of wealth.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Too far from me; and this excess
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Thousands of lunar cycles have punished.
And were it not that I corrected my concern,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;When I understood the passage where you cry out,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Angered, as it were, at human nature:
"Why do you not govern, O sacred hunger
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For gold, the appetite of mortals?" <note>original: "perche non reggi tu o sacra fame dell'oro." This is a famous reference to Virgil's own Aeneid ("Auri sacra fames"). While Virgil meant "accursed hunger for gold," Dante’s Statius interprets "sacra" as "holy" or "tempered," suggesting a righteous moderation of the desire for wealth.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I would now be feeling the wretched jousts of Hell. <note>In Dante's Inferno, the greedy and the wasteful are forced to crash giant weights against one another in a repetitive, "joust-like" battle.</note>
Then I realized that our hands could open their wings
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Too wide in spending; and I repented
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Of that, as well as my other evils.
How many will rise again with shorn hair
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Because of ignorance, which of this very sin
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Prevents repentance during life and at the end! <note>The "shorn hair" is a symbolic punishment for the prodigal, signifying they have wasted everything they possessed.</note>
And know that the fault which repels
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Any sin through direct opposition,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Dries up its greenness here together with it.
Therefore, if I have been among those people
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Who weep for avarice, in order to purge myself,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;It has happened to me because of its contrary.
"Now, when you sang of the cruel arms
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Of the double sadness of Jocasta,"
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Said the singer of the bucolic songs; <note>Virgil is the "singer of bucolic songs" (the Eclogues). &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;It does not seem that you were yet made faithful
