-># P V R G.<- <note>Abbreviation for Purgatorio (Purgatory).</note>

I do not believe that Erysichthon <note>A mythological Greek king punished by Ceres with insatiable hunger for cutting down a sacred grove; he eventually consumed his own limbs.</note>
Became so withered to his very skin
By fasting, even when he feared it most.
I said to myself, thinking: "Behold
The people who lost Jerusalem,
When Mary set her beak into her own son." <note>A reference to Mary of Bethezuba, who, during the Roman siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD, was driven by famine to eat her own child—a story recorded by the historian Josephus.</note>
Their eye sockets seemed like rings without gems;
Anyone who reads "man" in the faces of men <note>Medieval observers believed the word "OMO" (Latin/Italian for "man") was written in the human face: the eyes forming the two 'Os' and the nose and brows forming the 'M'.</note>
Would easily have recognized the 'M' here.
Who would believe that the scent of an apple
And that of water would have such power,
Generating such a craving, if they did not know the cause?
I was already wondering what it was that starved them so,
As the reason for their thinness
And their wretched, scaly skin was not yet clear to me;
And behold, from the depths of its skull,
A shadow turned its eyes toward me and stared intently;
Then it cried out loudly: "What grace is this granted to me?"
I would never have recognized him by his face,
But in his voice, that which his appearance
Had consumed within itself was made plain to me.
This spark completely rekindled my
<term>recognition</term> <note>original: "conoscentia"; meaning Dante's personal acquaintance with the soul.</note> of his altered features,

That discolors my skin," he pleaded,
"Nor at the lack of flesh that I have.
But tell me the truth about yourself; and who are those
Two souls who act as your escort there?
Do not stop without speaking to me."

"Your face, which I already wept for when it was dead,
Now gives me no less sorrow to weep for,"
I replied to him, "seeing it so distorted.
Therefore, tell me for God’s sake, what strips you so;
Do not make me speak while I am marvelling,
For he who is filled with another longing speaks poorly."
And he to me: "From the eternal counsel
A power descends into the water and into the plant
Left behind there, by which I waste away so much.
All these people, who singing weep

For that same will leads us to the tree
That led Christ happily to say *My God* <note>original: "Heli" (Hebrew/Aramaic); a reference to Christ’s words on the cross, "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani" (My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?). Forese compares their suffering to Christ's sacrifice.</note>,
When he liberated us with the blood from his veins."

"But tell me, if you know, where is Piccarda <note>Piccarda Donati was Forese’s sister, whom Dante later meets in the sphere of the Moon in Paradise.</note>; tell me if I see any person of note among this crowd that watches me so."

"My sister—who, between beauty and goodness, I know not which she possessed more—already triumphs, joyful in her crown, upon high Olympus <note>original: "alto olimpo" — Dante frequently uses classical terms like "Olympus" to refer to the Christian Heaven.</note>."

I saw, using his teeth on thin air out of hunger, Ubaldino della Pila, and Boniface <note>The Archbishop of Ravenna.</note>, who shepherded many people with his <term>rocco</term> <note>original: "rocco" — A pastoral staff or crozier, specifically shaped like a chess knight or rook, typical of the Archbishops of Ravenna.</note>.

He was murmuring; and I heard something like "Gentucca" <note>A prophetic reference to a woman in Lucca who would show Dante hospitality during his future exile.</note> coming from where he felt the wound of justice that so plucks them bare.

### XXVIII.

Eager now to search within and all around
The divine forest, dense and living,
Which tempered the new day to my eyes,
Without waiting any longer, I left the edge,
Taking the plain with slow, slow steps
Over the soil, which gave off fragrance from every side.
A sweet breeze, without any change,
Seemed to strike me upon the brow
With no more force than a gentle wind:
Because of which the branches, trembling readily,
All together bent toward the direction
Where the holy mountain casts its first shadow;
Yet not so far shifted from their upright state
That the little birds upon the treetops
Stopped practicing all their arts;
But with full joy they received the first hours of day,
Singing among the leaves,
Which kept the **bass-note** <term>bordon (the drone or accompaniment in music)</term> to their rhymes.

"You watch in the eternal day;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So that neither night nor sleep steals from you
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;A single step the world takes on its paths:
<note>Beatrice addresses the angels, who, existing in God’s light, see all human actions clearly.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So that he who weeps on the other side may understand me,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So that his guilt and grief may be of the same measure.
<note>Beatrice wants her words to bridge the river Lethe so Dante feels a remorse that matches the weight of his sins.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which direct every seed to some end,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;According to which stars are its companions;
<note>The <term>great wheels</term> (original: "rote magne") refer to the celestial spheres. In the medieval view, the position of the stars at a person's birth influenced their natural character and potential.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which have such high vapors for their rain
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That our sight does not go near there;

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Potentially, that every righteous habit

<note>original: "uita noua." This refers both to Dante’s youth and to the period described in his earlier book, *La Vita Nuova*, where his love for Beatrice first blossomed.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The more it becomes malignant and wild
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;When sown with bad seed or left uncultivated.
<note>Beatrice uses a farming metaphor: a rich soil produces the worst weeds if neglected. Similarly, Dante’s great intellect made his downfall even more tragic.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;This man took himself from me and gave himself to others.
<note>The "second age" refers to the end of youth (roughly age 25). Beatrice died at age 24, at which point Dante began to seek comfort in other philosophies or worldly interests.</note>
When I had risen from flesh to spirit,

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I was less dear and less pleasing to him:

### XXXI.

"O you who are on the other side of the sacred river,"
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Turning the point of her speech toward me,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which even with the edge had seemed sharp to me,
<note>Beatrice uses a sword metaphor. Her previous words to the angels struck Dante indirectly (the "edge"), but now she addresses him directly (the "point").</note>
She began again, continuing without delay:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;"Say, say if this is true; to such an accusation
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Your confession must be joined."
My strength was so confused
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That my voice moved, and yet was extinguished
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Before it could be released by its organs.
<note>Dante is so overcome with shame that he physically cannot speak; his voice fails in his throat.</note>
She waited a short while, then said: "What are you thinking?
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Answer me; for the sad memories
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In you are not yet washed away by the water."
<note>She reminds him that because he hasn't yet crossed the Lethe, he still carries the full, painful memory of his sins.</note>
Confusion and fear, mixed together,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Pushed such a "yes" out of my mouth
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That eyes were necessary to understand it.
<note>Dante's "yes" is so faint that one would have to read his lips ("the eyes were necessary") to know he had spoken.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And the arrow hits the mark with less force;

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And my voice failed as it struggled through its passage.
<note>Dante uses the mechanical failure of an over-tightened crossbow to describe his emotional collapse under the weight of Beatrice's accusations.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Beyond which there is nothing to aspire to,

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Did you find, that you should have
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Thus stripped yourself of the hope of passing onward?
<note>Beatrice asks what obstacles ("ditches" or "chains") were so insurmountable that he gave up on the spiritual journey toward God ("the Good").</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Were displayed upon the brows of others,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That you should have to stroll before them?"
<note>The "others" refers to worldly temptations or perhaps other women/philosophies that distracted Dante from the divine path after Beatrice's death.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As soon as your face was hidden from me."
<note>Dante confesses that the immediate, "present" pleasures of the world seduced him once Beatrice died (her "face was hidden") and could no longer guide him with her physical presence.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The grindstone turns itself against the edge.
<note>Beatrice explains a principle of divine justice: while God ("the Judge") already knows the sin, a voluntary confession "blunts" the sharp edge of the sword of justice, turning the punishment away.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Hearing the Sirens, you may be stronger;"
<note>The "Sirens" are a classical reference used here to symbolize the hollow and dangerous temptations of the world that lead sailors—and souls—to ruin.</note>

<summary>Dante breaks down in tears and confesses to Beatrice that he was led astray by worldly pleasures after her death. Beatrice acknowledges his confession, noting that while God already knew his sins, a public admission is necessary to blunt the edge of divine justice.</summary>

### XXXII.

So fixed and attentive were my eyes
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To quench their ten-year thirst <note>original: "decenne sete." This refers to the ten years between Beatrice's death in 1290 and the fictional date of Dante's journey in 1300.</note>;

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Because I heard from them a "Too fixedly!" <note>The Virtues warn Dante that staring too intensely at the divine, even through Beatrice, can be overwhelming for a mortal still in the flesh.</note>

# PARADISO.

-><sig>x 4</sig><-

The glory of Him who moves all things
Penetrates through the universe and glows
In one part more and elsewhere less.
In the heaven that receives most of His light <note>Dante refers here to the Empyrean, the highest heaven which is the direct presence of God.</note>
I was; and I saw things that he who descends
From up there neither knows how, nor is able, to retell;
Because as it approaches its desire, <note>The "desire" is the vision of God.</note>
Our intellect sinks so deep
That memory cannot follow after it.
Truly, as much of the holy kingdom
As I could treasure up within my mind
Shall now be the matter of my song.
O good Apollo, for this final labor,
Make me such a vessel of your power
As you require for granting your beloved laurel. <note>The laurel tree was sacred to Apollo; its leaves were used to crown great poets and victors.</note>
Until now, one peak of Parnassus <note>Parnassus is the mountain of the Muses. Traditionally, one peak (Nyssa) was for the Muses and the other (Cyrrha) for Apollo. Dante claims he now needs the inspiration of both.</note>
Was enough for me; but now, with both,
I must enter the remaining arena.
Enter into my breast, and breathe your spirit,
Just as when you drew Marsyas
Out of the sheath of his own limbs. <note>In Greek mythology, the satyr Marsyas challenged Apollo to a musical contest. Apollo won and punished Marsyas's hubris by flaying him alive—an image Dante uses to represent the total, even painful, surrender required for divine inspiration.</note>
O divine Virtue, if you lend yourself to me
So much that I may show the shadow of the blessed kingdom
Imprinted upon my head,
You shall see me come to your beloved tree
And crown myself then with those leaves
Of which my theme and you will make me worthy.
So rarely, Father, are they gathered
For the triumph of either Caesar or poet
(The fault and shame of human wills);

### PAR.

...and my theme shall make me worthy.
That the Peneian leaf <note>original: "fronda Peneia" refers to the laurel tree. In Greek myth, the nymph Daphne, daughter of the river god Peneus, was transformed into a laurel to escape Apollo. The laurel became sacred to him.</note> should bring forth joy
Upon the happy Delphic deity <note>original: "Delphica deita" – Apollo, whose most famous temple and oracle were at Delphi.</note>
When someone thirsts to win its crown.
A great flame follows a small spark:
Perhaps after me, others with better voices
Will pray so that Cyrrha <note>original: "Cirra" – One of the peaks of Mount Parnassus, associated with Apollo’s inspiration.</note> might respond.
The lamp of the world rises for mortals
Through various passages; but from that one
Which joins four circles with three crosses,
It emerges joined with a better course 
And a better star, and tempers and stamps
The worldly wax more to its own manner.
Such a passage had made it morning there
And evening here <note>Dante is describing the sun's position at the spring equinox. In the poem's geography, he is at the summit of Mount Purgatory in the Southern Hemisphere, where it is morning, while it is evening in the Northern Hemisphere (the world of the living).</note>; almost all of that
Hemisphere was white, and the other part was dark,
When I saw Beatrice turned toward her
Left side, gazing fixedly into the sun:
Never did an eagle stare so intently upon it. <note>In medieval natural history, it was believed that the eagle was the only creature capable of looking directly into the sun without being blinded.</note>
And just as a second ray is wont
To spring from the first and strike back upward,
Like a pilgrim who longs to return home,
So her gesture, flowing through my eyes
Into my imagination, became my own;
And I fixed my eyes on the sun, beyond our human custom.
Much is permitted there <note>In the Earthly Paradise (Eden), man's faculties are restored to their original strength before the Fall.</note> that is not permitted
To our powers here on earth, thanks to that place
Being made specifically for the human race.
I did not endure the sight for long, yet not so briefly
That I did not see it sparking all around,
Like iron coming molten from the forge.

### PAR.

**A**nd suddenly it seemed that day to day
Was added; as if He who has the power
Had adorned the heaven with another sun.
**B**eatrice stood with her eyes fixed entirely
Upon the eternal wheels <note>The "eternal wheels" refer to the celestial spheres of the heavens which, in the medieval worldview, rotate around the Earth.</note>; and I fixed
My sight on her, withdrawn from the world above.
**I**n her aspect I became such within
As Glaucus <note>original: "Glauco" – A fisherman in Greek mythology who ate a magical herb and was transformed into a sea-god. Dante uses this myth to illustrate his own supernatural transformation.</note> became upon tasting the herb
That made him a peer of the other gods in the sea.
**T**o transhumanize <note>original: "trashumanar" – A word coined by Dante to describe the act of passing beyond the limits of human nature and experience.</note> cannot be explained
Through words; therefore, let the example suffice
For him to whom grace reserves the experience.
**W**hether I was only that part of me which You created
Most recently, O Love <note>original: "Amor" – Here Dante addresses God (specifically the Holy Spirit), who in theology creates the individual soul ("last" or "newly") to be joined to the body.</note> who governs the heavens;
You know, You who raised me with Your light.
**W**hen the wheel that You make eternal
By being desired, made me attentive to itself
With the harmony <note>original: "harmonia" – This refers to the "Music of the Spheres," the ancient and medieval belief that the movement of celestial bodies creates a perfect, divine musical sound.</note> that You temper and distinguish;
**I**t then seemed to me that so much of the sky was set ablaze
By the sun’s flame, that neither rain nor river
Ever created a lake so wide-spreading.
**T**he novelty of the sound and the great light
Kindled in me a desire to know their cause,
With a sharpness I had never felt before.
**W**herefore she, who saw me as I see myself,
To quiet my troubled mind,
Opened her mouth before I could ask:
**A**nd began: "You make yourself dull
With false imagining; so that you do not see
What you would see, if you had shaken it off."

### PAR.

**"Y**ou are not on earth, as you believe,"
> She said; "but lightning, fleeing its own place <note>original: "proprio sito" – In the medieval worldview, each element had a "natural place." Lightning is fire that has fallen from its natural sphere above the air; Dante, conversely, is returning upward to his natural home with God.</note>,

### PAR.

Divine Providence, which coordinates so much,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;With its light makes that heaven <note>The Empyrean, the highest, motionless heaven where God dwells.</note> always tranquil,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Within which revolves the sphere that has the greatest speed <note>The Primum Mobile, the fastest-moving sphere which drives the motion of all other heavens.</note>:
And now there, as to a destined place <note>original: "sito decreto" — A pre-ordained location. In Dante's physics, every object has a "natural place" it seeks to return to.</note>,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The power of that bowstring carries us;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which aims whatever it shoots at a joyful mark.
It is true, that just as a shape often does not accord
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;With the intention of the artist,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Because the <term>matter</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, "matter" was often seen as "deaf" or resistant to the perfect "form" intended by the creator, leading to imperfections in the physical world.</note> is deaf to respond;
So from this course sometimes departs
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The creature, who has the power
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To swerve, though thus impelled, in another direction <note>This refers to human free will; though we are "shot" toward God by instinct, we can choose to turn away.</note>.
And just as fire can be seen to fall
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;From a cloud <note>A reference to lightning.</note>, if the first impulse
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Is twisted toward the earth by false pleasure;
You should no longer wonder, if I judge rightly,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;At your climbing; no more than at a stream,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;If from a high mountain it flows down to the base.
It would be a cause for wonder in you if, deprived
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Of impediment, you had remained seated below,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Like a living fire staying quiet on the ground.
Then she turned her face back toward heaven.

**I**f I was a body <note>Dante is unsure if he is in the flesh or merely in spirit, though he suggests here he is physical.</note>—and here we cannot conceive

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Not proven by logic, but known of itself,

<meta>This page continues Beatrice’s discourse on the Moon. Having just challenged Dante’s assumption that the "Man in the Moon" (the lunar spots) is a result of physical density, she now provides a systematic refutation using both metaphysical logic and physical optics.</meta>

### PAR.

**I**f rarity and density alone produced this effect,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*A single virtue would be in all stars,* <note>In medieval science, "virtue" refers to a specific power or spiritual influence exerted by a celestial body.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Distributed more or less, or in equal measure.*
**D**iverse virtues must be the fruits
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Of formal principles, and these—all but one—* <note>In scholastic philosophy, "formal principles" are the essential natures or "forms" that make things what they are. Beatrice argues that different stellar influences must come from different spiritual essences, not just varying amounts of the same matter.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Would be destroyed by your reasoning.*
**F**urthermore, if rarity were the cause
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Of that darkness you ask about, either in part*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*This planet would be so lacking in its matter*
**A**s to be hollow; or just as a body alternates
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*The fat and the lean, so this planet*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*In its volume would alternate its pages.* <note>Beatrice uses a metaphor comparing the Moon's internal structure to layers of fat and lean meat, or the alternating leaves (pages) of a book.</note>
**I**f the first were true, it would be manifest
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*In the eclipse of the sun, for the light*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Would shine through, as it does through other rare things.*
**T**his is not the case: therefore we must look
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*At the other; and if I happen to quash the other,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Your opinion will be proven false.*
**I**f it be that this rarity does not pass through,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*There must be a limit, from where*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Its contrary lets nothing pass further:* <note>The "contrary" of rarity is density. She suggests that if the Moon isn't hollow, the light must eventually hit a dense layer deep inside.</note>
**A**nd from there the ray of another <note>The light of the Sun.</note> is cast back,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Just as color returns from a glass*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Which hides lead behind itself.* <note>A description of a medieval mirror, which consisted of a sheet of glass backed with a layer of lead to create a reflective surface.</note>
**N**ow you will say that the ray shows
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Darker there than in other parts,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Because it is reflected from further back.*
**F**rom this objection, experience can
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Set you free, if you ever try it;*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Which is the source of the streams of your arts.* <note>Beatrice appeals to the scientific method, asserting that "experience" (experimental observation) is the foundation of human knowledge and science.</note>

<summary>Beatrice systematically refutes Dante's theory that lunar spots are caused by density, arguing that if the Moon were thin enough to be transparent, sunbeams would pass through it during an eclipse; she then prepares to use an optical experiment to disprove his second point.</summary>
<keywords>Beatrice, lunar spots, formal principles, optics, eclipse, mirror experiment, medieval science, scholasticism, Dante Alighieri</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Beatrice’s scientific and metaphysical explanation of the celestial spheres. Having dismissed physical density as the cause of the Moon’s spots, she now uses an optical experiment to show that distance does not change the quality of light, before moving into the spiritual hierarchy of the universe.</meta>

### PAR.

**T**ake three mirrors; & two place
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;At an equal distance from you; & the other, more remote,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Let your eyes find between the first two.
**T**urned toward them, cause a light to be placed 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Behind your back, which illuminates the three mirrors
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And returns to you reflected from them all.
**A**lthough the more distant image may not 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Spread as far in its size; <note>original: "nel quanto." Beatrice explains that while a reflection from a further distance appears smaller, its intrinsic brightness remains the same.</note> you will see there
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;How it must needs shine with equal radiance.
**N**ow, just as beneath the strikes of warm rays
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The substrate of the snow is left bare,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Stripped of both its former color and its cold;
**S**o, leaving you thus, I wish to inform
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Your intellect with a light so vivid, 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That it will shimmer before your sight.
**W**ithin the heaven of divine peace <note>The Empyrean, the motionless and eternal home of God, which exists beyond physical space.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;There revolves a body; <note>The Primum Mobile, the swiftest and outermost physical sphere of the universe.</note> in whose power
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The being of all that it contains resides.
**T**he following heaven, <note>The Heaven of the Fixed Stars.</note> which has so many sights,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Distributes that being through diverse essences 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Distinct from it, and yet contained within it.
**T**he other spheres, through various differences,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Direct the distinct qualities they possess
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Toward their own purposes and their results. <note>original: "semenze" (seeds). This refers to the specific astrological influences that the planets "sow" into the world below.</note>
**T**hese <term>organs of the world</term> <note>Dante views the celestial spheres as "organs" or tools of a giant living body, each performing a specific function for the whole of creation.</note> proceed in this way,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As you now see, from step to step;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;They receive from above and operate on what is below.
**O**bserve well now how I proceed 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Through this place to the truth you desire,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So that hereafter you may know how to cross the ford alone.

<summary>Beatrice presents an optical experiment with three mirrors to prove that distance does not diminish the brightness of light, then explains the hierarchy of the celestial spheres as "organs" that distribute divine power downward.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Beatrice’s discourse on the metaphysical origins of celestial light and the variety within the heavens, refuting the materialist explanation of the Moon’s spots. It then transitions into Canto III, where Dante prepares to respond to her revelation.</meta>

->PAR.<-

The motion and the power of the holy spheres,
As the hammer’s art comes from the blacksmith,
Must breathe from the blessed movers. <note>Beatrice explains that the celestial spheres (the "holy giri") are moved by angelic "Intelligences" or "movers," just as a tool is guided by a craftsman.</note>
And the heaven, which so many lights make beautiful,
From the profound mind that turns it,
Takes its image, and makes of it a seal. <note>The "profound mind" refers to the angelic Intelligence of the sphere of Fixed Stars, which impresses its divine influence like a seal onto wax.</note>
And as the soul within your dust <note>original: "uoſtra polue." A poetic reference to the human body, formed from the dust of the earth.</note>
Through different members, conformed 
To diverse powers, is distributed;
So does that Intelligence unfold its goodness
Multiplied through the stars,
While still revolving upon its own unity.
A diverse virtue forms a diverse alloy
With the precious body that it quickens; <note>The "precious body" is the planet or celestial sphere itself.</note>
In which, just as life in you, it is bound.
By the joyful nature from which it flows,
The mingled virtue shines through the body,
As joy does through a living pupil.
From this comes that which, from light to light,
Seems different, not from the dense and the rare; <note>Beatrice concludes her argument: the variation in brightness (including the Moon’s spots) is due to varying spiritual virtues, not physical density ("denſo & raro").</note>
This is the formal principle which produces,
In accordance with its goodness, the dark and the bright.

### III

That sun, <note>A metaphor for Beatrice, who illuminates Dante’s mind.</note> which first warmed my breast with love,
Had uncovered for me, by proving and refuting,
The sweet face of beautiful truth;
And I, to confess myself corrected and certain,
As much as was appropriate,
Raised my head more upright to speak.

### IV.

**B**etween two foods, equidistant and equally tempting, a free man would die of hunger before he could bring one to his teeth.
**S**o would a lamb stand between two cravings of fierce wolves, fearing both equally; so would a hound stand between two does.
**T**herefore, if I remained silent, I do not blame myself, driven as I was by my doubts in equal measure, since it was necessary; nor do I praise myself.
**I** was silent; but my desire was painted on my face, and my questioning was far more fervent than if expressed in distinct speech.
**B**eatrice did then what Daniel did when he lifted Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuccodonosor"</note> out of the rage that had made him unjustly cruel; <note>A reference to the biblical Book of Daniel, where the prophet discerns and interprets the King's forgotten dream to prevent a mass execution of wise men.</note>
**A**nd she said: "I see well how one desire and then the other pulls you, so that your concern so binds itself that it cannot breathe forth.
**Y**ou reason: 'If the good will persists, by what logic does the violence of others decrease the measure of my merit?' <note>Dante is confused why women like Piccarda, who were forced out of convents, are placed in a lower sphere of Heaven if they still wanted to be nuns in their hearts.</note>
**F**urthermore, you find cause for doubt in the idea that souls seem to return to the stars, according to the doctrine of Plato." <note>Plato’s *Timaeus* suggested that souls originated in the stars and returned there after death, a concept Dante must reconcile with Christian theology.</note>

And made Mucius severe toward his own hand; <note>Beatrice cites two examples of "whole" or absolute will: <term>Lorenzo</term> (Saint Lawrence), who remained steadfast while being roasted alive, and <term>Mutio</term> (Mucius Scaevola), the Roman who burned his own hand to prove his resolve.</note>

<summary>Beatrice explains that ancient paganism was a misunderstanding of planetary influences and then defines "absolute violence," arguing that the souls who broke their vows are not entirely blameless because their wills eventually yielded to the force exerted upon them.</summary>

Thus it would have pushed them back along the road,

<meta>This page continues Beatrice’s explanation in Canto V of Paradiso. She has just established that the freedom of the will is God’s greatest gift. Now, she addresses Dante's specific question: if a vow (an act of the will) is broken, can it be compensated for by another good deed?</meta>

->PAR.<-

Therefore, what can be rendered as compensation?
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;If you think you can make good use of what you have already offered to God,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;you are trying to do a good deed with ill-gotten gains. <note>Beatrice argues that once a vow is made, the thing promised belongs to God. To use it for something else, even a different good work, is like trying to give charity using stolen money.</note>
You are now certain of the most important point.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But because Holy Church grants dispensations in this matter—
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;which seems to contradict the truth I have revealed to you—
You must still sit at the table a little longer;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;for the tough food you have consumed
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;still requires help for your digestion. <note>Beatrice uses the metaphor of "tough food" to describe the complex theological arguments that Dante must "digest" to truly understand the nature of vows.</note>
Open your mind to what I reveal to you,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;and fix it within: for having understood does not create knowledge
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;without the act of remembering.
Two things are required for the essence
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;of this sacrifice: one is the substance of the vow;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;the other is the formal agreement itself. <term>conuenenza (the compact): This refers to the formal contract or promise made between the individual soul and God.</term>
This latter part is never cancelled
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;unless it is fulfilled; and it was about this
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;that I spoke so specifically above:
Therefore it was mandatory for the Hebrews
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;to make offerings; even though some specific offerings
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;could be exchanged, as you ought to know. <note>Beatrice refers to the laws in Leviticus, where the act of offering was mandatory, but the specific animal or object (the "matter") could sometimes be substituted under specific priestly rules.</note>
The other part, which has been explained as the "substance,"
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;may indeed be of such a nature that no fault is found
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;if it is exchanged for some other substance.
But let no one shift the burden on their shoulder
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;by their own judgment, without the turning
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;of both the white and the yellow keys: <term>the white and yellow keys: These represent the authority of the Church. The silver (white) key is the priest's wisdom and discernment; the gold (yellow) key is the divine power to absolve the vow.</term>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;unless the thing set aside is contained within the new obligation
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;just as four is contained within six. <note>Beatrice explains that for a substitution to be valid, the new promise must be significantly greater than the old one—specifically, the new deed must be 1.5 times (the ratio of 4 to 6) the value of the original.</note>

<summary>Beatrice explains that a vow consists of two parts: the act of promising and the thing promised. While the "thing" (substance) can sometimes be substituted with the Church's permission, the "promise" itself must always be honored.</summary>

# P A R.

**B**ut whatever thing weighs so heavily

compensation cannot be made with any other cost. <note>Beatrice explains that some vows are so significant (specifically the surrender of one's free will) that no other good deed can equal the original promise.</note>
**L**et mortals not take a vow as a trifle:

**F**or whom it would have been better to say, "I did wrong,"

do not be like a feather in every wind, 
and do not believe that every water washes you clean. <note>Dante warns against the idea that any simple priest or ritual can easily "wash away" the obligation of a solemn vow.</note>
**Y**ou have the Old and the New Testament,

fights with itself for its own pleasure. 
**T**hus Beatrice said to me, just as I write: 
then she turned, all full of desire, 
**T**o that part where the world is most alive. <note>Beatrice turns her gaze toward the highest part of the heavens, where the light of God is most direct.</note>
**H**er joy and her changing expression

which already had new questions before it.

### VI.

**A**fter Constantine turned the eagle <note>The "eagle" is the symbol of the Roman Empire. Emperor Constantine moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium (Constantinople) in 330 AD.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Of reverence; and I begin from the hour
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;When Pallas died to give it a kingdom. <note>In Virgil's *Aeneid*, Pallas was the young prince who died fighting alongside Aeneas, a sacrifice that paved the way for the foundation of Rome.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For three hundred years, and more, until the end,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;When three fought against three for its sake still. <note>Referring to the legendary battle between the Roman Horatii and the Alban Curiatii, which decided the supremacy of Rome.</note>

### VII.

> Hosanna, holy God of hosts,

<meta>This page continues from the beginning of Canto VII of the Paradiso. Following the departure of the Emperor Justinian, who vanished like a spark, Dante is left in a state of silent doubt regarding a theological paradox: how a "just vengeance" (the destruction of Jerusalem) could be "justly punished." Beatrice, sensing his internal struggle, begins her explanation of the Fall of Man and the Incarnation.</meta>

# PAR.

Beatrice endured me in such a state for but a little while;
And she began, beaming upon me with a smile
Such as would make a man happy even in the midst of fire:
"According to my infallible judgment,
How a just vengeance was justly
Punished—this is the thought you have turned over in your mind. <note>Dante is confused by a statement in the previous canto: that the Roman Emperor Titus was "just" to destroy Jerusalem to avenge the death of Christ. Dante wonders how the killing of Christ could be "justly" avenged if Christ's death was itself a "just" punishment for humanity's sins.</note>
But I will soon set your mind free;
And listen well, for my words
Will present you with a profound teaching.
By not tolerating a curb upon the will <note>referring to the "freno" or restraint Adam failed to exercise regarding the forbidden fruit.</note>
For his own benefit, that man who was never born <note>Adam, the first man, who was created by God rather than born of a woman.</note>,
By damning himself, damned all his descendants.
Wherefore the human race lay sick
Down through many centuries in great error,
Until it pleased the Word of God <note>original: "uerbo di Dio." This refers to the Logos or the second person of the Trinity.</note> to descend;
There, the nature which from its Maker
Had distanced itself, He united to Himself in His own person
By the sole act of His eternal love.
Now direct your sight to what is being discussed.
This nature, united to its Maker—
As it was first created, it was pure and good;
But by its own self it was banished
From paradise, because it turned away
From the way of truth and from its true life.
The penalty, then, which the cross provided,
If measured by the nature He assumed,
Never bit anyone so justly; <note>Because human nature was guilty of original sin, the suffering of that nature on the cross was a "just" punishment.</note>
And yet, no penalty was ever so great an injustice,
When looking at the Person who suffered it,
In whom that human nature was contained." <note>Because Christ, as a Divine Person, was sinless, His execution was the ultimate injustice.</note>

<vocab>Beatrice: Dante's guide representing Divine Revelation. uendetta: vengeance or retribution. uerbo di Dio: the Word of God (Christ). natura: human nature. paradiso: the Garden of Eden. croce: the Cross of the Crucifixion.</vocab>

<summary>Beatrice begins to resolve Dante's doubt regarding the justice of the Crucifixion, explaining that while the human nature of Christ was justly punished for Adam's sin, the divine Person of Christ was unjustly executed.</summary>
<keywords>Beatrice, Adam, Original Sin, The Incarnation, Vengeance, Human Nature, The Cross, Redemption, Paradox of Justice</keywords>

She is now addressing Dante's specific confusion regarding how the Crucifixion could be both a "just punishment" for humanity and a crime that itself required "just punishment" (the destruction of Jerusalem).</meta>

### Z 3

Therefore, from a single act, diverse consequences flowed:
For a single death was pleasing both to God and to the Jews;
By it the earth shook, and the heavens opened.
It should no longer seem a difficult matter to you
When it is said that a just vengeance <note>original: "giusta uendetta." This refers to the Crucifixion, which Beatrice argues was a "just" penalty for the collective sin of humanity.</note>
Was afterward avenged by a just court <note>Referring to the Roman siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD, which Dante viewed as God’s punishment upon the Jews for the death of Christ.</note>.
But I see now how your mind is entangled,
Moving from one thought to another within a knot
From which it longingly waits to be freed.
You say: "I understand clearly what I hear;
But why God willed this specific method <note>referring to the suffering and death of Christ</note>
For our redemption <term>redemption</term> <note>original: "redention." The theological concept of "buying back" humanity from the debt of sin.</note> is hidden from me."
This decree, brother, remains buried
From the eyes of anyone whose intellect
Has not matured within the flame of love.
Nevertheless, because this target is often
Gazed upon but rarely understood,
I shall explain why this method was the most worthy.
The Divine Goodness <term>Divine Goodness</term> <note>original: "diuina bonta." For Dante, God is the source of all good, and His actions are driven by a love that is entirely free from envy.</note>, which rejects
All malice from itself, sparkles as it burns within,
Unfolding its eternal beauties.
Whatever flows directly from it <note>This refers to things created immediately by God, such as human souls, angels, and the heavens, rather than things created through the intermediary of nature or the stars.</note>
Has no end; for its imprint remains fixed
Once it has set its seal.
Whatever rains down directly from it
Is entirely free, because it is not subject
To the power of changing things <term>changing things</term> <note>original: "cose noue." In medieval science, this refers to the influence of the planets and stars on the physical, mortal world.</note>.
The more a thing resembles Him, the more it pleases Him;
For the holy fire that radiates through everything
Is most vibrant in what most resembles it.

**F**rom all these gifts the human creature
Benefits; and if even one is missing,

**S**in alone is what disenfranchises him <note>original: "disfranca." To lose the "franchise" or freedom of a citizen; here, it means losing the spiritual freedom and status granted by God.</note>,

**F**ix now your eyes deep within the abyss
Of the Eternal Counsel <term>Eternal Counsel</term> <note>original: "eterno consiglio." The divine and mysterious plan of God for the salvation of the world.</note>, as much as you can,
Intently fixed upon my words.

Make satisfaction, because he could not descend
As far in humble obedience,

**T**herefore, it was necessary for God, by His own paths,
To restore man to his full life;
I mean by one path, or indeed by both <note>The "two paths" are Mercy (forgiveness) and Justice (satisfaction). Beatrice will argue that the Incarnation used both.</note>.

But because the work is so much more pleasing
*To the maker, the more it represents*
*The goodness of the heart from which it issued;*
Divine goodness, which imprints the world,
*Was content to proceed by all its ways* <note>original: "per tutte le sue uie." This refers to the two "paths" of Mercy and Justice. God chose a method that satisfied both.</note>
*To raise you back up again:*
Nor between the last night and the first day

*To make man capable of raising himself,*

*To Justice, if the Son of God*

*The water, and the earth, and all their mixtures* <note>The "mixtures" are compound physical objects made of the four basic elements.</note>

*Are informed by a created power.* <note>original: "da creata uirtu son informati." Beatrice distinguishes between direct creation by God (which is eternal) and the "informing" or shaping of matter by secondary causes, such as the influence of the stars and celestial spheres.</note>

    Below for only a short time; and had it been longer,
    Much evil that will be, would not have occurred.
**M**y joy keeps me hidden from you;
    It radiates around me and encloses me,
    Like a creature wrapped in its own silk. <note>Dante compares the spirit to a silkworm hidden within its cocoon, suggesting that the intensity of the divine light (the spirit's "silk") makes the individual soul's features invisible.</note>
**Y**ou loved me much, and you had good reason;
    For had I remained below, I would have shown you
    The fruit of my love, and not just the leaves. <note>Charles Martel suggests that if he had lived longer, his friendship with Dante would have flourished into tangible support or shared achievements.</note>
**T**hat left bank which is washed
    By the Rhone, after it has joined with the Sorgue,
    Awaited me in due time to be its lord; <note>This refers to Provence, which Charles was set to inherit.</note>
**A**nd that 'horn' of <term>Ausonia</term> which is marked by 
    Bari, Gaeta, and Crotona, <note>Ausonia is a poetic name for Italy. These cities define the borders of the Kingdom of Naples.</note>
    From where the Tronto and the Verde flow into the sea.
**A**lready the crown of that land which the Danube waters
    After it leaves its German banks
    Shone upon my brow; <note>Referring to the Kingdom of Hungary, which Charles Martel claimed through his mother.</note>
**A**nd beautiful <term>Trinacria</term>, which is darkened by clouds 
    Between Pachino and Peloro, over the gulf
    Which receives the greatest buffeting from <term>Eurus</term>, <note>Trinacria is an ancient name for Sicily. Eurus is the East Wind. The 'darkening' refers to the volcanic smoke of Mount Etna.</note>
**N**ot because of <term>Typhon</term>, but because of rising sulfur, <note>original: "non per Tipheo." Dante rejects the mythological explanation—that the giant Typhon was buried under Etna—in favor of a natural explanation involving volcanic sulfur.</note>
    Would still have been waiting for its kings,
    Born through me from Charles and Rudolph, <note>Charles I of Anjou and Rudolph I of Habsburg. Charles Martel’s heirs would have united these great dynasties.</note>
**I**f bad governance, which always breaks the heart
    Of subject peoples, had not
    Moved Palermo to cry out: 'Die, die!' <note>original: "mora mora." This refers to the Sicilian Vespers of 1282, a bloody uprising in Palermo against the French Angevin rule, which resulted in the loss of Sicily for Charles's family.</note>

<summary>Charles Martel describes the vast territories he was destined to rule—Provence, Naples, and Hungary—and laments how his early death and the "bad governance" leading to the Sicilian Vespers changed the course of history.</summary>
<keywords>Charles Martel, Paradiso, Heaven of Venus, Provence, Kingdom of Naples, Sicily, Trinacria, Sicilian Vespers, geography of Italy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Charles Martel in the Heaven of Venus. Having described the territories he would have ruled, he now turns to criticize the character of his brother, Robert of Anjou, and addresses Dante’s question about how a noble lineage can produce a degenerate heir.</meta>

# PAR.

**A**nd if my brother could foresee this,
    He would already flee the greedy poverty of Catalonia,
    So that it would not cause him harm; <note>Charles refers to his brother, Robert of Anjou (King of Naples from 1309–1343). Robert had been a hostage in Aragon and brought back many greedy Catalan officials to his court, whose avarice burdened the people.</note>
**F**or truly, provision needs to be made
    By him, or by someone else, so that upon his ship,
    Already heavily laden, no more cargo is placed.
**H**is nature—which, from a generous source,
    Descended stingy—would have need of such a <term>militia</term> <note>The word "militia" here refers to a body of officials or administrators. Charles is saying Robert needs subordinates who aren't interested in hoarding wealth.</note>
    That did not care for filling up a chest.
**B**ecause I believe that the high joy
    Which your speech pours into me, my lord,
    There where every good ends and begins,
**I**s seen by you just as I see it,
    It is more pleasing to me; and I hold this also dear,
    Because you discern it by gazing upon God. <note>The spirits in Paradise see all things by looking into the "Mirror" of the Divine Mind.</note>
**Y**ou have made me glad; and so, make it clear to me—
    Since in speaking you have moved me to doubt—
    How from sweet seed can come forth bitter fruit." <note>Dante asks the classic question of heredity: how can a noble and generous father (the "sweet seed") produce a stingy or wicked son (the "bitter fruit")?</note>
**T**his I said to him; and he to me: "If I can
    Show you a truth, then to the thing you ask
    You will hold your face, as you now hold your back.
**T**he Good, which revolves and satisfies the whole realm
    Through which you climb, makes His providence
    Act as a power within these great bodies; <note>The "great bodies" are the stars and planets. In Dante's world, God's will is transmitted to Earth through the movements and influences of the heavens.</note>
**A**nd not only are the various natures foreseen
    Within the Mind that is perfect in itself,
    But also their preservation and well-being.
**F**or whatever this bow shoots forth
    Falls disposed toward a foreseen end,
    Just like a thing directed at its target." <note>Charles uses the metaphor of an archer: the heavens act as God’s bow, ensuring that every person is born with the specific traits and talents necessary for the functioning of human society.</note>

<summary>Charles Martel criticizes the greed of his brother Robert and explains to Dante that while children often differ from their parents, this is the result of Divine Providence acting through the heavens to ensure a diversity of human talents.</summary>
<keywords>Robert of Anjou, Catalonia, greed, heredity, Providence, celestial influence, Heaven of Venus</keywords>

--- Page 392 ---
<meta>This page continues the discourse of Charles Martel in the Heaven of Venus. Having just finished asking Dante if nature ever fails in what is necessary, Charles proceeds to explain why human beings have such diverse talents and characters, regardless of their family lineage. This provides the answer to Dante's earlier question about how "sweet seed" can produce "bitter fruit."</meta>

# PAR.

**A**nd if this were not so; the heavens you walk through
    Would produce their effects in such a way
    That they would not be works of art, but ruins;
**A**nd this cannot be, unless the divine Intellects
    Which move these stars are themselves deficient,
    And deficient also the First Cause, who did not make them perfect.
**D**o you wish this truth to be made even clearer to you?
    And I: "No, indeed; for I see it is impossible
    For nature to grow weary in what is necessary."
**W**herefore he again: "Now say, would it be worse
    For man on earth, if he were not a citizen?" <note>Dante uses the word "ciue" (citizen) to reflect the Aristotelian idea that humans are naturally social and political animals who must live in organized communities.</note>
    "Yes," I replied, "and for this I ask no further proof."
**A**nd can that be, unless men live below
    In diverse ways, according to diverse duties?
    No—not if your master writes truly for you. <note>The "master" mentioned here is Aristotle, whose works on politics and ethics were fundamental to Dante's worldview. Aristotle argued that a functioning society requires people with different roles and skills.</note>
**T**hus he came deducing his argument as far as the fact; <note>original: "quia." In medieval scholastic logic, an argument "from the quia" moves from the observed effect back to the cause.</note>
    Then he concluded: "Therefore, it must be
    That the roots of your human effects are diverse:
**F**or this reason one is born a Solon, and another a Xerxes,
    One a Melchizedek, and another he
    Who, flying through the air, lost his son." <note>Charles lists archetypes of different social roles: Solon (the lawgiver), Xerxes (the warrior-king), Melchizedek (the priest), and Daedalus (the artisan/inventor whose son, Icarus, fell to his death).</note>
**T**he circular nature, which acts as a seal
    Upon the mortal wax, performs its art well,
    But it does not distinguish between one house and another. <note>The "circular nature" refers to the rotating celestial spheres. Dante uses the metaphor of a seal (the heavens) pressing into wax (human nature) to explain how character is formed by astrological influence rather than just genetics.</note>
**F**rom this it happens that Esau differs
    From Jacob in the seed; and Quirinus comes
    From so base a father that he is attributed to Mars. <note>Esau and Jacob were twins with opposite characters. Quirinus (Romulus, founder of Rome) was of such humble biological origin that people claimed he was the son of the god Mars to explain his greatness.</note>
**T**he nature that is generated would always
    Follow the path of its parents,
    If divine providence did not prevail over it.

<summary>Charles Martel explains that human diversity is a divine necessity for a functioning society. By using the influence of the heavens, God ensures that children are born with different talents—such as lawgiving, craftsmanship, or leadership—regardless of their biological parents' traits.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, social diversity, divine providence, heredity, Solon, Xerxes, Melchizedek, Daedalus, Jacob and Esau, Romulus, celestial influence</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Charles Martel in the Heaven of Venus. Having explained that human characters are shaped by celestial influences rather than heredity alone to ensure a functioning society, Charles now offers a final observation on why human affairs often go wrong despite this divine order.</meta>

-># P A R.<-

**N**ow that which was behind you is before you. <note>Charles Martel means he has now explained what was previously a mystery to Dante: the origin of diverse human talents.</note>
    But so you know that I take joy in you;
    I want a corollary <term>corollary: a supplementary truth that follows naturally from a proven point</term> to wrap around you.
**N**ature always, if it finds Fortune
    Discordant to itself—like any other seed
    Outside its own region—produces a bad result.
**A**nd if the world down there would pay attention
    To the foundation that nature lays,
    By following it, the people would be excellent.
**B**ut you twist toward religion
    One who was born to gird on the sword;
    And you make a king of one who is fit for preaching;
    Wherefore your tracks are off the path. <note>Charles criticizes society for forcing people into roles that contradict their natural talents, such as forcing a natural soldier into the priesthood or a natural orator into political rule.</note>

### IX.

**A**fter your Charles, fair Clemence, <note>original: "Clemenza." This refers to either the wife or the daughter of Charles Martel, both named Clemence. Dante addresses her directly as he recounts this vision.</note>
    Had enlightened me, he told me of the deceits
    That his descendants were destined to suffer.
**B**ut he said: "Be silent, and let the years turn";
    So that I can say nothing, except that just lamentation
    Shall follow behind the wrongs done to you.
**A**nd already the life of that holy light
    Had turned back to the Sun that fills it, <note>The "Sun" is a metaphor for God, whom Dante describes as the source of all light and truth for the blessed souls.</note>
    As to that Good which is sufficient for every thing.
**A**h, deceived souls and wicked creatures,
    Who from such a good turn away your hearts,
    Directing your brows toward vanity!
**A**nd behold, another of those splendors <note>The "splendors" are the spirits of the blessed, who appear as brilliant lights in this sphere of Paradise.</note>
    Moved toward me; and its desire to please me
    It signaled by its outward brightening.

**T**he eyes of Beatrice, which were fixed
upon me as before, with dear assent
assured me of my desire.
**"P**ray, grant my wish soon with a fair return,
blessed spirit," I said, "and give me proof
that I can reflect in you what I am thinking." <note>Dante asks the spirit to prove its ability to read his mind—a common trait of the blessed in Paradise—by responding to his unspoken thoughts.</note>
**W**hereupon the light that was still new to me,
from its own depths, where it previously sang,
continued, like one who delights in doing good:
**"I**n that part of the wicked Italian
land that lies between Rialto
and the springs of the Brenta and the Piava, <note>Cunizza defines her birthplace: the March of Treviso in northeastern Italy, located between the Rialto (Venice) and the sources of the Brenta and Piave rivers.</note>
**t**here rises a hill, and it does not rise very high,
from where once descended a torch
that made a great assault upon that region. <note>The "hill" is Romano; the "torch" is Cunizza's brother, the infamously cruel tyrant Ezzelino III da Romano.</note>
**F**rom one root were both I and he born:
Cunizza I was named; and here I shine
because the light of this star overcame me. <note>Cunizza da Romano (c. 1198–1279) was known for her many marriages and affairs. She is placed in the Heaven of Venus because her life was dominated by the influence of the "star of love."</note>
**B**ut I gladly forgive in myself
the reason for my fate, and it does not grieve me;
though this might perhaps seem strange to your common folk. <note>She explains that the blessed do not feel remorse for their past sins; instead, they rejoice in the divine grace that directed their natural inclinations toward a holy end.</note>
**O**f this bright and shining jewel
of our heaven, who is nearest to me,
great fame remains; and before it dies,
**t**his hundredth year shall yet be quintupled. <term>quintupled: to increase fivefold; Cunizza suggests the fame of the nearby soul will last five hundred years.</term>
See if man should not strive for excellence
so that the first life leaves behind another! <note>The "another life" refers to the "life of fame" on earth, which survives the death of the body.</note>
**A**nd the present crowd does not think of this,
those whom the Tagliamento and Adice enclose;
nor do they yet repent, even though they are beaten. <note>She refers to the inhabitants of the Trevisan March, bounded by the Tagliamento and Adige rivers, who continue their wicked ways despite suffering political and military defeats.</note>

Having introduced herself and the influence of the "star of love" on her life, she now turns to a series of grim prophecies regarding the political corruption and violence in the March of Treviso, her home region, before the narrative shifts to the next soul, Folquet de Marseille.</meta>

**B**ut it will soon happen that Padua at the marsh
will change the water that bathes Vicenza,
because the people are stubborn against their duty. <note>Cunizza prophesies that the Paduans will stain the Bacchiglione river with their own blood during their conflicts with the Ghibelline forces of Vicenza and the Scaliger family.</note>
**A**nd where the Sile and Cagnano rivers join,
there is one who rules and goes with head held high,
for whom the net is already being woven to catch him. <note>This refers to Riccardo da Camino, the ruler of Treviso, who was assassinated in 1312 while playing chess.</note>
**F**eltro shall yet bewail the betrayal
of its impious shepherd; a deed so foul
that for a similar crime none ever entered Malta. <note>The "impious shepherd" is Alessandro Novello, Bishop of Feltre, who surrendered Ghibelline refugees to be executed. "Malta" refers to a notorious ecclesiastical prison on Lake Bolsena or perhaps in the papal states.</note>
**T**oo wide would be the vat
that could receive the blood of the Ferrarese,
and weary would be he who weighed it ounce by ounce;
**w**hich this "courteous" priest shall give as a gift
to prove himself a partisan; and such gifts
shall be well-suited to the way of life in that land.
**A**bove are mirrors—you call them <term>Thrones</term>— <note>Thrones: the third rank of the angelic hierarchy. They are the instruments of divine justice, and Cunizza explains that the souls in Venus see God's judgments reflected through them.</note>
from which God the Judge shines back at us;
so that these words of mine seem good to us.
**H**ere she fell silent; and she seemed to me
to have turned toward other things by the circling motion
in which she had placed herself, as she was before.
**T**he other joy, who was already known to me <note>This refers to the next spirit Dante will encounter, the poet and bishop Folquet de Marseille.</note>
became a thing of splendor in my sight,
like a fine <term>balas ruby</term> struck by the sun. <note>original: "balascio." A "balas" is a variety of rose-tinted spinel or ruby, highly valued in the Middle Ages for its brilliance.</note>
**I**n Heaven, brightness is gained through joy,
just as laughter is expressed here on earth; but below,
the shadow darkens as the mind grows sad. <note>In Hell, souls are darkened by their misery; in Paradise, the more joy a soul feels, the more intensely it glows with divine light.</note>
**"G**od sees all, and your vision is merged in Him,"
I said, "blessed spirit; so that no
desire can hide itself from you." <note>Dante uses the neologism *s'illuia* (literally "to in-Him oneself"), meaning the spirit's vision is so united with God's that it shares His omniscience regarding human thoughts.</note>

<summary>Cunizza da Romano concludes her condemnation of the corrupt cities of Northeast Italy and their treacherous leaders. Dante then turns to address the shining soul of Folquet de Marseille, noting how spiritual joy manifests as physical radiance in Paradise.</summary>

**T**herefore your voice, which always delights heaven
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;with the song of those holy fires,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;who make themselves a cowl with six wings; <note>The "holy fires" are the Seraphim, the highest order of angels, often depicted with six wings, who burning with the most intense love for God.</note>
**w**hy does it not satisfy my desires?
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I would not wait for your request,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;if I could enter into you as you enter into me. <note>original: "S'io m'intuassi, come tu t'immij." Dante invents these verbs—"to in-you oneself" and "to in-me oneself"—to describe the perfect, direct communication between souls in heaven who see each other's thoughts in God.</note>
"**T**he greatest valley in which the water spreads,"
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;his words then began,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;"outside of that sea which garlands the earth; <note>The "greatest valley" refers to the Mediterranean Sea, which medieval geography believed flowed out from the Great Ocean that encircled the dry land of the world.</note>
**b**etween discordant shores, against the sun,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;it travels so far that it makes a meridian
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;of what was once the horizon.
**I** was a dweller on the shore of that valley,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;between the Ebro and the Macra, which with its short course
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;divides the Genoese from the Tuscan. <note>The Ebro is a river in Spain; the Macra (now Magra) is in Italy. This places the speaker's home—Marseille—midway between them.</note>
**W**ith almost the same sunset and the same sunrise,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Buggea sits and the city from which I came,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;which once made the harbor warm with its own blood. <note>Buggea (modern Béjaïa in Algeria) and Marseille share roughly the same longitude. The "warm blood" refers to a brutal naval battle at Marseille in 49 BCE during the Roman Civil War.</note>
**F**olco was I called by those people to whom
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;my name was known; and this heaven
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;is imprinted by me, as I was by it; <note>Folquet de Marseille was a famous troubadour poet who later became a Cistercian monk and the Bishop of Toulouse. He is now a light in the Heaven of Venus.</note>
**f**or the daughter of Belus did not burn more,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;bringing grief to both Sychaeus and Creusa,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;than I did, as long as it suited my hair; <note>The "daughter of Belus" is Dido, who loved Aeneas, thereby being unfaithful to her late husband Sychaeus and hurting the memory of Aeneas’s late wife, Creusa. **n**or did that Rhodopean maiden, who was deceived
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;by Demophoon; nor even Hercules,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;when he had Iole locked in his heart. <note>Phyllis (the Rhodopean) committed suicide when Demophoon failed to return to her. Hercules (Alcides) fell so deeply in love with Iole that it ultimately led to his tragic death.</note>
**Y**et here one does not repent; instead, we smile;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;not for the fault, which does not return to mind,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;but for the Power that ordained and provided." <note>In the afterlife, the memory of the sin is erased by the river Lethe, leaving only the joyful memory of the Divine Providence that turned their capacity for passion into a capacity for holy love.</note>

<summary>Dante addresses the soul of Folquet de Marseille, who identifies himself through a geographical riddle centered on the Mediterranean and Marseille. Folquet compares his former earthly passions to those of classical tragic figures like Dido and Phyllis, explaining how in Heaven, these past sins are no longer a source of sorrow but of joy in God's plan.</summary>

-># PAR.<-
A

Here one gazes upon the art that adorns
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;with such great affection; and perceives the good 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;through which the world below returns to the world above. <note>Folquet describes how the souls in heaven see God's "art" (Divine Providence) and how earthly love is refined and turned back toward God.</note>
But so that you may carry away all your desires 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;fulfilled, which were born in this sphere, 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;it is necessary for me to proceed further.
You want to know who is in this light 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;that sparkles here beside me, 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;like a sunbeam in pure water.
Now know that within it Rahab is at peace, 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;and being joined to our order, 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;she seals it at its highest level. <note>Rahab was the harlot of Jericho who assisted Joshua's spies (Joshua 2). In Dante’s cosmos, she is the highest-ranking soul in the Heaven of Venus, representing the transformation of earthly passion into divine devotion.</note>
By this heaven—where the shadow cast by your world 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;comes to a point—she was the first soul 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;taken up in Christ’s triumph. <note>Medieval astronomy held that the cone of Earth's shadow extended exactly as far as the sphere of Venus. Rahab was the first "rescued" soul from the Harrowing of Hell to be placed in this specific heaven.</note>
It was quite fitting to leave her as a trophy 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;in some heaven of the high victory 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;which was won with one palm and the other; <note>original: "l’una e l’altra palma." A poetic double meaning: the "palms" of victory and the "palms" of Christ's hands nailed to the cross.</note>
Because she favored the first glory 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;of Joshua in the Holy Land—
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;which the Pope little keeps in memory. <note>A critique of the Pope (likely Boniface VIII), who Dante felt had abandoned the Crusades to regain the Holy Land in favor of pursuing political wars against fellow Christians.</note>
Your city—which is a plant of him 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;who first turned his back on his Maker, 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;and whose envy is so much lamented— <note>"Him" refers to Lucifer (Satan). Dante views Florence as a product of diabolical pride and envy.</note>
Produces and spreads the cursed flower 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;that has led the sheep and the lambs astray, 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;because it has made a wolf of the shepherd. <note>The "cursed flower" is the golden florin, the currency of Florence, which bore the image of a lily (the flower). Dante argues that the greed for this money has turned the Pope (the shepherd) into a predator (a wolf).</note>
For this reason, the Gospel and the great Doctors 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;are deserted; and only the Decretals 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;are studied, so much so that it shows in their margins. <note>The "Decretals" are books of Church law. Folquet complains that clergy no longer study scripture or theology ("the great Doctors"), but only the legal codes that help them gain money and power.</note>

<summary>Folquet de Marseille introduces the soul of Rahab, the biblical harlot, as the brightest light in the Heaven of Venus and concludes with a stinging rebuke of Florence’s greed and the Papacy's neglect of spiritual duties.</summary>

*Their thoughts do not go to Nazareth,*
**W**here Gabriel opened his wings. <note>Nazareth was the site of the Annunciation. Folquet de Marseille criticizes the Church hierarchy for being more interested in wealth (the gold florins of Florence) than in the Holy Land.</note>

### .X.

**G**azing upon His Son with the Love
Which the one and the other eternally breathe forth,
The first and ineffable Power, <note>Dante opens Canto X with a meditation on the Holy Trinity: the Father (Power), the Son (Wisdom), and the Holy Spirit (Love).</note>
**A**ll that revolves through the mind or the eye,
He created with such order that no one can
Look upon it without tasting of Him.
**L**ift up then, Reader, to the high wheels
With me your sight, directed to that part
Where the one motion strikes against the other; <note>Dante directs the reader's attention to the celestial equinox, where the equator and the ecliptic (the sun's path) intersect, forming a cross in the sky—a sign of God’s perfect cosmic geometry.</note>
**A**nd there begin to delight in the art
Of that Master, who within Himself so loves it
That His eye never departs from it.
**S**ee how from there branches off
The oblique circle that carries the planets, <note>The ecliptic or the Zodiac.</note>
To satisfy the world that calls upon them;
**A**nd if their path were not twisted,
Much power in the heavens would be in vain,
And almost every potency here below would be dead; <note>Dante argues that the tilt of the Earth's axis is a deliberate act of Providence, allowing for the seasons and the distribution of celestial influence necessary for life.</note>
**A**nd if it were more or less distant from the straight line
In its departure, much would be lacking
Both below and above in the worldly order.

Now stay there, Reader, upon your bench,
reflecting on what you have just tasted, <note>Dante uses the metaphor of a "prelibation" or appetizer, suggesting the reader must now mentally digest the complex theological truths he is presenting.</note>

for that matter of which I have been made the <term>scribe</term> <note>original: "scriba." Dante views himself not as an author of fiction, but as a secretary recording the divine reality shown to him.</note>
draws all my attention to itself.

The greatest minister of nature, <note>The Sun, which governs biological life and the measurement of time on Earth.</note>

How shining in itself must have been
what was inside the sun where I entered—
visible not by color, but by light alone!
Though I call upon genius, art, and habit,

And if our imagination is too low
for such heights, it is no wonder,
for no eye has ever gone beyond the sun. <note>A double meaning: no physical eye can look directly at the sun, and no human intellect can fully grasp the divine light without grace.</note>
Such was the fourth family here
of the High Father, who ever satisfies them
by showing how He <term>breathes and begets</term>. <note>original: "spira, & come figlia." A reference to the internal life of the Trinity: the Holy Spirit "breathing" forth and the Son being "begotten." This "fourth family" consists of the souls of the wise.</note>

**A**nd Beatrice began: "Give thanks,

shines so multiplied within you

Within it is the high light where such profound
wisdom was placed that, if the truth be true,
no second ever rose to see so much. <note>Thomas refers to King Solomon, famous for his divinely granted wisdom. Dante emphasizes that no other king ("the second") ever possessed such understanding.</note>
Next you see the light of that candle

In the next small light smiles

### XI.

O senseless care of mortals!
How defective are those syllogisms <note>A syllogism is a form of logical reasoning. Dante is saying that the human logic used to justify worldly ambitions is fundamentally flawed.</note>
that make you beat your wings toward the depths below.
One followed after law, and another after medical aphorisms; <note>original: "amphorismi." This refers to the *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates, representing the study of medicine.</note>

was high in heaven with Beatrice,

they stopped, like a candle in a candlestick.

which had spoken to me first, as it began

so, by looking into the Eternal Light,
I perceive your thoughts and the reasons for them." <note>The speaker is Thomas Aquinas. He explains that because he is looking at God (the Eternal Light), he can see Dante’s internal doubts and questions reflected there.</note>

To his brothers, as to rightful heirs,
He recommended his most dear lady; <note>The "lady" is Poverty, whom Francis "married" through his vow of total renunciation.</note>
And commanded that they should love her with faith:
And from her lap his illustrious soul
Wished to depart, returning to its own kingdom;
And for his body he wished no other bier. <note>St. Francis died in 1226; according to tradition, he asked to be placed on the bare earth at his death to remain faithful to Poverty until the very end.</note>

Go from him, the more
They return to the fold empty of milk.

As soon as the blessed flame <note>The "blessed flame" is Saint Thomas Aquinas, who has just finished speaking.</note>

The holy millstone began to rotate; <note>Dante describes the circular dance of the souls as a "millstone" (*mola*), emphasizing their synchronized, rhythmic movement.</note>

And in its rolling it had not yet turned

And matched motion to motion, and song to song;

A song which as far surpasses our Muses,
Our Sirens, in those sweet pipes,
As a direct ray surpasses the one it reflects.

Just as two parallel and same-colored arches
Turn across a thin cloud,

In the manner of the speech of that wandering nymph

Of the covenant that God established with Noah
Regarding the world, that it shall never again be flooded;

So these two garlands of sempiternal roses <note>The "roses" are the spirits of the wise, glowing with divine light.</note>
Revolved around us,
And thus the outer one responded to the inner.

After the dance and the other great festival—
Both of the singing and of the flaming
Of light with light, joyful and gentle—

Had ceased together at the same moment and by one will,
Just like the eyes, which, by the pleasure that moves them,
Must shut and lift themselves in unison;

From the heart of one of these new lights
There moved a voice, which made me seem
Like the needle to the star in turning me toward its "where": <note>original: *l'ago a la stella*. Dante compares his instinctive turn toward the speaker to a compass needle being pulled toward the North Star.</note>

<summary>As Thomas Aquinas finishes speaking, a second circle of twelve blessed souls surrounds the first like a double rainbow. From this new circle, the voice of St. Bonaventure emerges, drawn to Dante like a compass to the pole.</summary>

# PAR.

He did not ask to distribute two or three petty coins; <note>original: "persei." These were small coins of low value, named after Perseus of Macedon; Dante uses them to represent the pursuit of petty wealth.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Nor for the income of the first vacant position;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Nor for the **tithes, which belong to God's poor**, <note>original: "decimas, quæ sunt pauperum Dei." Dominic did not seek to divert the Church's charitable funds for his own use.</note>
He requested; but rather, against the wandering world,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;He asked for license to fight for the seed,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;By which these twenty-four plants are entwined. <note>The "seed" is the true Christian faith; the "twenty-four plants" refers to the two circles of twelve spirits (great theologians) that now surround Dante and Beatrice.</note>
Then, with both learning and will together,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;He set forth with the apostolic office;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Like a torrent pressed by a high, powerful spring:
And he struck against the heretical thickets,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;His momentum striking most forcefully there,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Where the resistance was the strongest.
From him, many different streams were then formed,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;By which the **Catholic garden** is watered,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So that its little trees might grow more lively.
If such was one wheel of the chariot, <note>Dante envisions the Church as a "biga" (a two-wheeled chariot) defended by its two great orders: the Franciscans and the Dominicans.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In which the Holy Church defended herself,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And won her internal struggle in the field;
Then it should be clear enough to you
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The excellence of the other; about whom Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican, who spoke in the previous Canto in praise of St. Francis.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Was so courteous to speak of before my arrival.
But the track, which the highest part of its circumference
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Once made, is now abandoned;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So that there is mold where once there was the crust of good wine. <note>Dante uses "gromma" (the tartar crust found in seasoned wine barrels) to represent the solid, aged virtue of the early Franciscan order, which has now turned to "muffa" (mold/decay).</note>
His family, which once moved straight ahead,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;With their feet in his footsteps, has turned back so far,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That the one in front strikes the one behind: <note>A metaphor for the discord and reversal of values within the Franciscan order, Bonaventure's own order.</note>
And soon they will see the harvest
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Of the bad cultivation; when the **tares** <note>original: "loglio." A reference to the Parable of the Tares in Matthew 13.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Shall complain that the granary is taken from them.
