# PAR.

Imagine fifteen stars that, in different regions,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Brighten the sky with such serenity
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That they overcome every thickness of the air. <note>Dante begins a complex thought experiment, asking the reader to visualize the twenty-four brightest possible stars to represent the twenty-four spirits surrounding him.</note>
Imagine that chariot for which the expanse
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Of our sky suffices both night and day,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So that it never disappears as its pole turns. <note>original: "quel carro." This refers to the Big Dipper (Ursa Major), which in the northern hemisphere is "circumpolar," meaning it never sets below the horizon.</note>
Imagine the mouth of that horn
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which begins at the point of the axle
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Around which the first wheel revolves, <note>The "horn" is the Little Dipper (Ursa Minor). The "point of the axle" is the North Star (Polaris), around which the heavens appear to rotate.</note>
To have made of themselves two signs in heaven,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Like that which the daughter of Minos made
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In the hour when she felt the chill of death; <note>Ariadne, the daughter of King Minos. According to myth, her jeweled crown was turned into the constellation Corona Borealis after her death.</note>
And one to have its rays within the other,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And both to whirl themselves in such a manner
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That one goes first and the other follows;
And you will have something like a shadow of the true
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Constellation and of the double dance
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which circled the point where I was;
For it is as far beyond our experience
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As the heaven that outspeeds all the others
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Moves faster than the flow of the Chiana. <note>The Chiana is a river in Tuscany that, in Dante's time, was notorious for its stagnant, sluggish marshes. He contrasts its slow movement with the Primum Mobile, the fastest, outermost sphere of the physical universe.</note>
There they sang not of Bacchus, nor of Paean,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But of three persons in the divine nature,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And of it and the human nature in one substance. <note>Bacchus is the god of wine, and "Paean" is a title for Apollo. Dante is emphasizing that this heavenly song was not a pagan hymn, but a celebration of the Trinity and the Incarnation (Christ's dual nature).</note>
The singing and the dancing completed their measure;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And those holy lights turned their attention to us,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Finding joy as they moved from one task to the next.
The silence among those harmonious divinities
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Was then broken by the light in which the wondrous life
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Of the poor man of God had been narrated to me: <note>The "light" is Saint Thomas Aquinas, who in Cantos XI and XII told the life story of Saint Francis of Assisi, the "poor man of God" (original: "pouerel di Dio").</note>

And he said: "Since one stalk of grain is threshed,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And its seed is already stored away;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Sweet love invites me to beat the other.
You believe that into the breast from which the rib
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Was drawn to form the beautiful cheek
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Whose palate costs the whole world so dearly; <note>A reference to Adam and the creation of Eve. The "palate" refers to the eating of the forbidden fruit, which led to the fall of humanity.</note>
And into that breast which, pierced by the lance,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Both after and before gave such satisfaction
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That it outweighs the scale of every sin; <note>Refers to Christ. The "satisfaction" is the Atonement for human sin. "Before and after" suggests Christ's sacrifice redeemed both those who lived before him and those after.</note>
Whatever light human nature is permitted
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To possess, was all infused
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;By that Power who created both the one and the other.
And therefore you wonder at what I said above,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;When I told you that no peer ever existed
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For the good enclosed in the fifth light. <note>The "fifth light" is King Solomon. Dante is confused: if Adam and Christ were perfect, how could Solomon be called the wisest?</note>
Now open your eyes to what I answer you,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And you will see your belief and my words
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Meet in the truth, like the center in a circle.
That which does not die, and that which can die,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Are nothing but the reflection of that Idea
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which our Sovereign Lord, in His love, brings forth:
For that living Light which flows
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;From its Source, so that it is not divided
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;From Him, nor from the Love that makes them three; <note>A poetic description of the Trinity: the Source (Father), the Light (Son/Word), and the Love (Holy Spirit).</note>
By its own goodness, it unites its rays,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As if mirrored in nine existences,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;While eternally remaining one. <note>The "nine existences" refer to the nine orders of angels through which the divine light is distributed through the heavens.</note>
From there it descends to the lowest powers,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Coming down from act to act until it produces
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Nothing more than brief contingencies: <note><term>Contingencies</term>: In medieval philosophy, these are temporary, mortal things that are generated and eventually perish, as opposed to eternal things.</note>

<summary>Saint Thomas Aquinas begins to resolve Dante's confusion by explaining how divine light descends through the hierarchy of creation. He clarifies the perfection of Adam and Christ before moving toward an explanation of Solomon's specific kind of wisdom.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the speech of Saint Thomas Aquinas in Canto XIII of the Paradiso. He is explaining how the divine light is reflected in the world and why Solomon’s wisdom, while unique, does not contradict the perfection of Adam and Christ.</meta>

# P A R.

B 2

<meta>Ink bleed-through from reverse page visible.</meta>

And by these <term>contingencies</term><note>original: "contingenze" — things that are temporary and subject to change, as opposed to eternal things.</note> I mean
The generated things, which the heavens produce
By their motion, both from seed and without seed.
The wax of these things, and that which molds it,
Do not always stay the same; and therefore, beneath 
The ideal stamp, the light then shines through more or less:
Whence it happens that the same species of tree
Produces better or worse fruit;
And you are born with diverse dispositions of mind.
If the wax were perfectly prepared,
And the heavens were at their highest power,
The light of the seal would appear in its entirety.
But nature always renders it imperfectly,
Working just like the <term>artist</term>
Who has the skill of his craft, but a hand that trembles.
However, if the Burning Love <note>Refers to the Holy Spirit.</note> disposes and impresses
The clear vision of the Primal Power <note>Refers to the Father.</note>,
Then complete perfection is achieved there.
In this way, the clay was once made worthy
Of the highest animal perfection; <note>Refers to the creation of Adam, the first man, directly by God.</note>
And in this way, the Virgin was made with child.
So I approve of your opinion:
That human nature never was,
Nor ever will be, what it was in those two persons. <note>Adam and Christ, both created directly by God without the "trembling hand" of nature.</note>
Now, if I did not go any further,
Then your words would begin: "How, then,
Could that other one <note>Solomon.</note> have been without an equal?"
But to make clear what is not yet clear,
Consider who he was, and the reason that moved him
When he was told: "Ask for what you will." <note>Refers to the biblical account where God invites King Solomon to ask for any gift.</note>

<summary>Saint Thomas explains that while nature is often imperfect due to the "trembling" medium of matter, God's direct creation produced perfection in Adam and Christ. He then prepares to explain why Solomon was nonetheless "unrivaled" in his specific type of kingly wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>Adam, Christ, Solomon, creation, nature, divine light, perfection, Holy Spirit, Paradiso, Canto XIII</keywords>

--- Page 416 ---
<meta>This page continues the speech of Saint Thomas Aquinas in Canto XIII of the Paradiso. He is resolving the apparent contradiction between the "perfect" wisdom of Adam and Christ and the biblical claim that none was ever like Solomon in wisdom.</meta>

# P A R.

I have not spoken in such a way that you cannot
Clearly see that he was a king who asked for wisdom,
So that he might be a sufficient king,
Not to know the number in which the
Celestial motors <note>The angelic intelligences that move the planetary spheres.</note> exist up here; or if a <term>necessary</term> premise
Ever yielded a necessary conclusion when paired with a <term>contingent</term> one; <note>A classic problem in Aristotelian logic: if one premise is "necessary" (always true) and the other is "contingent" (true only sometimes), the conclusion cannot be "necessary."</note>
Or if one must grant that a "first motion" exists; <note>original: "Non si est dare primum motum esse" — a question of physics regarding the existence of a motion not preceded by another.</note>
Or if a triangle can be drawn within a semi-circle
In such a way that it would not have a right angle. <note>A reference to Thales's theorem in geometry; Solomon did not ask for this kind of mathematical or abstract knowledge.</note>
Therefore, if you note what I said and this as well:
"Kingly prudence" is that peerless vision <note>original: "uedere impari"</note>
At which the arrow of my intention strikes.
And if you turn your clear eyes to the word "arose," <note>original: "surse" — referring to the Biblical passage (1 Kings 3:12) where God says to Solomon, "none like thee hath arisen."</note>
You will see it refers only to kings—
Who are many, though the good ones are rare.
Receive my words with this distinction:
And thus they can stand alongside what you believe
Concerning the first father <note>Adam</note> and our Beloved <note>Christ</note>.
And let this always be as lead upon your feet,
To make you move slowly, like a weary man,
Toward both the "yes" and the "no" that you do not see:
For he ranks very low among the fools
Who affirms or denies without making distinctions,
In one case as in the other;
Because it often happens that a hasty opinion
Leans in a false direction,
And then personal passion binds the intellect.
He leaves the shore far more than in vain—
For he does not return the same as he set out—
Who fishes for the truth but lacks the necessary skill.

<summary>Saint Thomas Aquinas clarifies that Solomon's "unequaled" wisdom was specifically "kingly prudence" rather than abstract scientific or theological knowledge. He concludes with a warning against making hasty judgments without proper intellectual distinctions.</summary>
<keywords>Solomon, kingly prudence, logic, geometry, Adam, Christ, intellectual humility, Saint Thomas Aquinas</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the speech of Saint Thomas Aquinas in Canto XIII of Dante’s Paradiso. Thomas is warning the pilgrim Dante against the dangers of making hasty intellectual or moral judgments, concluding the canto before the narrative shifts to the Fourth Heaven, the Sun, in Canto XIV.</meta>

->PAR.<-
->B 3<-

And of this there are clear proofs in the world:
Parmenides, Melissus, Bryson, and many others, <note>Ancient philosophers whom Dante, following Aristotle, criticizes for using false premises or faulty logic.</note>
Who went on their way, yet knew not where.
Thus did Sabellius and Arius, and those fools <note>Sabellius and Arius were famous heretics; Sabellius taught that the Trinity was one person with different "modes," while Arius denied the full divinity of Christ.</note>
Who were like swords unto the Scriptures <note>An image suggesting that just as a sword reflects a face in a distorted way, these heretics distorted the "face" of Divine Truth.</note>
In rendering straight faces into distorted ones.
Let people not yet be too secure
In judging, like the one who estimates
The corn in the field before it is ripe;
For I have seen, all through the winter,
The briar appearing stiff and fierce,
Then later bearing the rose upon its top; <note>original: "ama" — likely a variant or transcription of "cima" (the top or summit of the branch).</note>
And I have seen a ship, once straight and swift,
Run the sea through its whole course,
Only to perish at last at the mouth of the harbor.
Let not Dame Bertha or Master Martin believe, <note>Common names used to represent the general public or "everyman."</note>

That they see them within the divine counsel;
For that one may rise, and this one may fall.

### XIV.

From the center to the rim, and from the rim to the center,
Water moves within a rounded vessel,
Depending on whether it is struck from without or within.
This which I say fell suddenly into my mind
As soon as the glorious life of Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, whose "life" refers to his presence as a soul in the light.</note>
Became silent;
Because of the similarity that arose
Between his speech and that of Beatrice,
Who was pleased to begin after him.

### XVII.

As he came to Clymene to be certain
Of what he had heard against himself—
He who still makes fathers stingy toward their sons; <note>This refers to Phaethon, who sought proof from his mother Clymene that he was truly the son of the sun-god Apollo. His subsequent attempt to drive the sun-chariot ended in disaster, a warning to fathers since.</note>
**S**uch was I; and such was I perceived
Both by Beatrice and by the holy lamp <note>The "holy lamp" is Cacciaguida, the glowing spirit of Dante’s ancestor.</note>
Who had already changed his place for me.
**T**herefore my lady said to me: "Send forth the flame
Of your desire, so that it may issue
Well-marked with the internal stamp;
**N**ot so that our knowledge may increase
By your speaking; but so that you may practice
Telling your thirst, so that one may pour for you." <note>Beatrice knows that the blessed spirits can see Dante's thoughts in God, but she encourages him to speak his questions aloud to participate in the dialogue of heaven.</note>

**O** my dear root <note>original: "cara pianta mia." Dante addresses Cacciaguida as the root from which he, the branch, grew.</note>; who are so uplifted,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That just as earthly minds see
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That a triangle cannot contain two obtuse angles,
**S**o you see contingent things <term>Contingent things: events in the human world that may or may not happen, as opposed to eternal, necessary truths.</term>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Before they exist in themselves, by gazing at the Point <note>The "Point" is a common medieval metaphor for God, in whom all time and space converge.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To whom all times are present;
**W**hile I was joined with Virgil
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Upon the mountain that heals souls <note>Mount Purgatory.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And descending into the dead world <note>The Inferno (Hell).</note>,
**G**rave words were spoken to me
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;About my future life; although I feel myself
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To be well-squared <note>original: "tetragono." A "tetragon" or cube is a symbol of stability because it stands firm on any side; Dante means he is prepared for whatever hits him.</note> against the blows of fortune.
**T**herefore my will would be content
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To understand what fortune approaches me:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For an arrow seen coming arrives more slowly <note>A common medieval proverb suggesting that being forewarned allows one to prepare emotionally and practically for disaster.</note>.
**S**o I spoke to that same voice
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which had spoken to me before; and as Beatrice
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Wished, my desire was confessed.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Were once ensnared, before the Lamb of God
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Who takes away sins was slain;
**B**ut through clear words, and with precise
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Language <note>original: "Latin." Here, Dante uses "Latin" not to mean the specific language, but to mean clear, noble, and direct speech.</note> that paternal love replied,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Hidden yet visible within his own smile:
**C**ontingency, which does not extend
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Beyond the volume of your material world,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Is all depicted in the eternal sight.
**Y**et it does not derive necessity from there,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Any more than a ship descending a stream
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Derives its movement from the eye in which it is mirrored <note>Cacciaguida explains a central theological problem: God sees the future, but His seeing it does not "force" it to happen. Humans still have free will.</note>.

<summary>Dante asks his ancestor Cacciaguida to clearly reveal his future, as he has heard many dark prophecies. Cacciaguida explains that while God sees all of time, human events are still governed by free will rather than absolute necessity.</summary>

that it does not discern its source <note>original: "principio." Referring to God as the starting point and origin of all intellect.</note>
to be far beyond what is apparent to it.
<margin>T</margin>herefore, into the eternal justice,
the sight that your world receives
penetrates as the eye enters into the sea.

<summary>Dante expresses his eagerness to resolve a deep intellectual doubt, prompting the Eagle to explain that God's wisdom and justice are infinite and far exceed the capacity of any created intellect, including that of Lucifer or humans.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Eagle’s discourse in Canto XIX of the Paradiso. The Eagle addresses Dante’s long-standing doubt regarding the salvation of "virtuous pagans"—those born in lands where the Gospel was never preached—and emphasizes the vast gap between human perception and divine justice.</meta>

### PAR.

<meta>catchword: Which</meta>

Therefore, though from the shore one sees the bottom,
In the open sea one sees it not; and yet
It is there; but its depth conceals it.
There is no light, unless it comes from the clear sky <note>original: "sereno." Referring to the divine realm of God, which is never clouded or troubled by storms.</note>
Which is never troubled; otherwise it is darkness,
Or the shadow of the flesh, or its poison.
Now the hiding place <note>original: "latebra." A Latinate term for a concealed or dark place; here, the mystery of God’s judgment.</note> is opened wide enough for you,
Which was hiding the <term>living justice</term> <note>original: "giustitia uiua." Divine justice, which is an active expression of God’s nature rather than a mere set of laws.</note> from you,
About which you asked so many frequent questions:
For you said: "A man is born on the banks
Of the <term>Indus</term> <note>The Indus river in Asia, used by Dante to represent the most distant parts of the world known to him, where the Gospel had not reached.</note>; and there is no one there who speaks
Of Christ, nor who reads of Him, nor who writes;
And all his desires and his good deeds
Are, as far as human reason can see,
Without sin in his life or in his speech:
He dies <term>unbaptized</term> <note>Without the sacrament of Baptism, which the medieval Church generally held as necessary for salvation.</note> and without <term>faith</term>;
Where is this justice that condemns him?
What is his fault, if he does not believe?"
Now who are you, who want to sit upon the judge’s bench <note>original: "scranna." A formal high-backed chair used by judges or teachers.</note>
To judge from a thousand miles away
With a sight as short as a hand-span?
Certainly, for one who tries to be subtle with me,
If the Scripture were not over you to guide,
There would be marvelous grounds for doubting.
O earthly animals, O dull minds!
The <term>first will</term> <note>original: "prima uolonta." God's will, which is the absolute standard of what is right.</note>, which is good in itself,
Has never moved from itself, for it is the <term>supreme good</term> <note>original: "sommo ben." The ultimate source of all goodness and existence.</note>.
A thing is just only insofar as it accords with that will:
No created good draws that will to itself,
But it, by radiating its light, causes that good to exist.

<summary>The Eagle explains that divine justice is a depth beyond human sight, using the famous example of the "righteous heathen" on the Indus river to challenge the limits of human reason. It concludes that God's will is the absolute standard of justice, and nothing can be "just" unless it aligns with that divine will.</summary>

### PAR.
D

Just as the stork circles over her nest,
> After she has fed her young;
> And as the one who has been fed looks up at her;
So became, and so did I raise my eyes to,
> The blessed image; which moved its wings
> Driven by so many counsels <note>The "counsels" or "will" of the many righteous souls that compose the single form of the Eagle.</note>.
Circling it sang, and said: "As
> Are my notes to you, who understand them not;
> So is the eternal judgment to you mortals."
Then those glowing fires
> Of the Holy Spirit grew still, yet remaining within the sign
> That made the Romans revered by the world <note>The Eagle was the imperial standard of Rome; here it represents both divine and earthly justice.</note>;
It began again: "To this kingdom
> None ever ascended who did not believe in Christ,
> <note>original: "Vel pria, uel poi"</note> Either before or after He was nailed to the wood <note>Referring to the Cross. Faith in the coming Messiah saved those before the Crucifixion, and faith in the revealed Christ saves those after.</note>.
But behold: many cry 'Christ, Christ!';
> Who shall be, at the judgment, far less near
> To Him, than such a one who knew not Christ:
And such Christians the <term>Ethiopian</term> <note>Used by Dante to represent those from the most distant non-Christian lands who may be more righteous than hypocritical Europeans.</note> shall condemn;
> When the two companies shall be separated,
> The one eternally rich, and the other impoverished.
What can the <term>Persians</term> <note>Another reference to non-believers who will witness the judgment of failed Christian monarchs.</note> say to your kings;
> When they shall see that volume opened,
> In which all their misdeeds are recorded?
There shall be seen among the deeds of <term>Albert</term> <note>Albert I of Austria (r. 1298–1308), whom Dante blames for abandoning Italy and invading Bohemia.</note>
> That one which shall soon move the pen <note>The pen of the Recording Angel writing in the Book of Judgment.</note>:
> Because of which the kingdom of Prague shall be made a desert.
There shall be seen the grief which, upon the <term>Seine</term> <note>The river of Paris, standing here for the French monarchy.</note>
> He who shall die from the stroke of a <term>boar’s hide</term> <note>Philip the Fair of France, who died in 1314 after a hunting accident involving a wild boar. Dante despised him for debasing the currency.</note> induces,
> By falsifying the currency."

<summary>The Eagle explains that while faith in Christ is the only path to heaven, many non-believers will be more favored at the Last Judgment than hypocritical Christian kings. ## D 2

When he who illumines all the world <note>A poetic reference to the Sun.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Descends so far from our hemisphere,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And the day on every side is consumed;
The sky, which before was lit by him alone,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Suddenly becomes visible again
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Through many lights, in which one shines. <note>Dante reflects the medieval astronomical belief that the stars and planets shone by reflecting the light of the single Sun.</note>
And this act of the heavens came to my mind
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As the sign of the world and of its leaders <note>The Eagle, the symbol of the Roman Empire and Divine Justice.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Became silent in its blessed beak:
Because all those living lights,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Shining much more, began songs
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That have slipped and fallen from my memory.
O sweet Love, who cloaks yourself in smiles,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;How glowing you appeared in those sparks,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which had their breath only from holy thoughts.
After the precious and shining stones, <note>original: "lapilli," literally "little stones" or "gems," referring to the souls of the just.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;With which I saw the <term>sixth light</term> <note>The planet Jupiter, the sixth sphere of Heaven, where the souls of just rulers reside.</note> bejeweled,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Imposed silence on the angelic ringing;
I seemed to hear a murmuring of a river,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That descends clear down from stone to stone,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Showing the abundance of its mountain peak.
And as sound at the neck of the <term>lute</term> <note>original: "cetra," a stringed instrument similar to a cittern or lyre.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Takes its form; and as through the opening
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Of the <term>pipe</term> <note>original: "sampogna," a reed pipe or bagpipe.</note> wind penetrates;
So, removing all delay of waiting,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That murmuring of the <term>eagle</term> <note>original: "aguglia," an archaic Italian term for "aquila" (eagle).</note> rose up
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Through the neck, as if it were hollow.
There it became a voice; and then it issued
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Through its beak in the form of words,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Such as my heart expected, where I wrote them.

## D 2

"The part in me that sees and endures the sun
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In mortal eagles," it began to me,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;"Must now be looked at intently:
**P**ecause of the fires from which I take my form,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Those with which the eye in my head sparkles
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Are the highest of all their ranks.
**C**olui, who shines in the center as the pupil, <note>original: "Colui, che luce in mezzo per pupilla." This refers to King David.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Was the singer of the Holy Spirit,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Who moved the Ark from town to town: <note>King David brought the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem; Dante calls him the "singer" because he was the traditional author of the Psalms.</note>
**H**e now knows the merit of his song,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Insofar as it was the fruit of his own will,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;By the reward which is equally great.
**D**f the five that form the circle of my eyebrow,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;He who stays closest to my beak
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Consoled the widow for her son: <note>This is the Roman Emperor Trajan. A popular medieval legend claimed he was so just that he delayed a war to help a widow whose son had been killed.</note>
**H**e now knows how dearly it costs
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Not to follow Christ, through the experience
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Of this sweet life and of its opposite. <note>Trajan, a pagan, was said to have been resurrected briefly by the prayers of Pope Gregory the Great so that he could convert and be saved; thus he knows both Limbo/Hell and Heaven.</note>
**A**nd he who follows in the circumference
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Of which I speak, along the upper arch,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Delayed death through true repentance:
**H**e now knows that eternal judgment
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Is not changed, even though a worthy prayer
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Makes today’s event happen tomorrow. <note>King Hezekiah, whose life was extended by fifteen years after he prayed to God. Dante notes that divine providence accounts for such prayers without "changing" its eternal nature.</note>
**T**he next who follows, with the laws and with me,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;With a good intention that bore bad fruit,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Made himself Greek in order to give way to the Shepherd: <note>The Emperor Constantine moved the capital of the Roman Empire to Byzantium (making himself "Greek") to leave Rome to the Pope (the "Shepherd"). Dante highlights that Constantine's intent was good, even if the result—the Church's temporal power—was disastrous.</note>
**H**e now knows how the evil resulting
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;From his good deed does not harm him,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Even though the world is brought to ruin by it."

## D 3

And he whom you see on the downward arc,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Was William; for whom that land laments
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which now weeps for the living Charles and Frederick: <note>William II "the Good," King of Sicily (1166–1189). Dante contrasts his just rule with his successors, Charles II of Anjou and Frederick II of Aragon, whom Dante despised as corrupt.</note>
Now he knows how heaven falls in love
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;With a just king; and by the appearance
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Of his radiance, he shows it still.
Who would believe, down in the erring world,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That Ripheus the Trojan in this circle <note>Ripheus is a character from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, described as "the most just among the Trojans." His presence in Heaven is a profound example of Dante's belief in the mysterious reach of God’s grace.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Should be the fifth of these holy lights?
Now he knows much of what the world
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Cannot see of divine grace;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Although his sight cannot discern the depths. <note>original: "non discerna il fondo." This refers to the "unfathomable" nature of God's judgment and the mystery of why some are saved and others are not.</note>
Like the little lark that soars in the air,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;First singing, and then falls silent, content
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;With the final sweetness that satisfies it;
So seemed to me the image of the imprint
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Of the eternal pleasure; by whose desire
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Each thing becomes exactly what it is.
And although I was to my own doubting
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Like glass to the color that covers it, <note>Dante means his doubt was perfectly visible on his face, just as a colored backing shows through glass.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;It could not endure to wait in silence:
But from my mouth, "What things are these?"
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;It pushed out with the force of its own weight:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Wherefore I saw great festivities of sparkling.
Then afterward with its eye more kindled,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The blessed sign replied to me,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So as not to keep me suspended in wonder:
"I see that you believe these things
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Because I say them; but you do not see how:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So that, though believed, they are hidden."

## d

**F**ai come quei; che la cosa per nome
*You act like one who learns a thing by name*
*Apprende ben; ma la sua quiditate*
*Quite well, but its true essence* <note>original: "quiditate." A Scholastic term referring to the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing.</note>
*Veder non puote, s'altri non la prome.*
*He cannot see, unless another reveals it.*
**R**egnum cælorum uiolentia pate
*The kingdom of heaven suffers violence* <note>original: "Regnum cælorum uiolentia pate." A reference to Matthew 11:12. Dante interprets this "violence" not as an assault, but as God's will being "conquered" by the intensity of human love and hope.</note>
*Da caldo amore, & da uiua speranza;*
*From burning love and from living hope,*
*Che uince la diuina uolontate,*
*Which overcomes the divine will,*
**N**on a guisa che l'huomo a l'huom souranza:
*Not in the way that one man overpowers another;*
*Ma uince lei, perche uol esser uinta:*
*But it overcomes it because it wishes to be overcome,*
*Et uinta uince con sua beninanza.*
*And, being overcome, it triumphs through its own goodness.*
**L**a prima uita del aglio & la quinta
*The first life of the eyebrow and the fifth* <note>The "eyebrow" of the Eagle. The first is the Emperor Trajan; the fifth is Ripheus the Trojan.</note>
*Ti fa marauigliar; perche ne uedi*
*Make you marvel, because you see*
*La region de gliangeli dipinta.*
*The region of the angels adorned by them.*
**D**' e corpi suoi non uscir, come credi,
*They did not leave their bodies, as you believe,*
*Gentili; ma Christiani in ferma fede*
*As Gentiles; but as Christians, firm in faith:*
*Quel de passuri, & quel de passi piedi:*
*One in the feet that were to suffer, and one in the feet that had already suffered.* <note>Ripheus believed in the future Christ (to suffer); Trajan believed in the Christ who had already lived and died (already suffered).</note>
**C**he l'una da l'inferno, u non si riede
*For the one returned from Hell, where no one ever returns*
*Giamai a buon uoler, torno a l'ossa;*
*To a state of good will, back to his bones;* <note>According to legend, St. Gregory the Great prayed for the soul of the Roman Emperor Trajan. Trajan was briefly resurrected to life so that he might choose Christ and be saved.</note>
*Et cio di uiua speme fu mercede,*
*And this was the reward of living hope,*
**D**i uiua speme; che mise sua possa
*Of living hope, which placed its power*
*N'e prieghi fatti a Dio per suscitarla;*
*In the prayers made to God to raise him up,*
*Si che potesse sua uoglia esser mossa.*
*So that his will might be moved.*
**L'** anima gloriosa, onde si parla,
*The glorious soul of whom we speak,*
*Tornata ne la carne, in che fu poco,*
*Having returned to the flesh, wherein he stayed but a short time,*
*Credette in lui, che poteua aiutarla:*
*Believed in Him who had the power to help him;*
**E** t credendo s'accese in tanto foco
*And by believing, he was kindled with such a fire*
*Di uero amor; ch' a la morte seconda*
*Of true love, that at his second death,*
*Fu degna di uenire a questo gioco.*
*He was worthy to come to this place of joy.*
**L'** altra per gratia; che da si profonda
*The other, through grace—which flows from a fountain*
*Fontana stilla, che mai creatura*
*So deep that no creature*
*Non pinse l'occhio infino a la prim' onda;*
*Ever pushed its eye to the first wave;* <note>This refers to Ripheus. Dante explains that the origins of Divine Grace are so deep they are hidden from all created beings.</note>

# PAR.
## D 4

He placed all his love below on righteousness:
Therefore, from grace to grace, God opened
His eye to our future <term>redemption</term>: <note>Dante is explaining how Ripheus, a minor character from Virgil's *Aeneid*, could be in Heaven. He suggests that God granted Ripheus a "revelation" of the future Christ as a reward for his perfect justice.</note>
Wherefore he believed in it; and no longer endured
From then on the stench of <term>paganism</term>;
And he rebuked the perverse people for it.
Those three ladies served as his <term>baptism</term>; <note>The "three ladies" are the Theological Virtues: Faith, Hope, and Charity. Dante suggests that for the righteous who lived before Christ, these virtues functioned as a spiritual baptism.</note>
Whom you saw by the right wheel;
More than a thousand years before baptizing began.
O <term>predestination</term>, how remote
Is your root from the sight of those
Who do not see the First Cause in its entirety!
And you mortals, hold yourselves back
From judging; for we, who see God,
Do not yet know all the <term>elect</term>: <note>The "elect" are those chosen by God for salvation. Even the souls in Paradise do not fully understand the mystery of who is saved and why.</note>
And such a deficiency is sweet to us:
Because our good is refined in this good;
That what God wills, we also will.
Thus from that <term>divine image</term>,
To clear my short-sighted vision,
A sweet medicine was given to me.
And as a good <term>lutanist</term> <note>original: "citharista." A player of the cithara or lute. Dante uses the image of a musician following a singer to describe how the spirits of Trajan and Ripheus synchronized their movements with the Eagle's voice.</note>
Makes the vibration of the string follow the good singer,
Whereby the song gains more pleasure;
So, while it spoke, I remember
That I saw the two blessed lights,
Just as the blinking of eyes is synchronized,
Move their little flames with the words.

<meta>This page transitions from the Heaven of Jupiter to the Heaven of Saturn (Canto XXI). The previous page concluded the discourse on divine justice and the salvation of the righteous. Here, Dante and Beatrice ascend to the sphere of the contemplative spirits.</meta>

# P A R.

Already my eyes were fixed again upon the face
Of my lady, and my soul with them;
And from every other intent it had withdrawn:
And she was not smiling; but, "If I were to smile,"
She began to me, "you would become like
<term>Semele</term> <note>In Greek mythology, Semele was a mortal lover of Jupiter who insisted on seeing him in his full divine glory; the sight was so intense that she was instantly incinerated.</note> was, when she turned to ashes:
Because my beauty, which along the stairs
Of the eternal palace kindles even more,
As you have seen, the higher one ascends;
If it were not tempered, it shines so brightly
That your mortal power, at its flash,
Would seem like a branch that a thunderbolt shatters.
We have risen to the <term>seventh splendor</term>; <note>The planet Saturn, the seventh of the nine celestial spheres in Dante's cosmos.</note>
Which, beneath the breast of the <term>burning Lion</term>, <note>The zodiac sign of Leo. In the spring of 1300, the setting of the poem, Saturn was positioned in Leo; the "valor" or influence of the planet is said to be "mingled" with the fiery nature of the constellation.</note>
Now radiates downward mingled with its power.
Fix your mind behind your eyes;
And make of them a mirror for the figure
Which in this mirror shall appear to you."
Anyone who knew what the nourishment
Of my sight was in her blessed countenance,
When I turned my attention to another task,
Would recognize how pleasing it was to me
To obey my <term>heavenly guide</term>, <note>Beatrice, Dante's guide through Paradise, who represents Divine Revelation.</note>
By weighing one side against the other.
Within the crystal that bears the name—
As it circles the world—of its beloved leader,
Under whom all malice lay dead; <note>A reference to the Golden Age of mythology, ruled by Saturn (Saturnus), a time of primordial peace and innocence.</note>
Of the color of gold, through which a ray shines,
I saw a <term>ladder</term> <note>The Jacob's Ladder of contemplation, representing the soul's ascent to God through meditative prayer.</note> raised so far upward
That my sight could not follow it.

I also saw descending down the steps

# P A R.

**Y**ou have mortal hearing, just as you have mortal sight;
> He replied to me: "Therefore, here we do not sing,
> For the same reason Beatrice does not smile." <note>Dante has just entered the Seventh Heaven, the sphere of Saturn. Here, the divine light is so intense that if Beatrice were to smile or if the souls were to sing, Dante’s mortal senses would be overwhelmed and destroyed.</note>

**I**ts power, joined with my vision,

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Saint Peter Damian in the Seventh Heaven. Having previously explained that the souls' actions are governed by divine love rather than individual preference, he now addresses Dante's specific question regarding why he, out of all the souls, was chosen by providence to greet the poet. # P A R.

**B**ut even that soul in heaven who is most enlightened,
> That <term>seraph</term> <note>original: "seraphin"; the highest order of angels, known for their burning love and most direct vision of God.</note> who has his eye most fixed on God,
> Will not satisfy your request:

**B**ecause what you ask is so deeply hidden
> Within the <term>abyss</term> <note>original: "abisso"; refers here to the unfathomable depth of God's wisdom.</note> of the eternal statute,
> That it is cut off from every created vision.

**A**nd when you return to the mortal world,
> Report this; so that humanity does not presume
> To move its feet toward such a goal any longer.

**T**he mind, which shines here, on earth smokes:
> Therefore, consider how it can do down there
> That which it cannot do even though heaven takes it in. <note>Damian argues that if even the most enlightened souls in Heaven cannot fully grasp God’s secret designs, it is impossible for human minds on earth—shrouded in the "smoke" of mortality—to understand them.</note>

**H**is words so restricted me
> That I left the question and drew back
> To ask humbly who he was.

"**B**etween two shores of Italy rise rocks,
> And not very far from your homeland,
> So high that the thunders sound much lower:

**A**nd they form a hump called **Catria**; <note>Mount Catria in the Apennines. The "two shores" are the Adriatic and the Tyrrhenian seas.</note>
> Below which a <term>hermitage</term> <note>original: "hermo"; specifically the monastery of Fonte Avellana.</note> is consecrated,
> Which used to be dedicated to <term>latria</term> <note>original: "latria"; a Greek-derived theological term for the supreme worship offered to God alone, as distinguished from the honor given to saints.</note> alone."

**T**hus he began his third speech to me:
> And then, continuing, he said: "There,
> In the service of God, I became so firm;

**T**hat with only food seasoned with the <term>liquor of olives</term> <note>original: "liquor d'uliui"; olive oil. This signifies his strictly vegetarian, ascetic diet.</note>
> I easily passed through the heats and frosts,
> Content in <term>contemplative</term> thoughts.

**T**hat <term>cloister</term> <note>original: "chiostro"; the monastery.</note> used to yield to these heavens
> A fertile harvest: but now it has become so barren
> That it must soon be revealed."

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Saint Peter Damian in the Seventh Heaven (Saturn). Having previously explained that the souls' actions are governed by divine love rather than individual preference, he now addresses Dante's specific question regarding why he, out of all the souls, was chosen by providence to greet the poet. This leads into Peter Damian’s autobiographical account of his life as an ascetic monk.</meta>

# P A R.

**I**n that place I was Peter Damian; <note>Peter Damian (c. 1007–1072) was a reformist monk and cardinal known for his strict asceticism.</note>
And I was Peter the Sinner in the House
Of Our Lady on the Adriatic shore. <note>original: "Pietro peccator"; Damian refers to himself by this humble title. The "House of Our Lady" refers to the monastery of Santa Maria in Porto near Ravenna.</note>
**L**ittle of mortal life was left to me
When I was called and drawn to that hat,
Which is only poured from bad to worse. <note>The "hat" refers to the cardinal’s red hat. Damian laments the corruption of the high Church offices in Dante's time.</note>
**C**ephas came, and the great vessel <note>original: "Cephas"; the Aramaic name for Saint Peter, meaning "rock." The "great vessel" (vasello) refers to Saint Paul, the "vessel of election."</note>
Of the Holy Spirit came, lean and barefoot,
Taking their food from whatever inn they found.
**N**ow the modern pastors want someone to prop them up
On either side, and someone to lead them—
They are so heavy!—and someone to lift them from behind.
**T**hey cover their horses with their flowing cloaks,
So that two beasts travel under a single skin:
O Patience, that you endure so much! <note>A biting satirical image: the priest and the horse are both "beasts" hidden under the same expensive fabric.</note>
**A**t this voice I saw many small flames
Descend from level to level and whirl about,
And every turn made them more beautiful.
**T**hey came around this soul and stopped,
And let out a cry of such a high sound
That it could not be compared to anything here;
**N**or did I understand it, so much did the thunder overcome me.

### XXII.

**O**verwhelmed with wonder, I turned to my guide
Like a little child who always runs back
To the place where he has the most confidence.
**A**nd she, like a mother who quickly succors
Her pale and breathless son
With her voice, which usually restores him, <note>Beatrice reassures Dante after the overwhelming "thunder" of the holy cry, which was a divine expression of outrage against Church corruption.</note>

**S**he said to me: "Do you not know you are in heaven?
And do you not know that heaven is entirely holy;
And that whatever is done here comes from righteous zeal?
**Y**ou can now imagine how their song would have transformed you,

**T**he sword of this place above does not strike in haste,

**A**s it pleased her, I directed my eyes;

**I** stood like one who suppresses within himself
The sting of desire, and does not dare
To ask; so much does he fear asking too much:
**A**nd the largest and most radiant
Of those pearls <term>margarite</term> <note>The souls are often described as "pearls" (margarite) due to their luminous, iridescent quality.</note> came forward,
To satisfy my will concerning itself.
**T**hen from within it I heard: "If you could see,
As I do, the charity that burns among us;
Your thoughts would have been expressed already.
**B**ut so that you, by waiting, do not delay
The reaching of your high goal; I will give you an answer
Even to the thought about which you are so hesitant."

<meta>This page continues the encounter in the Seventh Heaven (the Sphere of Saturn), where the contemplative souls reside. # P A R.

That mountain on whose slope Cassino lies
Was once frequented on its peak
By the deceived and ill-disposed people. <note>Saint Benedict refers to Monte Cassino in Italy; before he established his monastery there in 529 AD, the site was used for pagan worship of Apollo.</note>
**A**nd I am he who first carried up there
The name of Him who brought to earth
The truth that so uplifts us:

Men, kindled by that warmth
Which brings to life holy flowers and fruits.

Kept their feet firm and held their hearts steady.

**H**as so expanded my confidence,
As the sun does to the rose when it opens
As wide as its power allows.
**T**herefore I pray you—and Father, assure me—
If I may receive such grace that I
Might see you with your image unveiled." <note>Dante asks to see Benedict's actual human face, rather than the brilliant light that currently hides it.</note>
**W**hereupon he: "Brother, your high desire
Shall be fulfilled in the last sphere, <note>The Empyrean, the highest, non-physical heaven where God dwells and where the souls' true forms are visible.</note>

**T**here every desire is perfect, mature, and whole;
In that one alone
Is every part where it always was;

<meta>This page continues the speech of Saint Benedict in the Seventh Heaven (the Sphere of Saturn). Benedict is explaining to Dante that the ladder of contemplation leads to the Empyrean—the highest, motionless heaven—and laments how the monastic orders on earth have abandoned his Rule and fallen into corruption.</meta>

# P A R.

Because it is not in space, and has no poles: <note>Benedict refers to the Empyrean, the highest heaven, which unlike the other spheres is infinite and does not rotate on an axis.</note>
And our ladder reaches all the way to it;
Wherefore it vanishes thus from your sight.
High up there, the Patriarch
Jacob saw its upper part extending,
When it appeared to him so laden with angels. <note>A reference to the biblical "Jacob's Ladder" (Genesis 28), a symbol of the path to the divine.</note>
But to climb it now, no one lifts
His feet from the earth; and my Rule
Remains below as a waste of paper.
The walls that used to be an abbey
Have become dens; and the monastic hoods
Are sacks full of rotten flour. <note>original: "farina ria"; Benedict uses a baking metaphor to describe the spiritual decay of the monks.</note>
But heavy usury is not taken so much
Against God's pleasure, as that fruit
Which makes the hearts of monks so foolish. <note>Benedict argues that the monks’ greed and misuse of Church funds is even more offensive to God than the sin of usury (lending money at interest).</note>
For whatever the Church guards, belongs
Entirely to the people who ask in God's name,
Not to relatives, or other uglier things. <note>A critique of nepotism; Church wealth should go to the poor, not the families of the clergy.</note>
The flesh of mortals is so weak
That a good beginning does not last down there
From the sprouting of the oak to the forming of the acorn.
Peter began without gold or silver,
And I with prayer and with fasting,
And Francis humbly began his brotherhood. <note>Refers to Saint Peter (the first Pope), Saint Benedict, and Saint Francis of Assisi, emphasizing their original commitment to poverty.</note>
And if you look at the beginning of each,
Then look again at where it has strayed,
You will see the white has turned to dark.
Truly, the Jordan being turned back, <note>A reference to the miracle in Joshua 3 where the Jordan River stopped flowing.</note>
And the sea fleeing when God willed, were more
Wondrous to hear than help would be here. <note>Benedict suggests that while the Church's corruption seems absolute, God has performed greater miracles in the past and can intervene again.</note>

<meta>This page continues Dante’s journey through the Eighth Heaven, the Sphere of the Fixed Stars. Having just looked back at the smallness of the Earth, Dante now turns his gaze forward to witness a spectacular celestial vision prepared by Beatrice.</meta>

# P A R.

Like the bird among her beloved leaves,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;having rested on the nest of her sweet chicks
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;through the night that hides all things from us;
who, in order to see their longed-for faces
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;and to find the food with which to feed them—
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;a heavy labor that is a joy to her—

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;and alert, turned toward that region <note>The meridian, the highest point of the heavens where the sun appears to move slowest.</note>

so that seeing her in such suspense and longing,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I became like a man who, desiring something else,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;finds peace in his own hope.
But little time passed between one "when" and the other;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I mean the time of my waiting and the time of seeing
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;the heavens becoming brighter and brighter.
And Beatrice said: "Behold the hosts
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;of the triumph of Christ, and all the fruit
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;gathered from the revolving of these spheres!" <note>Beatrice explains that the souls now appearing are the result of the influence of the celestial heavens on humanity.</note>
It seemed to me her face was all aflame,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;and her eyes were so full of gladness
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;that I must pass over them without description. <note>original: "senza costrutto"; literally 'without construction,' meaning the poet lacks the words or "mental building blocks" to describe such beauty.</note>
As in the serene nights of the full moon,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Trivia <note>An epithet for the goddess Diana, used here to represent the Moon.</note> smiles among the eternal nymphs <note>The stars.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;who paint the sky through all its depths;
I saw, high above thousands of lamps,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;a single Sun that kindled them all,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;just as our sun kindles the sights we see above: <note>The "Sun" is Christ, whose light illuminates the "lamps," which are the souls of the blessed.</note>

<summary>In the Sphere of the Fixed Stars, Beatrice anticipates the appearance of Christ’s triumph, which manifests as a brilliant, overwhelming light—a "Sun"—illuminating thousands of radiant souls.</summary>

> Which opened the paths between heaven and earth,

> Of such gratitude; that it is never erased

**E**nding thus my depiction of paradise,
The sacred poem must leap ahead,
Like one who finds his path cut off. <note>Dante often uses this "ineffability topos," admitting that human language and memory are insufficient to describe the highest reaches of Heaven.</note>
**M**ut whoever considers the weight of the theme,
And the mortal shoulder that takes on the burden,

**N**on-trivial is the voyage for a small boat,
Which my daring prow goes cutting through,
Nor for a pilot who would spare himself. <note>Dante warns that his poem is now entering "deep waters" of theology and high mystery that require intense effort from both writer and reader.</note>
**P**erhaps it is because my face so enamors you,

Yielded myself once more
To the battle of my weak eyelids. <note>Dante refers to the "battle" of trying to see despite the overwhelming brightness of the divine light.</note>
**C**ome as a ray of sun, which streams pure
Through a broken cloud, has seen a meadow of flowers
While the eyes themselves were covered by shadow;
**V**isionary, I saw thus many crowds of splendors,
Struck from above by burning rays,
Without seeing the source of that brightness. <note>Dante sees the saints (the "flowers") illuminated by Christ (the "sun"). Christ has pulled His immediate presence upward so that Dante can look at the saints without being blinded by the direct source of the light.</note>
**O** kindly Power, who so stamps your mark upon them,
You raised yourself up to give space

**I**nvoking the name of the beautiful flower, which I always

My soul was drawn to observe the greatest flame. <note>The "beautiful flower" is Mary. After Christ ascended, she remains the brightest light in this heavenly vision.</note>

<summary>Dante describes the limitations of his poetry when facing the divine and shifts his focus from Beatrice to the "heavenly garden." He observes the saints illuminated by the light of Christ, specifically focusing on the Virgin Mary as the brightest "flower" among them.</summary>

**S**o spoke Beatrice: and those happy souls

**T**herefore the pen leaps, and I do not write it:

Let alone our speech, is too vivid a color. <note>Dante frequently uses this "ineffability topos"—the idea that heavenly beauty is so intense it exceeds the capacity of human language and thought to describe it.</note>

Devoutly through your burning affection,

# PAR.

"If he loves well, and hopes well, and believes,
> It is not hidden from you, for you have your vision there
> Where every thing is seen as if painted." <note>Saint Peter, being in the presence of God, can already see the state of Dante's soul. However, he requires a spoken profession of faith to fulfill the requirements of this heavenly examination.</note>

> Through true faith, to glorify it,

Just as the bachelor <term>bachelor: in medieval universities, a student of theology who had the right to debate but not yet the final authority to determine the truth of a question</term> arms himself and does not speak

<meta>This page continues Dante’s "exam" on the nature of Faith, conducted by Saint Peter. Dante has just begun to answer Peter's question by citing Saint Paul's definition of faith as the "substance of things hoped for and the evidence of things not seen."</meta>

# PAR.

And I followed: "The deep things,
> Which grant me here the sight of them,
> Are so hidden from the eyes of those below;
That their existence there lies in belief alone,
> Upon which our high hope is founded:
> And therefore it takes the nature of 'substance': <note>Dante is explaining Saint Paul’s definition. Because we cannot see heaven while on Earth, we must treat our "belief" as the solid ground or "substance" upon which we build our hope for salvation.</note>
And from this belief we must
> Reason, without having any other sight:
> Therefore it holds the nature of 'argument.'" <note>In medieval logic, an "argument" is a proof. Since we lack physical evidence of God, Faith serves as the logical proof or "evidence" that allows us to reason about the divine.</note>
Then I heard: "If all that is acquired
> Down there as knowledge were understood this way,
> The sophist’s <term>sophist: a person who uses clever but false arguments, typically to deceive</term> wit would find no place there."
These words breathed from that ignited love:
> Then he added: "The alloy and the weight
> Of this coin have already been well examined. <note>Saint Peter uses a monetary metaphor, comparing Dante's definition of faith to a coin that has been checked for its gold content (alloy) and its heaviness (weight) to ensure it is not counterfeit.</note>
But tell me if you have it in your purse."
> And I: "Yes, I have it so bright and so round,
> That in its minting nothing is uncertain to me."
Then issued from the deep light
> That was shining there: "This dear jewel,
> Upon which every virtue is founded;
Where did it come from to you?" And I: "The generous rain
> Of the Holy Spirit, which is poured
> Over the old and over the new skins, <note>original: "ueccie e'n ſu le nuoue cuoia". The "skins" refer to the parchment made of animal hides upon which the Old and New Testaments were written.</note>
Is a syllogism <term>syllogism: a form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two given premises</term> that has proven it to me
> So sharply, that compared to it,
> Every other demonstration seems blunt to me."
I heard then: "The ancient and the new
> Propositions, which conclude so for you,
> Why do you hold them to be divine speech?"

<summary>Dante explains the logical necessity of Faith as a foundation for hope and reasoning. Saint Peter approves of his definition and asks Dante where his faith comes from, to which Dante credits the inspiration of the Holy Spirit found in the Bible.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Dante’s "exam" on the nature of Faith, conducted by Saint Peter. Dante has just argued that the scriptures are the foundation of his belief. Saint Peter is now pushing him to provide logical proof for the validity of those scriptures.</meta>

# PAR.

**A**nd I replied: "The proof that unfolds the truth to me are the works that followed; for which nature never heated iron nor struck an anvil." <note>Dante is arguing that the miracles performed by the Apostles are the proof of the Bible's divine truth. He describes miracles as supernatural events that "nature" could never produce on its own, like metal that wasn't forged in a physical fire or on a physical anvil.</note>

**R**eply was made to me: "Tell me, who assures you that those works actually happened? The very thing that needs proving—the scripture itself—is your only witness; no one else swears it to you." <note>Saint Peter is playing the "devil's advocate" here, pointing out a circular argument: Dante is using miracles to prove the Bible, but he only knows about the miracles because they are written in the Bible.</note>

**S**hould the world have turned to Christianity," I said, "without miracles, that alone is such a miracle that all the others are not even a hundredth of it:

**F**or you entered the field poor and hungry to sow the good plant, which was once a fertile vine but has now become a thornbush." <note>Dante tells Peter that the greatest miracle was the conversion of the Roman world by a few poor, simple men. He adds a sharp critique of the Church of his own time, noting that the "vine" Peter planted has withered into a "pruno" (a thorny briar) due to corruption.</note>

**F**inished with this, the high holy court resounded through the spheres with a *'We praise Thee, O God'* <note>original: *Dio lodiamo*, referring to the hymn *Te Deum Laudamus*</note> in the melody that is sung up there in Heaven.

**A**nd that baron—who, examining me from branch to branch, had already led me so far that we were approaching the final leaves— <note>Dante refers to Saint Peter as a "baron," a term of high nobility in the celestial court, continuing the metaphor of their conversation as a tree of knowledge.</note>

**B**egan again: "Grace, which holds court with your lady <note>Dante refers to Beatrice, who is guiding him from above.</note>, has opened your mouth until now just as it ought to be opened;

**S**o that I approve of what has emerged from it; but now you must express what it is you believe, and the source from which your belief was offered to you."

"**O** holy father, spirit who sees what you once believed so strongly that you outdid younger feet in racing toward the tomb," <note>Dante refers to the Gospel of John (20:3–6). Although the "younger" Apostle John reached Jesus's empty tomb first, it was Peter who first had the faith and boldness to enter it.</note>

**I** began: "You wish for me to reveal the substance of my ready faith here, and you have also asked for the cause of it."

<summary>Dante argues that the conversion of the world to Christianity is itself the greatest miracle, proving the faith's divine origin. Saint Peter accepts this and asks Dante to move from the evidence of faith to the specific content of his personal creed.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Canto XXIV of Paradiso, where Dante finishes his "exam" on Faith given by Saint Peter. Having established the scriptures as his foundation, Dante now provides his personal profession of faith in the Trinity. The text then transitions into the famous opening of Canto XXV, where Dante reflects on his long labor writing the Divine Comedy and his hope for an end to his exile.</meta>

# P A R.

**A**nd I answer you: I believe in one God,
> Sole and eternal; who moves all the heavens,
> Himself unmoved, with love and with desire: <note>Dante draws on Aristotelian philosophy here, describing God as the "Unmoved Mover" who sets the universe in motion through the attraction of divine love.</note>
**A**nd for such belief I have not only proofs
> Physical and metaphysical; but it is also given to me
> By the truth that rains down from here
**T**hrough Moses, through prophets, through psalms,
> Through the Gospel, and through you [Apostles] who wrote,
> After the glowing Spirit made you holy. <note>The "glowing spirit" refers to the Holy Spirit descending as tongues of fire at Pentecost.</note>
**A**nd I believe in three eternal persons; and these
> I believe to be one essence, so singular and so threefold,
> That it admits the joined "they are" and "is." <note>original Latin: *sunt* (they are) and *este* (is). Dante is explaining the mystery of the Trinity: God is simultaneously three persons (plural) and one essence (singular).</note>
**O**f this profound Divine condition,
> Which I now touch upon, the Gospel doctrine
> Seals the image upon my mind many times.
**T**his is the principle: this is the spark
> Which then spreads into a living flame;
> And like a star in the sky, it scintillates within me.
**L**ike a lord who hears what pleases him,
> And then embraces his servant, congratulating him
> For the news, as soon as he is silent;
**S**o, blessing me and singing,
> The apostolic light—at whose command
> I had spoken—circled me three times
**A**s soon as I was silent; so much did I please him in my speech.

### XXV

**I**f it should ever happen that the sacred poem,
> To which both heaven and earth have set their hand,
> So that it has made me lean for many years, <note>Dante refers to the physical and mental exhaustion caused by the many years he spent writing the *Divine Comedy*.</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the end of Canto XXIV, where Saint Peter finishes examining Dante on the nature of Faith, into the beginning of Canto XXV. Having received Saint Peter's blessing, Dante begins with a poignant reflection on his exile from Florence before being introduced to Saint James for his next examination, this time on the subject of Hope.</meta>

# P A R.

Let the cruelty be overcome that locks me out
*From the fair sheepfold where I slept as a lamb,* <note>The "fair sheepfold" is Florence, Dante’s beloved home, from which he was exiled in 1302. The "wolves" are the political enemies who cast him out.</note>
*An enemy to the wolves that war against it;*
With another voice now, and with another fleece
*I shall return as a poet; and at the font*
*Of my baptism, I shall take the crown:* <note>Dante expresses his lifelong hope that his poetry would eventually allow him to return to Florence and be crowned as a Poet Laureate at the Baptistery of San Giovanni, where he was baptized.</note>
Because into the faith, which makes souls
*Known to God, I entered there; and then*
*Peter, for its sake, thus circled my brow.* <note>Referring to the end of the previous Canto, where Saint Peter circled Dante three times as a sign of approval.</note>
Then a light moved toward us
*From that circle whence the first-fruit came,*
*Whom Christ left among his vicars.* <note>The "first-fruit" refers to the early leaders of the Church; here, it signifies the Apostle James.</note>
And my lady, full of joy,
*Said to me: "Look, look! Behold the Baron,* <note>In medieval literature, the Apostles were often given the chivalric title of "Baron."</note>
*For whose sake Galicia is visited below."* <note>Galicia refers to Santiago de Compostela in Spain, the site of the famous pilgrimage to the tomb of Saint James.</note>
Just as when the dove alights
*Near its companion, and each one pours out*
*Its affection by circling and murmuring;*
So I saw one great, glorious prince
*Be received by the other,*
*Praising the food that is eaten up there.* <note>The "food" refers to the divine grace and joy found in Heaven.</note>

Had imposed silence on every side;

**A**nd the power that her gaze granted me
Tore me away from the <term>beautiful nest of Leda</term>,

<meta>This page continues Beatrice’s explanation as they enter the Primum Mobile, the ninth and outermost of the physical heavens. Having just left the Heaven of the Fixed Stars, Beatrice describes the nature of this swiftest sphere, which governs the motion of all the others beneath it, before shifting into a lament on the corruption of humanity on Earth.</meta>

# PAR.

**A**nd this heaven has no other "where"
Than in the Divine Mind, wherein is kindled
The love that turns it, and the power it rains down. <note>The "Primum Mobile" (First Mover) is the largest and fastest of the celestial spheres. In Dante’s universe, it is not contained by any physical space, but exists only within the mind of God.</note>
**L**ight and love enfold it in a single circle,
Even as it enfolds the others; and that border
Only He who girt it understands. <note>original: "quel precinto / Colui che'l uolge, solamente intende." The "precinct" or boundary of the highest heaven is known only to God, who surrounds all of creation with His light and love.</note>
**I**ts motion is not measured by another,
But all the others are measured by this one,
Just as ten is measured by its half and its fifth. <note>Dante uses a mathematical analogy: just as the number 10 is the product of its factors (5 and 2), the movement of the lower heavens (time) is calculated based on the movement of this sphere. It is the "universal clock" of the cosmos.</note>
**A**nd how time should have its roots
Within such a flower-pot, and in the others its leaves,
Can now be made manifest to you. <note>A beautiful metaphor for time: its "roots" are in the invisible Primum Mobile, while its visible "leaves" (days, months, years) are seen in the lower spheres like the Sun and Moon.</note>

The strength to raise their eyes above your waves!
**T**he will in men may blossom well,
But the constant downpour of worldly desire turns
The true plums into <term>blighted fruit</term>. <note>original: "bozzacchioni"; these are plums that have been stunted or shriveled by excessive rain or parasites, never reaching maturity. Dante uses this to describe how human potential is ruined by corruption.</note>

**A**nd another, stammering, loves and listens
To his mother, who, when he speaks plainly,
Then longs to see her buried in her grave.

At the first sight of the beautiful daughter
Of him who brings the morning and leaves the evening. <note>This "beautiful daughter" is a famously difficult image. Most scholars interpret it as human nature, which is the "daughter" of the Sun (symbolizing God). The passage laments how quickly human innocence turns to darkness under the influence of the world.</note>

<summary>Beatrice explains the metaphysical nature of the Primum Mobile as the source of time and motion, then delivers a scathing critique of human greed and the loss of childhood innocence.</summary>

**A**fter *she who "paradises" my mind* <note>original: "enparadisa." A beautiful neologism invented by Dante to describe how Beatrice elevates his intellect and soul to the state of Heaven.</note>

Here, in the spiritual realm, the speed increases as one gets *closer* to the center (God).</note>

<meta>This page continues Beatrice’s explanation in Canto XXVIII of the Paradiso. On the previous page, Dante noted a discrepancy: in the physical world, the outermost spheres move fastest and are most divine, but in this spiritual vision, it is the innermost ring—the one closest to the point of Light (God)—that is the swiftest and most brilliant. Here, Beatrice explains this paradox by distinguishing between physical size and spiritual power.</meta>

# PAR.

**B**ut in the sensible world one can <note>The "sensible world" refers to the physical universe perceivable by the senses.</note>
*See the spheres become so much more divine,*
*The further they are distant from the center.* <note>In the medieval Earth-centered model of the universe, the spheres furthest from the Earth (the center) were considered more perfect and holy.</note>
**T**herefore, if my desire is to find its end
*In this wondrous and angelic temple,*
*Which has only love and light for its boundary;* <note>The "angelic temple" is the Empyrean, the highest, non-physical heaven.</note>
**I** must still hear how the model
*And the original do not follow the same pattern:*
*For I, on my own, contemplate this in vain.* <note>original: "l’exemplo Et l’exemplare." Dante is struggling to understand why the physical "copy" of the universe (the model) does not look like the spiritual "original" (the exemplar) he is seeing now.</note>
**I**f your fingers are not sufficient for such a knot,
*It is no wonder;*
*For it has grown so hard from never being tried.* <note>Beatrice compares the intellectual problem to a tight knot that has become difficult to untie because no one has attempted to solve it.</note>
**S**o spoke my lady; then she said: "Take
*What I shall tell you, if you wish to be satisfied;*
*And sharpen your wits around it.*
**T**he physical circles are wide or narrow
*According to the greater or lesser power*
*Which is spread through all their parts.*
**G**reater goodness wishes to work greater well-being; <note>original: "salute," which can mean health, salvation, or well-being. Here it refers to the divine influence radiated by the heavens.</note>
*Greater well-being requires a greater body,*
*If its parts are equally perfected.*
**T**herefore this sphere, which sweeps along
*The whole high universe with it, corresponds*
*To the ring that loves the most and knows the most.* <note>Beatrice explains that the largest physical sphere (the Primum Mobile) corresponds to the smallest spiritual ring (the Seraphim) because both possess the highest degree of "virtue" or power.</note>
**F**or if you apply your measure to the power,
*And not to the outward appearance*
*Of the substances that appear round to you;*
**Y**ou will see a marvelous agreement
*Of greater to more, and smaller to less,*
*In every heaven, according to its governing intelligence.* <note>original: "intelligenza." In Dante's time, it was believed that each celestial sphere was moved and governed by an "Intelligence"—an angelic mind.</note>

<summary>Beatrice resolves Dante's confusion by explaining that while the physical universe is measured by size, the spiritual realm is measured by "virtue" or power, creating a perfect correspondence between the two.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Canto XXVIII of Dante Alighieri’s Paradiso. Having just received an explanation from Beatrice regarding the inverse relationship between the physical heavens and the spiritual angelic circles, Dante’s confusion clears. On this page, he witnesses the immense number of the angelic host and begins to learn the specific names of the hierarchies.</meta>

Just as the hemisphere of the air remains
Splendid and serene, when the North Wind <note>original: "Borea." The North Wind, specifically the North-East wind which was thought to clear the sky of clouds.</note> blows
From that cheek where he is mildest,
Because the mist is purged and dissolved,
Which before troubled the air, so that heaven smiles
With the beauties of all its regions; <note>original: "paroffia," literally "parish," used here to mean the various quarters of the sky.</note>
So did I become, after my lady provided me
With her clear answer;

While it boils, than the circles sparked.
Every spark followed the blaze;

Increases into the thousands more than the doubling of the chessboard. <note>original: "sciochi." To the fixed point that keeps them at their "where," <note>original: "ubi." A Latin philosophical term used to denote a fixed location or place in space.</note>

Within my mind, said: "The first circles
Have shown you the Seraphim and the Cherubim. <note>The Seraphim and Cherubim are the two highest orders in the celestial hierarchy.</note>
They follow their bonds <note>original: "uimi," literally "osier-ties" or "willow-bonds," referring to the divine attraction that pulls them.</note> so swiftly,
To resemble the Point <note>The "Point" is the infinitesimal point of blinding light representing God.</note> as much as they can;
And they can do so in proportion to the sublimity of their vision.
Those other loves that circle around them
Are called Thrones of the divine aspect,
Because they completed the first triad. <note>original: "ternaro." The first grouping of three angelic ranks: Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones.</note>
And you should know that they all have delight
In proportion to how deeply their vision penetrates
Into the Truth, in which every intellect finds peace."

<meta>This page continues Beatrice’s explanation in Canto XXVIII of the Paradiso. *Not on the act of love, which follows after:*
**A** nd the measure of this seeing is merit,
*Which grace brings forth, and good will:*
*Thus, from grade to grade, the soul proceeds.*
**T** he second triad <note>original: "ternaro." The angels are organized into three hierarchies, each containing three orders.</note>, which blossoms thus
*In this eternal springtime*
*That the nightly Ram does not despoil,* <note>The constellation Aries (the Ram) is visible at night in autumn. Dante is describing a celestial spring that never turns to winter or autumn.</note>
**P** erpetually sings "Hosanna" <note>original: "suerna." A poetic verb meaning to sing like a bird at the end of winter.</note>

**T** hen in the two penultimate dances,

*The last is entirely of Angelic games.* <note>original: "Angelici ludi." The lowest order is simply called "Angels." Dante refers to their movement as "games" or "play" to suggest their divine joy.</note>
**T** hese orders all gaze upward,
*And downward they prevail so that toward God*
*All are drawn, and all draw the others.*
**A** nd Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 1st-century convert who was traditionally (though incorrectly) credited with writing "The Celestial Hierarchy," the primary medieval source for these ranks.</note> with such great desire

*For he who saw it here above revealed it to him.* <note>Dante explains that Dionysius knew the "truth" because he was a student of St. Paul, who was believed to have seen the third heaven during his lifetime.</note>

### XXIX.

**W**hen both of the children of Latona, <note>The sun (Apollo) and the moon (Diana), the twin children of the goddess Latona. Dante is describing a moment when the sun and moon are perfectly balanced on opposite sides of the horizon.</note>

**S**o long, with a face painted with a smile,
*did Beatrice remain silent, looking*
*fixedly at the Point that had overwhelmed me;* <note>The "Point" is God, whom Dante saw as a piercingly bright light in the previous Canto.</note>
**T**hen she began: "I speak, and do not ask
*what you wish to hear; for I have seen it*
*where every 'where' and every 'when' is fixed as a point.* <note>Beatrice sees Dante's thoughts reflected in God, the eternal center where all space (where) and time (when) originate.</note>
**N**ot to gain any benefit for Himself,
*(which is not possible), but so that His splendor*
*could, in its reflection, say: 'I exist';* <note>original: "subsisto." God, being perfect, does not need to "gain" anything. He created the universe so that His light could have a conscious existence outside of Himself.</note>
**I**n His eternity, beyond the limits of time,
*beyond every other understanding, as it pleased Him,*
*Eternal Love opened into new loves.*
**N**or did He lie before then as if in sleep:
*for neither 'before' nor 'after' existed*
*before the movement of God upon these waters.* <note>A reference to the Book of Genesis. Dante explains that time itself was created along with the universe, so there was no "before" in a chronological sense.</note>
**F**orm and matter, both combined and pure,
*came forth into being, having no flaw,*
*like three arrows from a three-stringed bow:* <note>Dante uses the Aristotelian concepts of "Form" (pure spirit or soul) and "Matter" (physical substance). He suggests three things were created at once: pure spirit (angels), pure matter (the elements), and the combination of both (the physical heavens and humans).</note>
**A**nd as in glass, in amber, or in crystal,
*a ray of light shines so that from its arrival*
*to its full existence there is no interval;* <note>Dante emphasizes that the act of creation was instantaneous, like light passing through a transparent object.</note>

<summary>Beatrice begins a deep theological discourse on the creation of the universe, explaining that God created out of pure love to share His existence. She describes the instantaneous creation of spirit, matter, and the physical heavens, noting that time itself only began with this act.</summary>
<keywords>Creation, God, Beatrice, Latona, Sun and Moon, Form and Matter, Eternity, Divine Love, Angels</keywords>

Pure potentiality held the lowest part;
*in the middle, such a bond tied potential with act* <term>potentiality: the capacity of raw matter to become something</term>

*three fires of your desire are quenched.*
One could not reach twenty in counting

Those you see here were humble enough
to recognize themselves as products of that goodness

**F**or their vision was exalted
by illuminating grace and by their own merit,

**A**nd I do not want you to doubt, but be certain,

These substances, since they were made joyful <term>substances: the angels, who are "pure form" or spiritual substance</term>
