<summary>Beatrice explains that the faithful angels enjoy a permanent, uninterrupted vision of God, which eliminates their need for memory. She concludes by criticizing earthly philosophers and theologians for being led astray by vanity and complex, erroneous theories.</summary>

**E**ven this is tolerated here above
with less disdain than when Divine Scripture

**N**one think of how much blood it cost

**F**or the sake of display, everyone exerts their wit
and creates their own inventions; and these
are the themes of preachers, while the Gospel is silent.
**O**ne claims the moon turned back its course

**A**nd others claim the light withdrew itself
spontaneously; so that for Spaniards and for Indians,
just as for Jews, that eclipse took place. <note>Beatrice critiques the trivial "scientific" debates of the time regarding the darkness at the Crucifixion. **F**lorence does not have as many Lapi or Bindi <term>Lapi and Bindi: Very common nicknames in 14th-century Florence (short for Iacopo and Bernardo), similar to the modern English expression "every Tom, Dick, and Harry."</term>

from pulpits, year in and year out, on every side:
**S**o that the poor sheep, who do not know,
return from the pasture fed on nothing but wind; <note>The "sheep" are the faithful congregation; the "wind" represents the empty, useless words of the preachers that provide no spiritual nourishment.</note>
and not seeing their own loss does not excuse them.
**C**hrist did not say to his first assembly,
"Go and preach trifles to the world";
but gave to them a foundation of truth:
**A**nd that truth alone sounded from their lips;
so that, to do battle for the kindling of faith,
they made both shield and lance out of the Gospel.
**N**ow they go out to preach with jests and taunts;
and so long as they can raise a hearty laugh,
the preacher's hood puffs up, and nothing more is asked. <note>The "puffing of the hood" signifies the vanity and pride of the preacher who is satisfied merely by the applause of the crowd rather than the delivery of the truth.</note>

<summary>Beatrice delivers a stinging critique of contemporary preachers who prioritize entertainment and personal inventions over the Gospel. She contrasts these "fables" with the true mission of the Apostles, who used the Word of God as their only weapon.</summary>

### P A R.

**P**erhaps six thousand miles away from us <note>original: "semilia miglia". Dante uses a complex astronomical calculation to describe the hour before dawn. In medieval geography, 6,000 miles was approximately the distance the sun would be from the horizon an hour before it rises.</note>

Not only beyond our reach; but certainly I believe

**A**nd I saw light in the form of a river

Then, like people who have been under masks <note>original: "larue". In this context, it refers to masks or disguises used in pageantry or theater.</note>,

# PAR.

In the form, then, of a pure white rose
The holy militia <note>The "holy militia" refers to the Church Triumphant—the souls of the blessed who have triumphed over earthly sin and now reside in heaven.</note> was shown to me,
Whom Christ, with his own blood, made his bride.
But the other host <note>The angels.</note>, who as they fly behold and sing
The glory of Him who fills them with love,
And the goodness that made them so great;
Just like a swarm of bees, who dip into the flowers
In one moment, and in the next return
To where their hard work is turned into sweetness <note>original: "s’insapora" (becomes savory). This refers to the hive where honey is made; Dante compares the angels' return to God to bees returning to the hive.</note>;

To where their love <note>God.</note> always dwells.
Their faces were all of living flame,

That no snow ever reaches such a limit.
When they descended into the flower, from tier to tier,
They offered some of the peace and the ardor

Hinder the vision or the splendor:
For the divine light is so penetrating
Throughout the universe, according to its merit,
That nothing can stand in its way.
This secure and joyful kingdom,
Populated by people of both old and new times <note>Refers to those who believed in Christ to come (Old Testament figures) and those who believed in Christ after his coming (New Testament/Christian era).</note>,

O Triple Light <note>original: "trina luce". A reference to the Holy Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit).</note>, which in a single star
Sparkling in their sight, so satisfies them;
Look down here upon our storm <note>Dante contrasts the absolute peace of the Empyrean with the political and moral chaos of Earth ("our storm").</note>!

<meta>This page continues Dante’s first sight of the Empyrean, the highest heaven. Having just invoked the "Triple Light" of the Trinity, Dante now describes his overwhelming sense of awe by comparing his experience to that of a traveler from a remote land visiting the splendors of Rome.</meta>

# PAR.

If the Barbarians, coming from that region 
Which is covered every day by Helice <note>original: "Helice." In Greek mythology, this is Callisto, who was transformed into the constellation Ursa Major (the Great Bear).</note>

I, who had come to the divine from the human, 
To the eternal from time, 
And from Florence to a people just and sane, 
With what great wonder must I have been filled! 
Certainly, between that wonder and my joy, I was content 
To hear nothing and to remain silent.

And like a pilgrim who finds renewal 
By looking around the temple of his vow, 
And already hopes to tell others how it looked; 
So, walking through the living light, 
I moved my eyes along the rows <note>The tiers of the "white rose" where the blessed sit.</note>, 
Now up, now down, and now looking back again.

I saw faces made persuasive by charity, 
Graced by another’s light <note>The reflected light of God.</note> and their own smiles, 
And gestures adorned with every dignity. 
My gaze had already taken in 
The general form of paradise as a whole, 
But had not yet fixed my eyes on any one part:

And I turned with renewed desire 
To ask my lady <note>Beatrice.</note> about things 
That held my mind in suspense. 
I intended one thing, but another responded to me: 
I thought I would see Beatrice, but I saw an old man <note>original: "sene." This is Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, a famous medieval mystic who replaces Beatrice as Dante's final guide.</note> 
Dressed like those glorious people.

Benign joy was spread across his eyes and cheeks,

Without answering, I lifted my eyes

In the order formed by the third row of seats,
Rachel sits below Mary,
with Beatrice, just as you can see.
Sarah, Rebecca, Judith, and her <note>Refers to Ruth, the Moabite woman who married Boaz.</note>,

<meta>This page continues Canto XXXII of Paradiso. **N**ow behold the depth of divine providence <term>proueder diuino: the unfolding of God's plan for humanity</term>:
for both aspects of the faith <note>Those who believed in Christ before His coming and those who believed after.</note>
will fill this garden <term>giardino: a metaphor for the Celestial Rose or Heaven itself</term> in equal measure.

the midpoint of these two divisions <term>discretioni: the dividing lines of the Rose's seating</term> downwards,

**B**ut by the merit of others, under certain conditions;
for all these are spirits released <term>spiriti assolti: souls of the deceased</term>

**N**ow you are questioning, and in your doubt you are silent;

**F**or whatever you see is established

**T**he King, through whom this kingdom rests
in such love and in such delight

<center>H 2</center>

You are the one who so ennobled human nature
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;that its Creator <note>original: *fattore*</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;did not disdain to make Himself its creature <note>original: *fattura*. Dante highlights the paradox of the Incarnation, where God becomes a created being through Mary.</note>.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;higher toward the ultimate salvation <note>The direct vision of God.</note>.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;more than I do for his, offer all my prayers
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;to you, and pray they be not insufficient;
That you might scatter every cloud
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;of his mortality with your own prayers,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;so that the Supreme Pleasure <note>original: *sommo piacer*. God Himself.</note> may be unfolded to him.

<summary>This page contains the opening of Canto XXXIII, featuring Saint Bernard’s celebrated prayer to the Virgin Mary. He praises her role in the Incarnation and asks her to intercede so that Dante may behold the Divine Essence.</summary>
<keywords>Virgin Mary, Saint Bernard, prayer, Incarnation, Celestial Rose, intercession, Dante Alighieri, Paradiso</keywords>

--- Page 514 ---
<meta>This page continues from the conclusion of Saint Bernard’s prayer to the Virgin Mary in Canto XXXIII of the Paradiso. Having asked for Mary’s intercession, the narrative now shifts to the climax of the entire Divine Comedy: Dante’s direct vision of God.</meta>

# PAR.

**A**gain I pray to you, Queen, who can do
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;whatever you will; that you preserve his affections 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;sound after seeing so much.
**V**anquish his human impulses with your protection:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;See Beatrice, with so many of the blessed,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;folding their hands toward you to join my prayers.
**G**azing with eyes beloved and venerated by God,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;she <note>The Virgin Mary.</note> fixed her look upon those who prayed, showing us
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;how deeply pleasing devout prayers are to her.
**I**mmediately they were directed toward the eternal light;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;within which one cannot believe that any 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;creature's eye could penetrate so clearly.
**E**ven I, who was approaching the end of all desires <note>The "end of desires" refers to God, the ultimate object of all human longing.</note>,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;brought the heat of my longing
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;to its completion within me, as was only right.
**B**ernard signaled to me and smiled,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;indicating that I should look upward; but I was 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;already, of my own accord, doing as he wished:
**C**onsequently, my vision, becoming pure,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;entered deeper and deeper into the ray
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;of that high light, which is Truth in itself.
**D**irectly from that point on, my seeing was greater
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;than our speech, which fails at such a sight;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;and memory fails before such an overwhelming experience <note>original: *oltraggio*. Here Dante uses the term to mean an "excess" or "transgression" of the normal limits of human capacity.</note>.
**Q**uite like a man who sees things in a dream,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;and after the dream is over, the feeling it impressed 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;remains, while the rest does not return to the mind;
**C**learly so am I: for almost all of my vision 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;has faded away, yet the sweetness 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;born from it still drips into my heart.

<summary>In these lines from the final Canto of the Paradiso, Mary grants Saint Bernard's prayer, allowing Dante to look directly into the Light of God. Dante describes the "ineffability" of the experience—how his vision exceeded the capacity of human speech and memory to record it.</summary>
<keywords>Virgin Mary, Saint Bernard, Beatrice, Eternal Light, Ineffability, Divine Vision, Dante Alighieri, Paradiso</keywords>

--- Page 515 ---
<meta>This page continues from the final Canto of the Paradiso. Dante has just been granted the ultimate grace: the ability to look directly into the "Eternal Light" of God. This passage marks the beginning of his attempt to describe an experience that is essentially beyond human words and memory. Catchword: Dicendo; bleed-through from reverse page visible.</meta>

# PAR.

**H 3**

**T**hus the snow is unsealed by the sun;
**T**hus in the wind, on the light leaves,
**T**he Sibyl's prophecy was lost. <note>original: *sententia di sibilla*. Dante refers to the Cumaean Sibyl, who wrote her oracles on leaves. When the wind blew them away, the prophecy’s meaning was lost—just as Dante’s memory of his divine vision is fading.</note>
**O** supreme light, who rises so high
**A**bove mortal concepts, to my mind
**G**rant again a little of how you appeared;
**A**nd make my tongue so powerful
**T**hat even a single spark of your glory
**I** might leave to the people of the future:
**F**or by returning somewhat to my memory,
**A**nd by sounding a little in these verses,
**M**ore will be understood of your victory.
**I** believe that, because of the keenness I endured
**F**rom the living ray, I would have been lost
**I**f my eyes had turned away from it.
**A**nd I remember that I was more emboldened
**B**ecause of this to endure so much, until I joined
**M**y gaze with the infinite Goodness.
**O** abundant grace, through which I presumed
**T**o fix my look through the eternal light
**S**o far that I consumed my vision there.
**I**n its depths I saw contained,
**B**ound by love into a single volume,
**T**hat which is scattered in pages throughout the universe;
<term>Substance</term> <note>In the Aristotelian philosophy of Dante's era, "substance" refers to something that exists in itself (like a person or a rock).</note>, and <term>accident</term> <note>"Accidents" are qualities that only exist within a substance (like the color of a rock or the height of a person).</note>, and their relations,
**A**ll fused together in such a way
**T**hat what I describe is a simple light.
**T**he universal form of this knot <note>Dante uses the word "knot" (*nodo*) to describe the complex, miraculous way that God binds all the disparate parts of the universe into a single, unified whole.</note>
**I** believe I saw; because, in saying this,
**I** feel my joy expand more and more.

<summary>Dante describes how his memory of God is fading like melting snow or scattered leaves, yet he recounts the profound moment when he saw the entire universe—its objects, qualities, and relations—bound together in a single book of divine love.</summary>
<keywords>Dante Alighieri, Divine Vision, Sibyl, Scholasticism, Substance and Accident, Unity, Metaphor of the Book</keywords>

--- Page 516 ---
<meta>This page continues the final Canto of the Paradiso. On the previous page, Dante described seeing the entire universe "bound by love into a single volume," reconciling the concepts of substance and accident. Here, he struggles with the fading of this divine memory and begins to describe the vision of the Trinity.</meta>

# PARADISO

**V**n single moment brings me greater forgetfulness 
Than twenty-five centuries have brought to the enterprise 
That made Neptune wonder at the shadow of the Argo. <note>Dante uses "lethargy" (*lethargo*) to mean oblivion. He claims that a single moment after his vision caused him to forget more than humanity has forgotten of the voyage of the *Argo*—the first ship—which amazed the sea god Neptune 2,500 years ago.</note>
**C**oasely my mind, held in total suspense, 
Gazed fixed, motionless, and intent; 
And grew ever more inflamed by its very gazing. 
**A**t that light one becomes such 
That to turn away from it for any other sight 
Is impossible for the will to ever consent: 
**P**erceiving that the Good, which is the object of the will, 
Is all gathered therein; and outside of it, 
That which is perfect there is elsewhere defective. 
**H**enceforth my speech will be shorter, 
Even for those things I remember, than that of an infant 
Who still bathes his tongue at the breast; 
**N**ot because there was more than a single appearance 
Within the living light that I gazed upon, 
For that light is forever what it was before; 
**M**at because my own sight was gaining strength 
In me as I looked, a single appearance 
Was transformed as I myself was changing. 
**N**ear the profound and clear <term>subsistence</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, "subsistence" refers to something that exists in its own right—the essential reality of God.</note> 
Of the high light, there appeared to me three circles 
Of three colors and one dimension: 
**E**nd one seemed reflected by the other, as a rainbow by a rainbow, <note>original: *iri da iri*. Dante uses the rainbow (Iris) to describe the relationship between God the Father and God the Son.</note> 
And the third seemed like fire 
Breathed forth equally from the one and the other. 
**O** how brief is speech, and how feeble 
Compared to my thought; and that thought, compared to what I saw, 
Is such that "little" is not enough to say.

<summary>Dante describes the overwhelming nature of his divine vision, which transcends human memory and language, before detailing the appearance of the Holy Trinity as three distinct yet unified circles of light.</summary>
<keywords>Paradiso, Neptune, Argo, memory, divine light, Trinity, three circles, Holy Spirit, Father and Son, rainbow analogy</keywords>

--- Page 517 ---
<meta>This page concludes the 1515 Aldine edition of Dante's *Paradiso* and the entire *Divine Comedy*. It contains the final lines of Canto XXXIII, where the poet attempts to understand the mystery of the Incarnation before his intellectual powers are overwhelmed by divine grace, ending with the famous closing line of the poem.</meta>

# PAR.

**O** light eternal, who alone dwell in yourself,
Who alone understand yourself, and who, understood
And understanding, smile upon yourself! <note>Dante here addresses the Trinity: the Father (who dwells), the Son (the understanding), and the Holy Spirit (the love/smile between them).</note>
**T**hat circle which appeared to be conceived
Within you as a reflected light,
When surveyed by my eyes for a while,
**S**eemed to me, within itself and in its own color,
To be painted with our human image: <note>original: *nostra effige*. This is the climax of the vision: Dante sees a human face within the divine light, representing Christ.</note>
Because my sight was entirely fixed upon it.
**A**s is the geometer who applies himself entirely
To measure the circle, and does not find,
Through thinking, that principle which he lacks; <note>This refers to the ancient mathematical problem of "squaring the circle," which was proven impossible in the 19th century but was a symbol of an unsolvable puzzle in Dante's time.</note>
**S**uch was I at that new sight:
I wished to see how the human image fitted the circle,
And how it finds its place there. <note>original: *si s'indoua*. Dante is trying to comprehend how the human and divine natures coexist in one person (the mystery of the Incarnation).</note>
**B**ut my own wings were not meant for this:
Except that my mind was struck
By a flash of light, in which its wish arrived.
**H**ere power failed the high fantasy; <note>Dante admits that his imagination and poetic ability cannot describe the ultimate union with God.</note>
But already my desire and my will were revolved,
Like a wheel that is moved evenly,
By the Love that moves the sun and the other stars.

<meta>This page contains lines 94–123 of the final Canto (XXXIII) of the *Paradiso*. # P A R.

A single moment brings more forgetfulness to me than twenty-five centuries have brought to that enterprise which made **Neptune** <note>The Roman god of the sea.</note> wonder at the shadow of the **Argo**. <note>The *Argo* was the first ship in Greek mythology; Dante suggests that his vision of God was so profound that he forgot more of it in a second than the world has forgotten of the 2,500-year-old story of the first sailors.</note>
Thus my mind, held in total suspense, gazed fixedly, motionless and attentive, and became more inflamed by the very act of gazing.
In that light, a person becomes such that it is impossible to ever consent to turn away from it toward any other sight:
Because the good, which is the object of the will, is all gathered within that light; and outside of it, everything that is perfect there is defective.
From now on, my speech will be briefer, even concerning what I remember, than that of an infant who still bathes his tongue at the breast. <note>Dante compares his linguistic inadequacy to the babbling of a nursing baby.</note>
It was not because there was more than a single appearance within the living light I was watching—for that light is always as it was before;
But as my own sight gained strength while I looked, a single appearance was transformed for me as I myself was changing. <note>Dante explains that God is unchanging; the "movement" or "change" in the vision was actually the poet’s own spiritual perception maturing.</note>
Within the profound and clear **subsistence** <note>original: *sussistenza*. A technical philosophical term meaning something that exists independently and in its own right.</note> of the high light, there appeared to me **three circles** of three colors and one dimension:
And one seemed reflected by the other, as a rainbow is by a rainbow, and the third seemed like fire breathed forth equally from the one and the other. <note>The *tre giri* (three circles) represent the Trinity: the Father, the Son (the reflection), and the Holy Spirit (the fire of love).</note>
Oh, how meager is my speech, and how weak compared to my memory! And even my memory, compared to what I truly saw, is such that calling it "little" is not enough.

<summary>Dante describes the overwhelming nature of the Divine Vision, explaining how his own evolving perception allowed him to see the Trinity as three distinct yet unified circles of light.</summary>
<keywords>Neptune, Argo, Trinity, divine light, ineffability, Canto XXXIII, Paradiso</keywords>

--- Page 519 ---
<meta>This page concludes Canto XXXIII of the *Paradiso* and the entire *Divine Comedy*. It follows the previous page where Dante describes seeing the Trinity as three distinct circles of one dimension. Here, he focuses on the mystery of the Incarnation—how the human form fits within the divine—before his vision ends in a final moment of grace.</meta>

# P A R.

O eternal light; who dwell in yourself alone, <note>original: *sidi*. An archaic form of *siedi* (dwell/sit).</note>
who alone understand yourself, and being understood by yourself
and understanding yourself, you smile upon me; <note>In many editions, this is "smile upon yourself" (*a te arridi*), but this 1515 Aldine edition reads *a me* (upon me), suggesting the light reflects back to the observer.</note>
That circle, which seemed to be conceived
within you as a reflected light,
when surveyed by my eyes for a while,
seemed to me, within itself and in its very own color,
to be painted with our human image: <note>This is the climax of the vision: Dante sees a human face—the Incarnate Christ—within the second circle of the Trinity.</note>
because my sight was completely fixed upon it.
Like the geometer who sets himself entirely <note>A mathematician.</note>
to measure the circle, and does not find,
through thinking, that principle which he lacks; <note>This refers to the "squaring of the circle," a famous mathematical problem that was unsolveable in Dante’s time; it represents the limits of human reason when faced with the divine.</note>
such was I at that new sight:
I wanted to see how the human image fitted the circle,
and how it found its place there. <note>original: *s'indoua*. A word invented by Dante meaning "to find its 'where' (dove)."</note>
But my own wings were not sufficient for this: <note>Dante often uses "wings" as a metaphor for his intellectual or poetic power.</note>
except that my mind was struck
by a flash of light, in which its will was fulfilled.
Here power failed the high imagination;
but already my desire and my will were being turned,
like a wheel that is moved evenly,
by the love that moves the sun and the other stars. <note>The famous final line of the poem, signifying that Dante is now in perfect harmony with God’s cosmic order.</note>
